docs.title: 5.1 — What Middleware Is
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 4.11 Project structure · Next: 5.2 Middleware order

Markers: 🔥 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Middleware is a piece of code that sits in the path of every HTTP request. It receives the request, can act on it, and then decides whether to pass it along to the next piece or stop and answer immediately.

  • The pieces form a pipeline, in the order you register them.
  • Each one can run code before and after the rest of the pipeline, because it calls the next one and waits.
  • That "before and after" shape makes the pipeline nested, not flat — which is why order matters so much.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is in ASP.NET Core What it means Middleware a component in the request path Code that receives a request, optionally acts on it, and chooses whether to call the next component. Pipeline the assembled chain All your middleware, in registration order, nested inside each other. RequestDelegate a delegate type Task RequestDelegate(HttpContext). What every middleware reduces to. next a RequestDelegate parameter The rest of the pipeline. Calling it hands the request onward. HttpContext a class Everything about this request and response. See 5.8. IApplicationBuilder an interface What you call Use... on to add middleware. WebApplication implements it. app.Use(...) a method Adds middleware that can call next. app.Run(...) a method Adds terminal middleware — it never calls next. See 5.3. Short-circuit a behaviour Not calling next, so the pipeline stops and the response is sent from there. Terminal middleware a role The last piece. Produces the response. Usually the endpoint. Endpoint the final destination Your controller action or minimal API handler.

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
Think of an airport. A passenger passes a series of desks: check-in, security, passport control, the gate. Each desk does its job and passes them on. Any desk can stop them — security finds something, and they never reach the gate.

Middleware works the same way. Each component:

  1. Sees the request
  2. Can do work before passing it on
  3. Calls the next component — or refuses to
  4. Can do work after the rest of the pipeline has finished

That fourth step is the part people miss, and it is what makes middleware powerful.

docs.title: Why "nested", not "a list"
docs.text:
Here is the shape of every middleware:

async Task Middleware(HttpContext context, RequestDelegate next)
{
    // ── BEFORE: on the way in ──

    await next(context);          // run EVERYTHING below this point

    // ── AFTER: on the way back out ──
}

await next(context) does not mean "hand over and finish". It means "run the entire rest of the pipeline and wait for it". When it returns, something further down has already produced the response, and you get a chance to look at it.

So three middleware are not three steps in a row. They are three boxes inside each other:

flowchart TD
    A1["A: before"] --> B1["B: before"]
    B1 --> C1["Endpoint: produce response"]
    C1 --> B2["B: after"]
    B2 --> A2["A: after"]

Run order: A-before, B-before, endpoint, B-after, A-after.

The first middleware registered is the outermost — first to see the request and last to see the response.

docs.title: Proving it to yourself
docs.text:
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("A: before");
    await next();
    Console.WriteLine("A: after");
});

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("B: before");
    await next();
    Console.WriteLine("B: after");
});

app.Run(async context =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("C: the endpoint");
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("Hello");
});

Output for one request:

A: before
B: before
C: the endpoint
B: after          ← unwinding
A: after          ← unwinding

Note the symmetry. It behaves exactly like nested try/finally blocks, which is why one middleware near the top can catch exceptions thrown anywhere below it. That is how global exception handling works — see 5.11.

docs.title: The simple version — what it replaced
docs.text:
In classic ASP.NET the equivalent was HTTP modules and handlers, registered in web.config:

<httpModules>
  <add name="MyModule" type="MyApp.MyModule" />
</httpModules>

Three problems. The order came from config files including machine-level ones. You could not see the pipeline by reading code. And modules hooked into a fixed set of lifecycle events rather than simply wrapping the next thing.

Middleware fixed all three. The pipeline is C# code, in one file, in explicit order:

app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseStaticFiles();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

Read it top to bottom and you know exactly what happens to a request.

docs.title: How it actually works — everything is a RequestDelegate
docs.text:
Underneath, middleware is one delegate type:

public delegate Task RequestDelegate(HttpContext context);

"Take a context, do something, return a task." That is the whole contract.

The pipeline is built by composing these, from the last registered backwards to the first:

// Conceptually, what Build() does:
RequestDelegate pipeline = endpointDelegate;              // innermost

pipeline = ctx => middleware2(ctx, pipeline);             // wrap it
pipeline = ctx => middleware1(ctx, pipeline);             // wrap again

// Serving a request is now just:
await pipeline(httpContext);

Each layer closes over the next one. That is why next is available inside your middleware — it is a captured reference to the already-composed remainder (1.13).

docs.title: The deeper detail — what middleware is good for
docs.text:
Middleware handles concerns that apply to every request, regardless of endpoint:

Concern Examples Cross-cutting Logging, correlation IDs, timing Security Authentication, HTTPS redirection, security headers Protocol CORS, compression, static files Reliability Global exception handling, rate limiting

What it is not good for: anything needing to know which action was selected. Middleware runs before model binding and before the action is invoked, so it has no idea about your method's parameters or return type.

That is what filters are for — see 5.13.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The three ways to write middleware, in increasing formality:

// 1. Inline — fine for something tiny
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-Request-Id"] = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
    await next();
});

// 2. A conventional class — the usual choice. See 5.5.
public class TimingMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, ILogger<TimingMiddleware> logger)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();

        await next(context);              // run everything below

        // Runs on the way back out, so the status code is known by now
        logger.LogInformation("{Method} {Path} → {Status} in {Ms}ms",
            context.Request.Method,
            context.Request.Path,
            context.Response.StatusCode,
            sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
}

app.UseMiddleware<TimingMiddleware>();

// 3. An extension method, so Program.cs reads consistently
public static class TimingMiddlewareExtensions
{
    public static IApplicationBuilder UseTiming(this IApplicationBuilder app)
        => app.UseMiddleware<TimingMiddleware>();
}

app.UseTiming();

The third form is how every built-in middleware is exposed, and worth copying so your own reads the same as UseAuthentication().

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?

It is a component sitting in the path of every HTTP request. Each piece receives the HttpContext, can act on it, and decides whether to call the next component. Because it calls the next one and awaits it, control comes back afterwards — so a single middleware can run code before the rest of the pipeline and again after the response has been produced. The pipeline is assembled in Program.cs in explicit order, which replaced the HTTP modules and handlers of classic ASP.NET, where ordering came from config files and was effectively invisible.

Q: Explain the shape of the pipeline.

It is nested rather than flat. Each middleware wraps the rest, so registering A then B then the endpoint produces A-before, B-before, endpoint, B-after, A-after. The first registered is the outermost — first to see the request and last to see the response. Structurally it behaves like nested try/finally blocks, which is exactly why one middleware at the top can catch exceptions thrown anywhere below it, and how global exception handling is implemented.

Q: What does await next() actually do?

It runs the entire remaining pipeline and waits for completion. It is not "hand off and return" — when that await finishes, something downstream has already produced a response and your code gets a chance to inspect or add to it. That is why timing middleware works: capture the time, call next, and by the time control returns you know the duration and the status code.

Q: What is middleware not suitable for?

Anything requiring knowledge of which endpoint or action was selected, or its parameters. Middleware runs before model binding and before the action executes, so it sees a raw request rather than a bound model. Validating a specific action's arguments, or caching based on an action's return value, belongs in filters, which run inside MVC with the action context available.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Order is registration order, and it matters enormously. See 5.2.
  • Forgetting to call next() silently ends the pipeline — the request never reaches your endpoint and the caller gets an empty 200.
  • Writing to the response after await next() usually throws, because the response has already started. See 5.8.
  • Conventional middleware is a singleton. Injecting a scoped service into its constructor is a captive dependency — see 5.6.
  • Middleware cannot see the selected action. Use a filter.
  • Exceptions propagate up the nesting, so only middleware registered above the throwing code can catch them.

docs.title: 5.2 — Middleware Order
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.1 What middleware is · Next: 5.3 Use, Run, Map

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Middleware runs in the order you register it, and getting that order wrong causes bugs that produce no error message — just silently wrong behaviour.

  • Authentication must come before Authorization, or User is empty when the decision is made.
  • Exception handling goes first, so it wraps everything below it.
  • Static files go early, before authentication, so image requests do not pay for auth they do not need.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Registration order the order of your app.Use... calls Determines pipeline position. The only thing that decides order. Upstream / downstream relative positions Upstream = registered earlier = outer. Downstream = later = inner. UseExceptionHandler a middleware method Catches exceptions from everything below it. Must be near the top. UseHsts a middleware method Sends the Strict-Transport-Security header. Production only. UseHttpsRedirection a middleware method Redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS. UseStaticFiles a middleware method Serves wwwroot. Short-circuits on a match. UseRouting a middleware method Works out which endpoint matches this request. Does not run it. UseCors a middleware method Applies cross-origin policy. Must sit between routing and auth. UseAuthentication a middleware method Works out who you are and populates context.User. UseAuthorization a middleware method Decides whether you may proceed. Needs User already populated. MapControllers a method Adds the endpoint execution step at the end. Auto-inserted middleware a WebApplication behaviour Routing and endpoints are added automatically if you do not add them yourself.

docs.title: Why order is not a detail
docs.text:
Middleware is nested (5.1). Each one wraps everything registered after it. So the order decides:

  • Who sees the request first
  • Who can stop it
  • Who can catch exceptions from whom
  • What information is available when a decision is made

That last one causes the classic bug. Consider:

app.UseAuthorization();      // "is this user allowed?"
app.UseAuthentication();     // "who is this user?"

Authorization runs first, and asks whether the user is allowed. But authentication has not run yet, so context.User is an empty, unauthenticated principal. Every [Authorize] endpoint returns 401 regardless of how valid the token was.

And there is no error. No exception, no warning, no log entry saying "you have these the wrong way round". Just an API that rejects everyone.

A picture: airport security placed after the departure gate. Every step still happens, in a technically valid order — it just achieves nothing useful.

docs.title: The canonical order 🎯
docs.text:
This is worth memorising. It is the order Microsoft documents and the order almost every real application uses:

var app = builder.Build();

// 1. Exception handling — FIRST, so it wraps everything below
if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
else
{
    app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");
    app.UseHsts();
}

// 2. Forwarded headers — before anything reads IP or scheme
app.UseForwardedHeaders();

// 3. HTTPS redirect
app.UseHttpsRedirection();

// 4. Static files — early, so assets skip everything below
app.UseStaticFiles();

// 5. Routing — decide WHICH endpoint matches
app.UseRouting();

// 6. CORS — after routing, before auth
app.UseCors();

// 7. Who are you?
app.UseAuthentication();

// 8. Are you allowed?
app.UseAuthorization();

// 9. Anything needing an authenticated user
app.UseSession();
app.UseResponseCaching();

// 10. Endpoints — run the selected action
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

docs.title: The rules behind the order
docs.text:
You do not need to memorise the list if you understand the four rules that produce it.

Rule 1 — Exception handling wraps what it protects. It can only catch exceptions from middleware registered below it. Put it at the bottom and it protects nothing.

Rule 2 — Authentication before Authorization. UseAuthorization reads context.User. UseAuthentication is what populates it. Reverse them and the decision is made with no information.

Rule 3 — Cheap short-circuits go early. UseStaticFiles returns immediately on a match (5.7). Placed after authentication, every image on your page runs JWT validation and a claims lookup first. Forty assets means forty wasted authentication cycles per page load.

Rule 4 — Anything reading request metadata goes before whoever reads it. UseForwardedHeaders rewrites the client IP and scheme, so it must precede rate limiting, logging and HTTPS redirection — otherwise those see the proxy's values (4.2).

docs.title: How it actually works — routing sits in the middle
docs.text:
UseRouting and the endpoint execution step are separate, and authentication and authorization sit between them.

flowchart TD
    A["UseRouting<br/>which endpoint matches?"] --> B["UseAuthentication<br/>who are you?"]
    B --> C["UseAuthorization<br/>may you reach THAT endpoint?"]
    C --> D["Endpoint<br/>run the action"]

The reason: authorization needs to know which endpoint was selected before it can check the policy on it. Routing selects but does not execute; that gap is where the security decisions happen with full information available.

In minimal hosting, WebApplication inserts UseRouting and the endpoint step automatically, so you rarely write them. But if you call UseRouting() explicitly, it is placed where you put it — which is how you get middleware to run before or after route matching deliberately.

See 8.2.

docs.title: The deeper detail — the bugs each mistake causes
docs.text:
Wrong order Symptom UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication Every authenticated endpoint returns 401, tokens are ignored UseExceptionHandler last Unhandled exceptions produce a raw 500 with a stack trace leaked to the client UseStaticFiles after UseAuthentication Assets work but every one runs full auth — slow, and 401s if auth is required UseCors after UseAuthentication Preflight OPTIONS requests get rejected before CORS can answer them UseForwardedHeaders late Rate limiting and logs record the proxy's IP for every request UseRouting after UseAuthorization Throws at startup — authorization has no endpoint to check UseHttpsRedirection behind a TLS proxy Infinite redirect loop

The CORS one is subtle and worth knowing. A browser preflight is an OPTIONS request with no credentials. If authentication runs first, it rejects the request with 401 before CORS middleware can reply with the allow headers — so the browser blocks the real request and you see a CORS error that is actually an ordering bug. See 10.10.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The failure mode, side by side:

// ✗ BROKEN — no error, just an API that rejects everyone
app.UseAuthorization();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.MapControllers();

// ✓ CORRECT
app.UseAuthentication();     // populate context.User
app.UseAuthorization();      // now decide, with information
app.MapControllers();

And a realistic production pipeline with the reasoning inline:

var app = builder.Build();

// Outermost — catches everything below, including its own downstream middleware
app.UseExceptionHandler();

// Must precede anything reading IP or scheme
app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
{
    ForwardedHeaders = ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto
});

if (!app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    app.UseHsts();

// Assets short-circuit here and skip everything below
app.UseStaticFiles();

app.UseRouting();

app.UseCors("Default");          // before auth, so preflight is answered
app.UseRateLimiter();            // after forwarded headers, so it sees real IPs

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");

app.Run();

Notice UseRateLimiter sits after UseForwardedHeaders and after UseRouting. After forwarded headers so it rate-limits real clients rather than the proxy; after routing so per-endpoint limits know which endpoint they apply to.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why does middleware order matter?

Because the pipeline is nested — each middleware wraps everything registered after it. So the order decides who sees the request first, who can stop it, who can catch exceptions from whom, and crucially what information is available when a decision is made. The classic example is authorization before authentication: authorization reads context.User, but authentication is what populates it, so reversing them means every authenticated endpoint returns 401 with no error message explaining why.

Q: What is the canonical order and why?

Exception handling first so it wraps everything, then forwarded headers before anything reads the client IP or scheme, then HTTPS redirection, then static files, then routing, then CORS, then authentication, then authorization, then endpoints. You can derive it from four rules rather than memorising: exception handling only catches what is below it; authorization needs the user that authentication populates; cheap short-circuits like static files go early so they skip work; and anything rewriting request metadata must precede whoever reads it.

Q: Why do authentication and authorization sit between routing and the endpoint?

Because authorization needs to know which endpoint was selected before it can evaluate the policy attached to it. UseRouting performs the match but does not execute anything, and the endpoint step at the end runs it. That gap is deliberately where the security decisions happen, with the routing result available. In minimal hosting WebApplication inserts both automatically, so you normally just write authentication and authorization in the right order.

Q: You get a CORS error in the browser but your CORS policy looks correct. What might be wrong?

Very likely UseCors is registered after UseAuthentication. A browser preflight is an OPTIONS request sent without credentials, so if authentication runs first it rejects that preflight with 401 before CORS middleware ever gets to answer with the allow headers. The browser then blocks the real request and reports it as a CORS failure, when the actual cause is middleware ordering. Moving UseCors above the auth middleware fixes it.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication produces 401 on everything, with no error.
  • UseExceptionHandler registered late leaves everything above it unprotected and can leak stack traces.
  • UseCors after authentication breaks preflight requests and looks like a CORS misconfiguration.
  • UseStaticFiles after authentication runs full auth for every image, script and stylesheet.
  • UseForwardedHeaders late means logs and rate limiting see the proxy IP.
  • UseRouting after UseAuthorization throws at startup.
  • Service registration order does not matter. Only pipeline order does — people confuse the two halves of Program.cs.
  • Middleware added inside Map branches has its own order, independent of the main pipeline (5.3).

docs.title: 5.3 — Use vs Run vs Map vs MapWhen vs UseWhen
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.2 Middleware order · Next: 5.4 Inline middleware

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Five methods for adding middleware, and they differ in whether the pipeline continues and whether it rejoins.

  • Use — can call next. The normal one.
  • Run — terminal. Never calls next. The pipeline ends here.
  • Map / MapWhen — branch off permanently. The branch never rejoins the main pipeline.
  • UseWhen — branch conditionally, and rejoin the main pipeline afterwards.

The Map versus UseWhen distinction is the one that gets asked about.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Use an extension method Adds middleware that receives next and may call it. The default. Run an extension method Adds terminal middleware. Receives no next, so nothing after it runs. Map an extension method Branches on a URL path prefix. The branch does not rejoin. MapWhen an extension method Branches on any predicate over HttpContext. Does not rejoin. UseWhen an extension method Runs extra middleware when a predicate matches, then rejoins the main pipeline. Branch a separate sub-pipeline Its own chain of middleware, with its own order. Rejoin a behaviour Whether control returns to the main pipeline after the branch. PathString a struct Typed URL path. Map matches against it and strips the prefix. PathBase a property on the request Where Map moves the matched prefix to. Terminal a role Middleware that produces the response and does not delegate onward.

docs.title: The one distinction that matters
docs.text:
All five add middleware. They differ on two questions:

  1. Does it call next? — Use can, Run cannot.
  2. Does the branch rejoin? — UseWhen rejoins, Map and MapWhen do not.

A picture: a road with a fork.

  • Use is a checkpoint on the road. Everyone passes through and continues.
  • Run is the destination. The road ends.
  • Map is a permanent turn-off. Once you take it, you are on a different road and never come back.
  • UseWhen is a detour — a loop that rejoins the main road further along.

That difference decides whether the rest of your pipeline — authentication, authorization, your endpoints — still runs.

docs.title: Use — the normal one
docs.text:
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    // before
    await next();          // continue down the pipeline
    // after
});

Skipping next() short-circuits the pipeline, which is sometimes exactly what you want — see 5.7.

⚠️ There are two overloads and one is a performance trap:

// Older: next is a Func<Task>. Allocates a closure per request.
app.Use(async (context, next) => { await next(); });

// Newer (.NET 7+): next is a RequestDelegate. No per-request allocation.
app.Use(async (HttpContext context, RequestDelegate next) => { await next(context); });

The second form is preferred in hot paths. Note it takes next(context) rather than next().

docs.title: Run — terminal
docs.text:
app.Run(async context =>
{
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("This is the end of the line");
});

No next parameter at all — the signature makes it impossible to continue. Anything registered after it never runs.

⚠️ app.Run(handler) and app.Run() are completely different things. The one with no arguments starts the web server and blocks (4.3). The overload taking a delegate adds terminal middleware. Same name, unrelated jobs, and it confuses people constantly.

docs.title: Map — branch on a path prefix
docs.text:
app.Map("/admin", adminApp =>
{
    adminApp.Use(async (context, next) =>
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Only admin requests reach here");
        await next();
    });

    adminApp.Run(async context =>
        await context.Response.WriteAsync("Admin area"));
});

// Main pipeline continues for everything that is NOT /admin
app.UseAuthentication();
app.MapControllers();

Two things happen that surprise people:

The branch does not rejoin. A request to /admin/users enters the branch and never comes back — so UseAuthentication and MapControllers below do not run for it. If the branch does not produce a response, the request ends with a 404.

The matched prefix is stripped. Inside the branch, /admin/users has Request.Path == "/users" and Request.PathBase == "/admin". That is deliberate — it lets you mount a self-contained sub-application at a path — but it breaks link generation if you are not expecting it.

docs.title: MapWhen — branch on any condition
docs.text:
app.MapWhen(
    context => context.Request.Query.ContainsKey("debug"),
    debugApp =>
    {
        debugApp.Run(async context =>
            await context.Response.WriteAsync("Debug mode"));
    });

Same non-rejoining behaviour as Map, but the predicate can inspect anything on the context — headers, query string, method, host. The path is not stripped.

docs.title: UseWhen — branch and rejoin ⭐
docs.text:
This is the one people reach for when they mistakenly use Map:

app.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/api"),
    apiApp =>
    {
        apiApp.UseMiddleware<ApiKeyValidationMiddleware>();
    });

// This DOES run for /api requests — the branch rejoined
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

An /api request runs the API-key middleware and then continues through authentication, authorization and on to its endpoint.

That is almost always what you actually want: "run this extra middleware for some requests" rather than "send some requests somewhere else entirely".

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
Method Condition Calls next? Rejoins? Strips path? Use always optional n/a no Run always never n/a no Map path prefix branch decides no yes MapWhen any predicate branch decides no no UseWhen any predicate branch decides yes no 
flowchart TD
    R["Request"] --> U["Use / UseWhen<br/>continues"]
    U --> M{"Map / MapWhen<br/>matched?"}
    M -->|"yes"| B["Branch pipeline<br/>DEAD END — never returns"]
    M -->|"no"| C["Rest of main pipeline"]
    C --> E["Endpoint"]

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The mistake and the fix. Requiring an API key on /api routes only:

// ✗ WRONG — Map does not rejoin.
// /api requests never reach authentication or the controllers below.
app.Map("/api", apiApp =>
{
    apiApp.UseMiddleware<ApiKeyMiddleware>();
});

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();      // /api requests NEVER GET HERE → 404

The symptom is baffling: your API returns 404 for every route, while the routes clearly exist and non-API routes work fine.

// ✓ CORRECT — UseWhen rejoins
app.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/api"),
    apiApp => apiApp.UseMiddleware<ApiKeyMiddleware>());

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();      // /api requests DO get here

docs.title: A legitimate use of Map
docs.text:
Map is right when the branch really is a separate application that produces its own response:

// A completely self-contained health/metrics endpoint
app.Map("/internal", internalApp =>
{
    internalApp.UseMiddleware<InternalNetworkOnlyMiddleware>();

    internalApp.Run(async context =>
    {
        context.Response.ContentType = "application/json";
        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new
        {
            status  = "ok",
            version = typeof(Program).Assembly.GetName().Version?.ToString(),
            uptime  = Environment.TickCount64 / 1000
        });
    });
});

Here not rejoining is correct — these requests should never touch your application's authentication or controllers.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between Use and Run?

Use adds middleware that receives a next delegate and can choose to call it, continuing down the pipeline. Run adds terminal middleware — its signature has no next at all, so nothing registered after it can execute. You use Run for the final component that produces a response. Worth noting that app.Run(handler) with a delegate is entirely different from app.Run() with no arguments, which starts the server and blocks; the shared name confuses people regularly.

Q: What is the difference between Map and UseWhen?

Both create a branch, but Map is a dead end and UseWhen rejoins. With Map, once a request matches the path prefix it enters the branch and never returns to the main pipeline — so anything registered afterwards, including authentication and your endpoint mapping, does not run for it. UseWhen runs the extra middleware when its predicate matches and then continues down the main pipeline. In practice UseWhen is what people usually want, because the intent is normally "apply this extra middleware to some requests" rather than "route these requests to a different application".

Q: You add app.Map("/api", ...) with some middleware and now every API route returns 404. Why?

Because Map branches permanently. Requests to /api enter that branch and never rejoin the main pipeline, so MapControllers further down never runs for them — nothing matches, and the result is a 404. The routes exist and non-API routes work fine, which makes it confusing. The fix is UseWhen, which applies the middleware and then lets the request carry on to routing and endpoints as normal.

Q: What does Map do to the request path?

It strips the matched prefix. Inside a Map("/admin", ...) branch, a request to /admin/users has Request.Path of /users and Request.PathBase of /admin. That is deliberate — it lets you mount a self-contained sub-application at a path without it needing to know where it is mounted — but it surprises people, and it affects link generation if code inside the branch builds URLs from Request.Path.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Map and MapWhen never rejoin. Everything registered after them is skipped for matched requests.
  • Map strips the matched prefix from Request.Path and moves it to PathBase.
  • app.Run(handler) versus app.Run() are unrelated despite the shared name.
  • Forgetting next() in a Use silently ends the pipeline with an empty 200.
  • The older Use overload allocates a closure per request. Prefer the RequestDelegate form in hot paths.
  • A Map branch that produces no response returns 404, because the request cannot continue.
  • Branches have their own middleware order, independent of the main pipeline.
  • Map matches whole segments only. Map("/api") matches /api/users but not /apixyz.

docs.title: 5.4 — Inline Custom Middleware
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.3 Use, Run, Map · Next: 5.5 Conventional middleware

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Inline middleware is middleware written as a lambda directly in Program.cs, rather than as its own class.

  • Written with app.Use(async (context, next) => { ... }).
  • Good for something small, obvious and unlikely to grow — adding a header, a quick check.
  • Once it needs dependencies, unit tests, or more than a few lines, move it to a class (5.5).

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Inline middleware a lambda in Program.cs Middleware defined at the point of registration rather than in its own type. app.Use(...) an extension method Takes a lambda receiving HttpContext and next. context an HttpContext This request and response. See 5.8. next a delegate The rest of the pipeline. Two overloads exist — Func<Task> and RequestDelegate. RequestDelegate overload the newer form (.NET 7+) next takes the context. Avoids a per-request closure allocation. Func<Task> overload the older form next() takes nothing. Allocates a closure per request. context.RequestServices a property The DI container for this request. How inline middleware gets scoped services. OnStarting a method on the response Registers a callback that runs just before the response is sent.

docs.title: Why inline exists
docs.text:
Not every piece of middleware deserves a file. Adding one response header is three lines, and a class with a constructor, an InvokeAsync method and an extension method is more ceremony than the logic warrants.

Inline middleware lets you write it where it is registered:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-App-Version"] = "1.4.2";
    await next();
});

That is complete and readable, and it sits exactly where someone reading Program.cs will look for it.

A picture: a sticky note versus a filing cabinet. A sticky note is perfect for one short reminder. It is the wrong home for a contract.

docs.title: The line to draw
docs.text:
Move to a class when any of these becomes true:

  • It needs an injected dependency other than through RequestServices
  • It is more than roughly ten lines
  • You want to unit test it
  • The same logic is needed in more than one place
  • Program.cs is getting hard to scan

The last one matters more than people expect. Program.cs is the file where the whole application's shape is visible (4.3). Two hundred lines of inline lambdas destroys that.

docs.title: The simple version
docs.text:
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    // ── before: on the way in ──
    var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

    await next();          // run the rest of the pipeline

    // ── after: on the way back out ──
    var ms = Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start).TotalMilliseconds;
    Console.WriteLine($"{context.Request.Path} took {ms:F1}ms");
});

The structure is always the same: work, await next(), more work. Either half can be empty.

docs.title: The two overloads
docs.text:
// Older — next is Func<Task>, called with no arguments
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    await next();
});

// Newer (.NET 7+) — next is RequestDelegate, called with the context
app.Use(async (HttpContext context, RequestDelegate next) =>
{
    await next(context);
});

The newer form avoids allocating a closure object on every request. In middleware that runs for every single request, that allocation is real GC pressure (3.4) — worth using in anything hot, and irrelevant in something that runs occasionally.

Note the explicit type annotations. Without them the compiler picks the older overload.

docs.title: ⚠️ Getting services into inline middleware
docs.text:
Inline middleware has no constructor, so there is nothing to inject into. You resolve from the request's own container:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    // RequestServices is the scoped container FOR THIS REQUEST
    var logger = context.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<ILogger<Program>>();
    var db     = context.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

    logger.LogInformation("Handling {Path}", context.Request.Path);
    await next();
});

context.RequestServices is safe for scoped services, because it is the request scope. That is different from capturing a service in a closure, which would pin one instance for the life of the application — the captive dependency problem (6.4):

// ✗ WRONG — resolved once at startup, shared by every request forever
var db = app.Services.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    db.Orders.Add(...);        // one DbContext for the whole app. Not thread-safe.
    await next();
});

Resolving from RequestServices inside the lambda is the fix, and it is the one thing about inline middleware worth being careful with.

docs.title: The deeper detail — modifying the response
docs.text:
Writing to the response after await next() usually fails:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    await next();

    context.Response.Headers["X-Duration"] = "42ms";
    // ✗ InvalidOperationException: "Headers are read-only, response has already started."
});

Once any bytes have been written, headers are on the wire and cannot change. The fix is OnStarting, which registers a callback that runs just before the first byte is sent:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

    context.Response.OnStarting(() =>
    {
        var ms = Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start).TotalMilliseconds;
        context.Response.Headers["X-Duration"] = $"{ms:F0}ms";
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    });

    await next();
});

Register the callback before calling next(), so it is in place before anything downstream starts writing. See 5.8.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Genuinely good uses of inline middleware — each small, obvious, and unlikely to grow:

// 1. A correlation ID for tracing across services
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var correlationId = context.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault()
                        ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString();

    context.Items["CorrelationId"] = correlationId;          // available downstream
    context.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"] = correlationId;

    await next();
});

// 2. Security headers
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var headers = context.Response.Headers;
    headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff";
    headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "DENY";
    headers["Referrer-Policy"] = "no-referrer";

    await next();
});

// 3. Blocking a path outright — short-circuits, so next() is never called
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/.git"))
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound;
        return;                       // deliberately no next()
    }

    await next();
});

And one that should not be inline:

// ✗ Too much for a lambda — needs a class
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var apiKey = context.Request.Headers["X-Api-Key"].FirstOrDefault();
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(apiKey)) { /* ... */ }

    var repo = context.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<IApiKeyRepository>();
    var key = await repo.FindAsync(apiKey);
    if (key is null || key.IsRevoked || key.ExpiresAt < DateTimeOffset.UtcNow) { /* ... */ }

    // ...and twenty more lines of rate limiting and audit logging
});

That has dependencies, branching, and logic worth testing. It belongs in a class — 5.5.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you write middleware inline rather than as a class?

When it is small, self-contained and unlikely to grow — adding a response header, setting a correlation ID, blocking a path. The benefit is that the logic sits in Program.cs where someone reading the pipeline will find it, without the ceremony of a class, a constructor and a registration extension method. I would move it to a class as soon as it needs dependencies beyond a quick RequestServices lookup, exceeds around ten lines, or is worth unit testing — and also to protect Program.cs, since its value is that the whole application's shape is visible at a glance.

Q: How does inline middleware get access to services?

Through context.RequestServices, which is the dependency injection scope for that specific request. That is important because it means scoped services like DbContext are resolved correctly, one per request. The mistake to avoid is resolving from app.Services outside the lambda and capturing the result in a closure — that gives you a single instance shared across every request for the life of the application, which for a DbContext is both a memory leak and a thread-safety bug.

Q: Why can't you set a response header after await next()?

Because by then the response has usually already started — headers are sent before the body, so once any bytes have been written they are on the wire and immutable. Attempting it throws an InvalidOperationException saying the headers are read-only. The fix is context.Response.OnStarting, which registers a callback that runs immediately before the first byte is sent, so you can still set headers based on work done during the request. The callback has to be registered before calling next, so it is in place before anything downstream writes.

Q: What is the difference between the two Use overloads?

The older one gives you next as a Func<Task> called with no arguments; the newer one, from .NET 7, gives you a RequestDelegate that you call with the context. The newer form avoids allocating a closure on every request, which matters in middleware that runs for every single request in a high-throughput service. You have to annotate the lambda parameter types explicitly, otherwise the compiler resolves to the older overload.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Capturing a service resolved from app.Services pins one instance for the whole app. Use context.RequestServices inside the lambda.
  • Forgetting await next() ends the pipeline silently with an empty 200.
  • Setting headers after await next() throws. Use OnStarting, registered before next.
  • Program.cs filling with lambdas destroys the readability that makes it useful.
  • Inline middleware cannot be unit tested without spinning up the app.
  • The older Use overload allocates per request. Annotate types to get the newer one.
  • return without writing a response produces an empty 200, not a 404.

docs.title: 5.5 — Conventional Middleware Classes
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.4 Inline middleware · Next: 5.6 IMiddleware factory

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Conventional middleware is middleware written as a class with a constructor taking RequestDelegate next, and a method called InvokeAsync.

  • It implements no interface. The framework finds InvokeAsync by name, using reflection.
  • The class is created once, at startup — it is effectively a singleton.
  • Scoped services go in the InvokeAsync parameters, not the constructor. That is the one rule that matters.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Conventional middleware a class shape A class with a RequestDelegate constructor parameter and an InvokeAsync method. InvokeAsync a method, found by name Where the work happens. Must return Task and take HttpContext first. Invoke the older name Also accepted. InvokeAsync is preferred; defining both throws. RequestDelegate next a constructor parameter The rest of the pipeline, captured once at startup. UseMiddleware<T>() an extension method Registers the class into the pipeline. Convention-based a discovery style Found by name, not by an interface. Misspelling compiles and silently fails. Singleton lifetime what middleware gets One instance for the whole application, shared by every concurrent request. Method injection the fix for scoped services Extra InvokeAsync parameters are resolved per request from the request scope. Registration extension a static method UseSomething(this IApplicationBuilder). Makes your middleware read like the built-in ones.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
public class RequestTimingMiddleware
{
    private readonly RequestDelegate _next;
    private readonly ILogger<RequestTimingMiddleware> _logger;

    // Constructor — runs ONCE, at startup
    public RequestTimingMiddleware(
        RequestDelegate next,
        ILogger<RequestTimingMiddleware> logger)
    {
        _next = next;
        _logger = logger;
    }

    // InvokeAsync — runs on EVERY request
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

        await _next(context);

        var ms = Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start).TotalMilliseconds;
        _logger.LogInformation("{Path} → {Status} in {Ms:F0}ms",
            context.Request.Path, context.Response.StatusCode, ms);
    }
}

Registered with:

app.UseMiddleware<RequestTimingMiddleware>();

With C# 12 primary constructors it is shorter:

public class RequestTimingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<RequestTimingMiddleware> logger)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();
        await next(context);
        logger.LogInformation("{Path} took {Ms:F0}ms",
            context.Request.Path, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start).TotalMilliseconds);
    }
}

docs.title: ⚠️ It implements no interface
docs.text:
This is the first thing to know, and it mirrors the Startup.cs convention (4.4).

There is no IMiddleware to implement here. The framework looks for a method named InvokeAsync (or Invoke) using reflection.

public class MyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    // Typo — compiles fine, never runs
    public async Task InvokAsync(HttpContext context)   // missing 'e'
    {
        await next(context);
    }
}

app.UseMiddleware<MyMiddleware>() throws at startup with "No public 'InvokeAsync' or 'Invoke' method found" — which is at least loud, unlike the Startup.cs equivalent that fails silently.

Rules for the method:

  • Named InvokeAsync or Invoke — not both, or it throws
  • Returns Task
  • First parameter must be HttpContext
  • Further parameters are resolved from DI per request

docs.title: The simple version — created once
docs.text:
The class is instantiated a single time, when the pipeline is built. Not per request.

That means:

  • The constructor runs once, at startup
  • The instance is shared by every concurrent request
  • Any field you set is shared across all of them
public class CountingMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    private int _count;                       // ⚠️ shared by ALL requests

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        _count++;                             // ⚠️ RACE CONDITION
        await next(context);
    }
}

That _count++ is three operations and two threads can interleave (2.18). Use Interlocked.Increment, or better, do not keep mutable state in middleware at all.

docs.title: How it actually works — the scoped service problem ⚠️
docs.text:
This is the most important thing in the note.

Because the class is a singleton, injecting a scoped service into the constructor captures it forever:

// ✗ BROKEN
public class AuditMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, AppDbContext db)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        db.AuditLog.Add(new AuditEntry(context.Request.Path));
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        await next(context);
    }
}

The middleware is built once, so db is resolved once and held for the application's lifetime. That DbContext is now shared by every concurrent request — it is not thread-safe, and its change tracker grows without limit. This is the captive dependency problem (6.4).

In Development you usually get a startup exception, because scope validation is on. In production it is off by default, so the app starts and misbehaves under load — which is exactly why this bug reaches production.

The fix: put scoped services in the InvokeAsync signature.

// ✓ CORRECT
public class AuditMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, AppDbContext db)
    {
        //                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
        // Resolved fresh from THIS REQUEST's scope, every time
        db.AuditLog.Add(new AuditEntry(context.Request.Path));
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        await next(context);
    }
}

Extra parameters on InvokeAsync are resolved per request from context.RequestServices, so each request gets its own instance.

The rule to remember: singletons in the constructor, scoped in InvokeAsync.

Loggers, IOptions<T>, IHttpClientFactory and configuration are all singletons — constructor is correct for those.

docs.title: The deeper detail — the extension method
docs.text:
Every built-in middleware is exposed through an extension method, and yours should be too:

public static class RequestTimingMiddlewareExtensions
{
    public static IApplicationBuilder UseRequestTiming(this IApplicationBuilder app)
        => app.UseMiddleware<RequestTimingMiddleware>();
}

// Program.cs now reads consistently
app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseRequestTiming();          // ← indistinguishable from built-in
app.UseAuthentication();

Two benefits beyond style: the middleware class can be internal, keeping it out of your public API surface, and you can validate configuration or add related services inside the extension method.

docs.title: Passing options
docs.text:
UseMiddleware<T> forwards extra arguments to the constructor:

public class RateLimitMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, int maxPerMinute)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context) { /* ... */ }
}

app.UseMiddleware<RateLimitMiddleware>(100);

But prefer IOptions<T> for anything non-trivial, because it participates in configuration binding and validation (7.6):

public class RateLimitMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    IOptions<RateLimitOptions> options)
{
    private readonly RateLimitOptions _options = options.Value;
}

⚠️ Note IOptions<T> is a singleton and safe in the constructor. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped and must go in InvokeAsync instead — a subtle version of the same trap.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A complete, realistic middleware with its extension method:

internal class CorrelationIdMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<CorrelationIdMiddleware> logger)      // singleton — constructor is fine
{
    private const string HeaderName = "X-Correlation-Id";

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var correlationId = context.Request.Headers[HeaderName].FirstOrDefault()
                            ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N");

        context.Items[HeaderName] = correlationId;

        // Set the header before anything downstream writes the response
        context.Response.OnStarting(() =>
        {
            context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = correlationId;
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        });

        // Put it in the log scope so EVERY log line for this request carries it
        using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
        {
            ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId
        }))
        {
            await next(context);
        }
    }
}

public static class CorrelationIdMiddlewareExtensions
{
    public static IApplicationBuilder UseCorrelationId(this IApplicationBuilder app)
        => app.UseMiddleware<CorrelationIdMiddleware>();
}

app.UseCorrelationId();      // register it early, so everything below is in scope

Three deliberate choices worth explaining:

  • OnStarting rather than setting the header after next, because by then the response has started and headers are read-only (5.8).
  • BeginScope wrapping next, so every log entry produced anywhere downstream carries the correlation ID automatically (18.4).
  • internal, because the extension method is the public surface.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
Unlike inline middleware, this is straightforwardly unit testable:

[Fact]
public async Task Adds_correlation_id_when_none_supplied()
{
    var context = new DefaultHttpContext();
    var nextCalled = false;

    var middleware = new CorrelationIdMiddleware(
        next: _ => { nextCalled = true; return Task.CompletedTask; },
        logger: NullLogger<CorrelationIdMiddleware>.Instance);

    await middleware.InvokeAsync(context);

    Assert.True(nextCalled);
    Assert.True(context.Items.ContainsKey("X-Correlation-Id"));
}

DefaultHttpContext is a real, usable HttpContext for tests, and next is just a delegate you supply — so there is no framework to stand up. That testability is the main reason to prefer a class over inline.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you write custom middleware as a class?

You write a plain class with a constructor taking a RequestDelegate — the rest of the pipeline — and a method named InvokeAsync that takes HttpContext and returns Task. Inside it you do your work, call the delegate to continue down the pipeline, and optionally do more work after it returns. You register it with app.UseMiddleware<T>(), usually wrapped in an extension method so it reads like the built-in ones. Notably the class implements no interface — the framework locates InvokeAsync by name using reflection.

Q: What lifetime does conventional middleware have?

Singleton. The class is instantiated once when the pipeline is built, not per request, so a single instance is shared across every concurrent request. That has two consequences: any mutable field is shared state needing thread safety, and injecting a scoped service into the constructor captures one instance for the life of the application. For a DbContext that is both a thread-safety bug and a memory leak, because its change tracker never resets.

Q: How do you use a scoped service like DbContext in middleware?

Put it in the InvokeAsync signature rather than the constructor. Extra parameters on that method are resolved per request from the request's own DI scope, so each request gets its own instance. The rule I remember is singletons in the constructor, scoped services in InvokeAsync. A subtlety worth knowing is that IOptions<T> is a singleton and safe in the constructor, but IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped and has to go in the method.

Q: What happens if you misspell InvokeAsync?

You get an exception at startup saying no public InvokeAsync or Invoke method was found, so the failure is loud and immediate. That is better than the equivalent mistake in the old Startup.cs convention, where a misspelled ConfigureServices compiled and simply never ran. Worth also knowing that defining both Invoke and InvokeAsync on the same class throws, because the framework cannot decide which one you meant.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Injecting a scoped service into the constructor is a captive dependency. Development catches it; production does not, by default.
  • The class is a singleton, so mutable fields are shared across concurrent requests.
  • IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped and cannot go in the constructor, unlike IOptions<T>.
  • Defining both Invoke and InvokeAsync throws at startup.
  • The first InvokeAsync parameter must be HttpContext. Other orders fail.
  • InvokeAsync must return Task, not void or ValueTask.
  • Forgetting to call next ends the pipeline silently.
  • Setting headers after await next throws — use OnStarting.

docs.title: 5.6 — Factory-Based Middleware (IMiddleware)
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.5 Conventional middleware · Next: 5.7 Short-circuiting

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
IMiddleware is the interface-based alternative to conventional middleware. Instead of the framework creating one instance at startup, it asks the DI container for one per request.

  • Because it is resolved per request, scoped services work in the constructor — no method injection needed.
  • It is strongly typed: implement the interface and the compiler checks you got it right.
  • You must register it in DI yourself, and forgetting that is the one gotcha.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means IMiddleware an interface in Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http Has one method: InvokeAsync(HttpContext, RequestDelegate). Factory-based middleware a middleware style The instance is produced by a factory — the DI container — on each request. IMiddlewareFactory an interface What creates the instance. The default implementation resolves from DI. Conventional middleware the other style A class found by convention, created once. See 5.5. Per-request activation a lifetime behaviour A new instance for every request, so constructor injection of scoped services is safe. AddScoped<T>() a registration method How you normally register IMiddleware implementations. AddTransient<T>() a registration method Also works. Effectively the same here, since one instance is used per request. UseMiddleware<T>() an extension method Same call as conventional — the framework detects that T implements IMiddleware.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
Conventional middleware is created once, at startup (5.5). That makes it effectively a singleton, so you cannot inject scoped services into its constructor — you have to add them as InvokeAsync parameters instead.

That works, but it has costs:

  • The class's dependencies are split across two places, which reads oddly.
  • Method injection is not obvious to someone unfamiliar with the convention.
  • Nothing about the class says it is a singleton.

IMiddleware fixes all three by changing when the instance is created. Ask DI for a fresh instance per request, and constructor injection just works like it does everywhere else in your application.

A picture: conventional middleware is one permanent employee handling every customer. Factory-based middleware is hiring a temp for each customer — more overhead per customer, but each one can carry that customer's paperwork without any risk of mixing it up.

docs.title: The simple version — the shape
docs.text:
public class AuditMiddleware : IMiddleware
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _db;                    // SCOPED — and that is fine
    private readonly ILogger<AuditMiddleware> _logger;

    public AuditMiddleware(AppDbContext db, ILogger<AuditMiddleware> logger)
    {
        _db = db;
        _logger = logger;
    }

    // The interface method. Note 'next' is a PARAMETER, not a constructor argument.
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, RequestDelegate next)
    {
        _db.AuditLog.Add(new AuditEntry(context.Request.Path, DateTimeOffset.UtcNow));
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync();

        await next(context);
    }
}

Two structural differences from conventional middleware:

  • No RequestDelegate in the constructor. It arrives as a method parameter instead.
  • AppDbContext in the constructor is safe, because a new instance is created per request.

docs.title: ⚠️ Registration — the gotcha
docs.text:
Factory-based middleware requires two steps, not one:

// 1. Register it in DI — EASY TO FORGET
builder.Services.AddScoped<AuditMiddleware>();

var app = builder.Build();

// 2. Add it to the pipeline
app.UseMiddleware<AuditMiddleware>();

Miss the first step and you get a runtime exception on the first request:

No service for type 'AuditMiddleware' has been registered.

Conventional middleware needs no registration at all, so people forget. It is a loud failure, at least — but it happens on the first request rather than at startup.

You can validate at startup by enabling ValidateOnBuild (4.5).

docs.title: Conventional vs factory-based
docs.text: Conventional Factory-based (IMiddleware) Implements an interface No — found by name Yes Instances One, at startup One per request RequestDelegate Constructor parameter Method parameter Scoped services InvokeAsync parameters only Constructor — normal DI Must register in DI No Yes Compile-time checked No Yes Allocation per request None One instance

docs.title: How it actually works — the factory
docs.text:
The framework resolves an IMiddlewareFactory and calls it per request:

// Roughly what happens per request
var factory = context.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<IMiddlewareFactory>();
var middleware = factory.Create(typeof(AuditMiddleware));   // resolves from request scope

try
{
    await middleware.InvokeAsync(context, next);
}
finally
{
    factory.Release(middleware);
}

The default factory resolves from context.RequestServices — the request scope — which is exactly why scoped constructor injection works.

You can supply your own IMiddlewareFactory if you need pooling or a custom container, though that is rare.

docs.title: The deeper detail — which should you use?
docs.text:
Conventional is the default, and what you will see in most codebases and documentation.

Choose IMiddleware when:

  • The middleware has several scoped dependencies and method injection would be unwieldy
  • You want the compiler to verify the shape rather than relying on a method name
  • You want the middleware itself registered in DI so it can be replaced or decorated

Stay with conventional when:

  • It has no scoped dependencies, or only one
  • It runs on every request and you care about the extra allocation
  • You want the simpler registration story

⚠️ The performance difference is real but small. Factory-based allocates one object per request plus a DI resolution. On a service handling thousands of requests per second that is measurable GC pressure (3.4); on a typical application it is irrelevant. Measure before deciding it matters.

⚠️ One genuine limitation: you cannot pass extra constructor arguments through UseMiddleware<T>(args) with IMiddleware, because the container constructs it. Configuration has to come through IOptions<T> — which is better practice anyway (7.6).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The same middleware written both ways, so the trade-off is visible.

Conventional — dependencies split across constructor and method:

public class TenantResolutionMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<TenantResolutionMiddleware> logger)     // singleton — constructor
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(
        HttpContext context,
        ITenantRepository tenants,                  // scoped — must go here
        ITenantContext tenantContext)               // scoped — and here
    {
        var host = context.Request.Host.Host;
        var tenant = await tenants.FindByHostAsync(host, context.RequestAborted);

        if (tenant is null)
        {
            logger.LogWarning("Unknown tenant host {Host}", host);
            context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound;
            return;                                 // short-circuit
        }

        tenantContext.Current = tenant;
        await next(context);
    }
}

Factory-based — everything in the constructor, as normal:

public class TenantResolutionMiddleware(
    ITenantRepository tenants,
    ITenantContext tenantContext,
    ILogger<TenantResolutionMiddleware> logger) : IMiddleware
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, RequestDelegate next)
    {
        var host = context.Request.Host.Host;
        var tenant = await tenants.FindByHostAsync(host, context.RequestAborted);

        if (tenant is null)
        {
            logger.LogWarning("Unknown tenant host {Host}", host);
            context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound;
            return;
        }

        tenantContext.Current = tenant;
        await next(context);
    }
}

builder.Services.AddScoped<TenantResolutionMiddleware>();     // required
// ...
app.UseMiddleware<TenantResolutionMiddleware>();

The second reads more like ordinary C#. With three dependencies, two of them scoped, that is worth the per-request allocation.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Both are testable, but IMiddleware is slightly cleaner because next is a parameter:

[Fact]
public async Task Returns_404_for_unknown_tenant()
{
    var tenants = Substitute.For<ITenantRepository>();
    tenants.FindByHostAsync(Arg.Any<string>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
           .Returns((Tenant?)null);

    var middleware = new TenantResolutionMiddleware(
        tenants,
        Substitute.For<ITenantContext>(),
        NullLogger<TenantResolutionMiddleware>.Instance);

    var context = new DefaultHttpContext();
    context.Request.Host = new HostString("unknown.example.com");

    var nextCalled = false;
    await middleware.InvokeAsync(context, _ => { nextCalled = true; return Task.CompletedTask; });

    Assert.Equal(404, context.Response.StatusCode);
    Assert.False(nextCalled);          // short-circuited, as intended
}

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is IMiddleware and how does it differ from conventional middleware?

It is an interface with a single InvokeAsync method taking the context and the next delegate. The difference is when the instance is created: conventional middleware is instantiated once at startup and is effectively a singleton, whereas an IMiddleware implementation is resolved from the DI container on every request. That means scoped services can go in the constructor like normal, instead of having to be method-injected into InvokeAsync. It is also strongly typed, so the compiler verifies the shape rather than the framework locating a method by name.

Q: Why can't you inject a DbContext into conventional middleware's constructor?

Because conventional middleware is created once when the pipeline is built, so the constructor runs a single time and whatever it captures lives for the application's lifetime. A scoped DbContext captured that way is shared across every concurrent request, which is both a thread-safety problem and a memory leak as its change tracker grows. That is the captive dependency problem. The conventional fix is to add the DbContext as a parameter on InvokeAsync, which is resolved per request; the IMiddleware alternative sidesteps it entirely.

Q: What is the catch with factory-based middleware?

You have to register it in the DI container yourself, usually with AddScoped. Conventional middleware needs no registration, so it is easy to forget, and the failure appears on the first request rather than at startup — an exception saying no service for that type has been registered. There is also a small per-request cost, since you allocate an instance and perform a container resolution for every request, which only matters at high throughput. And you cannot pass extra constructor arguments through UseMiddleware, so configuration has to come through IOptions.

Q: Which would you choose?

Conventional by default, because it needs no registration, allocates nothing per request, and is what most codebases and documentation use. I would switch to IMiddleware when the middleware has several scoped dependencies, since splitting them between the constructor and the method reads badly, or when I want the middleware registered in DI so it can be decorated or replaced. The performance difference is real but small enough that I would let readability decide unless profiling said otherwise.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting to register it in DI. Fails on the first request, not at startup.
  • RequestDelegate goes in the method, not the constructor, unlike conventional middleware.
  • You cannot pass extra constructor arguments via UseMiddleware<T>(args). Use IOptions.
  • One allocation and one DI resolution per request. Only matters at high throughput.
  • Registering it as a singleton defeats the point — and reintroduces the captive dependency problem it was meant to solve.
  • Mixing the two styles in one class does not work. A RequestDelegate constructor parameter plus IMiddleware will not behave as expected.
