docs.title: 5.7 — Short-Circuiting and Terminal Middleware
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.6 IMiddleware factory · Next: 5.8 HttpContext

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Short-circuiting means a middleware decides not to call next, so the request stops there and that middleware produces the response itself.

  • It is done simply by not calling next() — usually with an early return.
  • Everything registered below is skipped. Everything above still gets its "after" half.
  • This is how static files, authorization failures, rate limiting and caching all work.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Short-circuit a behaviour Not calling next, so the rest of the pipeline is skipped. Terminal middleware a role Middleware that never calls next at all — the end of the line. app.Run(handler) an extension method Adds terminal middleware. Its signature has no next. Unwinding what happens next Control returns up through the middleware that already called next. return a C# statement How you short-circuit. Simply stop before reaching next. Empty 200 a failure symptom What the caller gets when you short-circuit without writing a response. context.Response.StatusCode a property Set this before writing, or the default 200 is sent. Results / TypedResults static classes Helpers for producing responses in minimal APIs and endpoint filters. ShortCircuit() an endpoint method (.NET 8+) Marks an endpoint to skip most of the pipeline for performance.

docs.title: It is just an early return
docs.text:
There is no special API for short-circuiting. You simply do not call next:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/blocked"))
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden;
        await context.Response.WriteAsync("Not allowed");
        return;                       // ← the short circuit. No next().
    }

    await next();                     // the normal path
});

That is the entire mechanism.

A picture: a security desk in a corridor of desks. Normally they check you and wave you through to the next desk. When something is wrong they hand you a rejection slip and turn you around — you never see the desks further down.

docs.title: What still runs
docs.text:
This is the part worth being precise about. Short-circuiting skips everything downstream, but middleware upstream has already called next and is waiting — so their "after" code still runs as the call unwinds.

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("A: before");
    await next();
    Console.WriteLine("A: after");        // ← STILL RUNS
});

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("B: short-circuiting");
    context.Response.StatusCode = 403;
    return;                               // no next()
});

app.Run(async context =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("C: never reached");
});

Output:

A: before
B: short-circuiting
A: after            ← A's after half still executes

That is essential, and it is why logging, timing and exception-handling middleware keep working even when a request is rejected early. They are wrapped around the short-circuit, not bypassed by it.

docs.title: The simple version — where it already happens
docs.text:
Most short-circuiting in your app is done by middleware you did not write:

Middleware Short-circuits when UseStaticFiles The path matches a file in wwwroot — serves it and stops UseAuthorization The user fails the policy — returns 401 or 403 UseRateLimiter The limit is exceeded — returns 429 UseCors A preflight OPTIONS request — answers it directly UseResponseCaching A cached response exists — returns it without hitting the endpoint UseHttpsRedirection The request is HTTP — returns a 307 redirect

Static files is the one to understand, because it explains the ordering rule from 5.2. A request for /logo.png matches a file, so that middleware writes it and returns. Authentication, authorization and routing below it never execute — which is why placing static files early saves real work, and why files in wwwroot are not protected by [Authorize] (4.10).

docs.title: ⚠️ The empty 200 trap
docs.text:
The most common bug here:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    if (!IsValid(context))
    {
        return;             // ✗ short-circuits, but writes NOTHING
    }
    await next();
});

The caller gets HTTP 200 with an empty body. No error, no status code, nothing to debug from — because StatusCode defaults to 200 and you never changed it.

Always set a status code and ideally write a body:

if (!IsValid(context))
{
    context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest;
    context.Response.ContentType = "application/problem+json";
    await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new ProblemDetails
    {
        Status = StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest,
        Title  = "Invalid request"
    });
    return;
}

Using ProblemDetails keeps your error shape consistent with the rest of the API — 10.8.

docs.title: Terminal middleware — app.Run
docs.text:
Run is short-circuiting made structural. Its delegate has no next parameter, so continuing is impossible:

app.Run(async context =>
{
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("This always ends here");
});

app.UseAuthentication();     // ⚠️ unreachable — nothing after Run ever executes

Registering middleware after Run compiles fine and silently never runs. Covered in 5.3.

Your endpoints are effectively terminal middleware — MapControllers sits at the end of the pipeline and produces the response.

docs.title: The deeper detail — the .NET 8 ShortCircuit() optimisation
docs.text:
.NET 8 added a way to skip most of the pipeline for specific endpoints:

app.MapGet("/healthz", () => Results.Ok()).ShortCircuit();

// Or with a status code, skipping even the handler
app.MapGet("/robots.txt", () => "User-agent: *").ShortCircuit(200);

Normally routing happens early and the endpoint runs at the end, so a health check still passes through authentication, authorization, CORS and everything else. ShortCircuit() tells the routing middleware to execute the endpoint immediately after matching, skipping the middleware in between.

Use it for high-volume endpoints that need no pipeline — health checks polled every few seconds, robots.txt, favicon.ico.

⚠️ Be careful. It skips authentication and authorization too. Applying it to anything sensitive removes your security middleware from that path entirely. Health endpoints are the intended case precisely because they are meant to be unauthenticated.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic short-circuiting middleware — an API key check:

internal class ApiKeyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, ILogger<ApiKeyMiddleware> logger)
{
    private const string HeaderName = "X-Api-Key";

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, IApiKeyValidator validator)
    {
        // Only guard /api — everything else passes straight through
        if (!context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/api"))
        {
            await next(context);
            return;
        }

        if (!context.Request.Headers.TryGetValue(HeaderName, out var provided))
        {
            await WriteProblemAsync(context, StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized,
                "Missing API key");
            return;                                    // short-circuit
        }

        if (!await validator.IsValidAsync(provided!, context.RequestAborted))
        {
            logger.LogWarning("Rejected invalid API key from {Ip}",
                context.Connection.RemoteIpAddress);

            await WriteProblemAsync(context, StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden,
                "Invalid API key");
            return;                                    // short-circuit
        }

        await next(context);                           // valid — carry on
    }

    private static async Task WriteProblemAsync(HttpContext context, int status, string title)
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = status;
        context.Response.ContentType = "application/problem+json";
        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new ProblemDetails
        {
            Status = status,
            Title  = title
        });
    }
}

Three things worth noticing:

  • Every short-circuit path sets a status code and writes a body. No silent empty 200s.
  • The non-matching path calls next and returns, so unrelated requests are unaffected.
  • context.RequestAborted is passed down, so a disconnected client stops the validation work (2.14).

docs.title: Checking whether the response already started
docs.text:
Before short-circuiting after calling next, check that nothing has been written:

await next(context);

if (!context.Response.HasStarted)
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-Handled-By"] = "MyMiddleware";
}

Once the response has started, headers and status code are already on the wire and any modification throws. See 5.8.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does it mean to short-circuit the pipeline?

It means a middleware decides not to call the next delegate, so the request stops there and that middleware produces the response itself. There is no special API — you simply return before reaching next. Everything registered below is skipped, but middleware above has already called next and is awaiting it, so their code after that await still runs as the call unwinds. That is important, because it means logging, timing and exception handling continue to work for requests that are rejected early.

Q: Where does short-circuiting already happen in a typical app?

In most of the built-in middleware. Static files short-circuits when the path matches a file in wwwroot, serving it without running anything below — which is why placing it early saves work and why files there are not protected by authorization. Authorization short-circuits with 401 or 403 when a policy fails. Rate limiting returns 429, response caching returns a cached body without touching the endpoint, and CORS answers preflight requests directly.

Q: What is the most common bug when writing short-circuiting middleware?

Returning without writing anything. The caller then gets an HTTP 200 with an empty body, because the status code defaults to 200 and you never set it — so there is nothing to diagnose from. Every short-circuit path should set an explicit status code and ideally write a body, and using ProblemDetails keeps the error shape consistent with the rest of the API.

Q: What is ShortCircuit() in .NET 8?

An endpoint-level optimisation. Normally routing matches early but the endpoint executes at the end of the pipeline, so even a health check passes through authentication, authorization and everything else. Calling .ShortCircuit() on an endpoint tells the routing middleware to run it immediately after matching, skipping the middleware in between. It suits high-volume endpoints that need no pipeline — health checks, robots.txt. The caveat is that it skips authentication and authorization too, so it must never be applied to anything sensitive.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Returning without writing a response gives an empty 200. Always set a status code.
  • Middleware after app.Run(handler) never executes. It compiles and silently does nothing.
  • Short-circuiting does not skip upstream "after" code. Those middleware still unwind.
  • Modifying the response after it has started throws. Check HasStarted first.
  • ShortCircuit() skips authentication and authorization. Only for genuinely public endpoints.
  • Short-circuiting before UseExceptionHandler means your error is not formatted by it.
  • Forgetting return after writing a response lets execution continue to next, producing a second response and an exception.

docs.title: 5.8 — HttpContext
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.7 Short-circuiting · Next: 5.9 Request body buffering

Markers: 🔥 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
HttpContext is the object holding everything about one HTTP request and its response. Every middleware, filter and action receives it.

  • One instance per request. It is created when the request arrives and disposed when the response completes.
  • It is not thread-safe, and storing it anywhere is a bug.
  • The parts you use daily: Request, Response, Items, User, RequestServices, RequestAborted.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means HttpContext an abstract class Everything about one request and response. Created per request. Request a property (HttpRequest) Incoming data — path, method, headers, query string, body. Response a property (HttpResponse) Outgoing data — status code, headers, body. Items a property (IDictionary<object, object>) A scratchpad for passing data between middleware within one request. User a property (ClaimsPrincipal) Who the caller is. Populated by UseAuthentication. Never null, but may be unauthenticated. RequestServices a property (IServiceProvider) The request-scoped DI container. RequestAborted a property (CancellationToken) Fires when the client disconnects. Features a property (IFeatureCollection) Low-level server capabilities. The extensibility mechanism underneath everything. Connection a property Remote IP address, port, client certificate. TraceIdentifier a property (string) A per-request ID the framework generates. Useful in error responses. Response.HasStarted a property (bool) Whether any bytes have been sent. Once true, headers are immutable. OnStarting a method Registers a callback to run just before the first byte is written. IHttpContextAccessor an interface Reaches the current context outside a controller. Use sparingly — see 21.12.

docs.title: One object, one request
docs.text:
When a request arrives, ASP.NET Core creates one HttpContext and passes the same instance through every middleware, then to the filter pipeline and finally your action. When the response finishes, it is disposed and often pooled for reuse.

That last detail matters more than it sounds — see the trap section.

A picture: a job docket travelling through a workshop. Everyone who touches the job writes on the same docket. It carries the original order, notes added along the way, and eventually the finished result. When the job ships, the docket is filed and the clipboard reused for the next job.

docs.title: What replaced HttpContext.Current
docs.text:
Classic ASP.NET had a static HttpContext.Current reachable from anywhere. Convenient, and a genuine design flaw — it made code untestable and coupled every layer to the web (4.1).

ASP.NET Core has no static context. You receive it as a parameter, which means a method's dependencies are visible in its signature and it can be tested with a DefaultHttpContext.

docs.title: The simple version — the parts you use
docs.text:
public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    // ── the request ──
    context.Request.Method;                    // "GET"
    context.Request.Path;                      // "/api/orders/42"
    context.Request.QueryString;               // "?page=2"
    context.Request.Query["page"];             // "2"
    context.Request.Headers["Authorization"];
    context.Request.ContentType;
    context.Request.Body;                      // a Stream — see 5.9

    // ── the response ──
    context.Response.StatusCode = 200;
    context.Response.Headers["X-Custom"] = "value";
    context.Response.ContentType = "application/json";
    await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new { ok = true });

    // ── the caller ──
    context.User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated;    // bool
    context.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value;
    context.Connection.RemoteIpAddress;

    // ── infrastructure ──
    context.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();
    context.RequestAborted;                    // client-disconnect token
    context.TraceIdentifier;                   // "0HN7B1..." per-request id
    context.Items["key"] = value;              // scratchpad
}

docs.title: Items — passing data down the pipeline
docs.text:
Items is a dictionary scoped to one request. It is how middleware hands information to code further down:

// Early middleware writes
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Items["CorrelationId"] = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
    await next();
});

// A controller reads
public IActionResult Get()
{
    var correlationId = HttpContext.Items["CorrelationId"] as string;
    return Ok(new { correlationId });
}

⚠️ It is untyped and stringly-keyed, so a typo gives you null rather than a compile error. Use a constant for the key, or a typed wrapper:

public static class HttpContextExtensions
{
    private const string CorrelationIdKey = "__CorrelationId";

    public static void SetCorrelationId(this HttpContext ctx, string id)
        => ctx.Items[CorrelationIdKey] = id;

    public static string? GetCorrelationId(this HttpContext ctx)
        => ctx.Items[CorrelationIdKey] as string;
}

Prefer a scoped service for anything substantial. A scoped service is typed, injectable and testable; Items is right for small, incidental values that only middleware cares about.

docs.title: ⚠️ HasStarted — the response is one-way
docs.text:
The single most common HttpContext error:

await next(context);

context.Response.Headers["X-Duration"] = "42ms";
// ✗ InvalidOperationException:
//   "Headers are read-only, response has already started."

HTTP sends headers before the body. Once any byte of body has gone out, the headers are on the wire and cannot change. Same for the status code.

Two fixes:

// 1. Check first
await next(context);
if (!context.Response.HasStarted)
    context.Response.Headers["X-Duration"] = "42ms";

// 2. Better — register a callback that runs just before the first byte
context.Response.OnStarting(() =>
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-Duration"] = $"{sw.ElapsedMilliseconds}ms";
    return Task.CompletedTask;
});

await next(context);        // register BEFORE calling next

OnStarting is the correct answer when you need to set a header based on work done during the request. Register it before next, so it is in place before anything downstream writes.

docs.title: The deeper detail — Features
docs.text:
HttpContext is a friendly facade over a feature collection — a set of interfaces the server implements. Request and Response are convenience wrappers over those features.

// Ask the server whether it supports a capability
var bodyFeature = context.Features.Get<IHttpRequestBodyDetectionFeature>();
var syncIo = context.Features.Get<IHttpBodyControlFeature>();

if (syncIo is not null)
    syncIo.AllowSynchronousIO = true;      // off by default, for good reason

This design is why the same HttpContext works over Kestrel, IIS and HTTP.sys — each server supplies its own feature implementations, and code asks for a capability rather than assuming it. It is rare to touch directly, but knowing it exists explains a lot of the framework's extensibility.

AllowSynchronousIO is the feature you are most likely to meet. Synchronous reads and writes are disabled by default because they block a thread-pool thread (2.13). If a library throws "Synchronous operations are disallowed", that is why — and enabling it is a workaround, not a fix.

docs.title: ⚠️ Never store HttpContext
docs.text:
// ✗ CATASTROPHIC
public class BadService
{
    private static HttpContext? _context;

    public void Remember(HttpContext ctx) => _context = ctx;
}

Two reasons this breaks badly:

It is not thread-safe. One instance belongs to one request on one execution flow.

It is pooled and reused. After the response completes, the framework may reset the object and hand it to a different request. Your stored reference now points at someone else's request — potentially exposing one user's data to another. That is a security bug, not just a correctness one.

The same applies to capturing it in a background task:

// ✗ WRONG — the request may finish before this runs
_ = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await DoWorkAsync(context.User.Identity!.Name);   // context may be recycled
});

// ✓ Copy the values you need FIRST
var userName = context.User.Identity?.Name;
_ = Task.Run(async () => await DoWorkAsync(userName));

And in ASP.NET Core, fire-and-forget from a request is usually the wrong pattern anyway — 2.15 and 21.1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A middleware using the pieces properly:

internal class RequestContextMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<RequestContextMiddleware> logger)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        // Prefer an incoming correlation id so traces span services
        var correlationId = context.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault()
                            ?? context.TraceIdentifier;

        context.Items["CorrelationId"] = correlationId;

        // Register BEFORE next, so it is in place before the response starts
        context.Response.OnStarting(() =>
        {
            context.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"] = correlationId;
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        });

        using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
        {
            ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId,
            ["UserId"] = context.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value ?? "anonymous",
            ["ClientIp"] = context.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "unknown"
        }))
        {
            await next(context);
        }
    }
}

Every log line written anywhere downstream now carries the correlation ID, user and client IP, with no extra code in your controllers — 18.4.

docs.title: Testing with DefaultHttpContext
docs.text:
var context = new DefaultHttpContext();
context.Request.Path = "/api/orders";
context.Request.Method = "GET";
context.Request.Headers["X-Api-Key"] = "test-key";
context.Response.Body = new MemoryStream();       // capture what gets written

context.User = new ClaimsPrincipal(new ClaimsIdentity(
    [new Claim(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier, "user-1")],
    authenticationType: "Test"));                 // ← makes IsAuthenticated true

⚠️ That authenticationType argument matters. A ClaimsIdentity created without one has IsAuthenticated == false, so [Authorize] still rejects it — a common source of confusing test failures.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is HttpContext?

It is the object holding everything about a single HTTP request and its response — the path, method, headers and body coming in, the status code and body going out, the authenticated user, the request-scoped DI container, and a cancellation token that fires if the client disconnects. One instance is created per request and passed through every middleware, filter and action. It replaced classic ASP.NET's static HttpContext.Current, which was convenient but made code untestable and coupled every layer to the web.

Q: Why can't you set a response header after calling next?

Because HTTP sends headers before the body, so once any byte of the body has been written the headers are already on the wire and immutable — attempting to change them throws. You can guard with Response.HasStarted, but the better answer is Response.OnStarting, which registers a callback that runs immediately before the first byte is sent. You register it before calling next, so it is in place before anything downstream starts writing, and it can then set headers based on work measured during the request.

Q: Why must you never store an HttpContext?

Two reasons. It is not thread-safe — one instance belongs to one request on one execution flow. More seriously, the framework pools and reuses these objects: after a response completes it may be reset and handed to a different request, so a stored reference ends up pointing at someone else's request. That is a security problem, not just a correctness one, because you could read another user's data. If you need values in a background task, copy the primitives you need before starting it.

Q: What is HttpContext.Items for, and when would you use something else?

It is a dictionary scoped to one request, used to pass small pieces of data from middleware to code further down the pipeline — a correlation ID, a resolved tenant. Its weakness is that it is untyped and keyed by string, so a typo gives you null rather than a compile error. For anything substantial I would use a scoped service instead, which is typed, injectable and testable. Items earns its place for incidental values that only the pipeline cares about.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Storing HttpContext anywhere. It is pooled and reused — you may end up reading another user's request.
  • Setting headers or status after the response has started throws. Use OnStarting.
  • Items is untyped and string-keyed. Typos fail silently. Use constants or a typed wrapper.
  • context.User is never null but may be unauthenticated. Check User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated.
  • A ClaimsIdentity with no authenticationType is not authenticated, which breaks tests in confusing ways.
  • Request.Body can only be read once unless you enable buffering — see 5.9.
  • Synchronous IO is disabled by default. Enabling AllowSynchronousIO is a workaround, not a fix.
  • Capturing the context in a fire-and-forget task races with the request completing.

docs.title: 5.9 — Reading and Rewinding the Request Body
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.8 HttpContext · Next: 5.10 Built-in middleware

Markers: ⚠️ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Request.Body is a forward-only stream. Reading it consumes it — so if your middleware reads the body, the model binder finds nothing and your action gets a null model.

  • EnableBuffering() makes the stream re-readable by keeping a copy.
  • After reading you must rewind it with Body.Position = 0, or the next reader still sees nothing.
  • Buffering costs memory or disk. Do not do it for every request unless you have measured the cost.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Request.Body a Stream property The raw bytes of the request body. Forward-only by default. Forward-only stream a stream property Can be read once, start to finish. No seeking, no rewinding. EnableBuffering() an extension method Swaps in a stream that remembers what it read, making it seekable. FileBufferingReadStream a class What EnableBuffering installs. Buffers in memory, spilling to disk past a threshold. Rewind an action Setting Body.Position = 0 so the next reader starts at the beginning. bufferThreshold a parameter Bytes kept in memory before spilling to a temp file. Default 30 KB. bufferLimit a parameter Maximum total size. Exceeding it throws. leaveOpen a StreamReader parameter Whether disposing the reader also disposes the stream. Must be true here. Model binding a framework step Reads the body to construct your action's parameters. See 11.2. MaxRequestBodySize a Kestrel limit The hard ceiling on body size. Default 30 MB.

docs.title: Why the body can only be read once
docs.text:
The request body arrives over a network socket. ASP.NET Core exposes it as a Stream that reads directly from that socket as data arrives — nothing is stored.

That is a deliberate design for efficiency. A 2 GB file upload does not sit in memory; it flows through as it arrives.

The consequence: once bytes are read, they are gone. There is no buffer to re-read from.

A picture: water from a tap. You can fill a glass as it flows. What you did not catch has gone down the drain — you cannot ask the tap to send the same water again.

docs.title: The bug this causes
docs.text:
// Logging middleware reads the body
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(context.Request.Body);
    var body = await reader.ReadToEndAsync();
    logger.LogInformation("Body: {Body}", body);      // works — logs correctly

    await next();
});

// The action gets nothing
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult Create([FromBody] CreateOrderRequest request)
{
    // request is NULL — the body was already consumed upstream
}

With [ApiController] you get an automatic 400 saying the body is required, which at least points somewhere. Without it, you get a null reference deeper in your code.

The middleware works and breaks the application. That is what makes it a good interview question.

docs.title: The simple version — EnableBuffering
docs.text:
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Request.EnableBuffering();          // ← swap in a re-readable stream

    using var reader = new StreamReader(
        context.Request.Body,
        encoding: Encoding.UTF8,
        detectEncodingFromByteOrderMarks: false,
        leaveOpen: true);                       // ← do NOT dispose the body stream

    var body = await reader.ReadToEndAsync();
    logger.LogInformation("Body: {Body}", body);

    context.Request.Body.Position = 0;          // ← REWIND for the next reader

    await next();
});

Three details, and all three are required:

EnableBuffering() replaces Request.Body with a FileBufferingReadStream, which keeps what it reads so the stream becomes seekable.

leaveOpen: true stops StreamReader's disposal from closing the body stream. Without it the stream is disposed and model binding throws ObjectDisposedException.

Body.Position = 0 rewinds. EnableBuffering alone only makes rewinding possible — you still have to do it. Forget this and the symptom is identical to not buffering at all, which makes it maddening to debug.

docs.title: How it actually works — where the buffer lives
docs.text:
FileBufferingReadStream buffers in memory up to a threshold, then spills to a temp file:

context.Request.EnableBuffering(
    bufferThreshold: 1024 * 100,          // 100 KB in memory
    bufferLimit: 1024 * 1024 * 10);       // 10 MB hard ceiling — throws beyond

Defaults are a 30 KB threshold and no limit.

The design is sensible: small bodies stay in memory, large ones go to disk rather than exhausting RAM. But both have costs.

⚠️ The memory cost. Buffering every request means holding every request body in memory simultaneously. At 500 requests per second with 50 KB bodies, that is roughly 25 MB of live allocation churning constantly — straight into GC pressure (3.4).

⚠️ The disk cost. Bodies above the threshold write to a temp file. That is disk IO on every large request, and in a container with a read-only or memory-backed filesystem it can fail outright.

⚠️ The denial-of-service angle. Buffering with no bufferLimit lets an attacker send large bodies to force allocation. Always set a limit, and keep Kestrel's MaxRequestBodySize sensible (4.9).

docs.title: The deeper detail — don't buffer everything
docs.text:
The right instinct is to buffer selectively:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var shouldLog =
        context.Request.ContentLength is > 0 and < 10_000 &&     // small only
        context.Request.ContentType?.Contains("json") == true && // JSON only
        context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/api");         // API only

    if (!shouldLog)
    {
        await next();          // no buffering — no cost at all
        return;
    }

    context.Request.EnableBuffering();
    // ... read, log, rewind ...
    await next();
});

And ask whether you need the body at all. Most of the time the answer is no:

  • Debugging a specific problem? Enable it temporarily, behind a config flag.
  • Auditing? Log the bound model from a filter instead — it is typed, and the framework did the parsing (12.8).
  • Diagnosing failures only? Buffer only when the response status indicates an error.

docs.title: ⚠️ Logging bodies is a data-protection problem
docs.text:
Request bodies contain passwords, card numbers, personal data and tokens. Logging them wholesale means writing all of it to a log aggregator that many people can read and that is retained for months.

At minimum, redact:

private static readonly string[] SensitiveKeys =
    ["password", "token", "secret", "cardNumber", "ssn", "apiKey"];

private static string Redact(string json)
{
    try
    {
        var node = JsonNode.Parse(json);
        if (node is JsonObject obj)
        {
            foreach (var key in SensitiveKeys)
            {
                var match = obj.FirstOrDefault(p =>
                    p.Key.Contains(key, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));

                if (match.Key is not null)
                    obj[match.Key] = "***REDACTED***";
            }
        }
        return node?.ToJsonString() ?? json;
    }
    catch
    {
        return "[unparseable body — not logged]";   // never log raw on failure
    }
}

Note the catch: if the body will not parse, log nothing rather than dumping raw bytes that might contain anything. See 18.10.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic body-logging middleware that is safe to run in production:

internal class BodyLoggingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<BodyLoggingMiddleware> logger,
    IOptions<BodyLoggingOptions> options)
{
    private readonly BodyLoggingOptions _options = options.Value;

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        if (!ShouldCapture(context))
        {
            await next(context);
            return;
        }

        context.Request.EnableBuffering(
            bufferThreshold: _options.BufferThresholdBytes,
            bufferLimit: _options.MaxBodyBytes);

        string body;
        using (var reader = new StreamReader(
            context.Request.Body, Encoding.UTF8,
            detectEncodingFromByteOrderMarks: false,
            leaveOpen: true))
        {
            body = await reader.ReadToEndAsync(context.RequestAborted);
        }

        context.Request.Body.Position = 0;      // ESSENTIAL — rewind

        await next(context);

        // Log only when something went wrong, to keep volume down
        if (context.Response.StatusCode >= 400)
        {
            logger.LogWarning(
                "Request {Method} {Path} failed with {Status}. Body: {Body}",
                context.Request.Method,
                context.Request.Path,
                context.Response.StatusCode,
                Redact(body));
        }
    }

    private bool ShouldCapture(HttpContext context) =>
        _options.Enabled &&
        context.Request.ContentLength is > 0 &&
        context.Request.ContentLength <= _options.MaxBodyBytes &&
        context.Request.ContentType?.Contains("json", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) == true;
}

Four production-shaped decisions worth explaining:

  • Config-driven Enabled flag, so it can be switched on to investigate and off again without a deploy.
  • A size ceiling, so a large upload cannot force a large allocation.
  • Only logs on failure, which cuts volume enormously while keeping the diagnostic value.
  • Redaction, because request bodies contain credentials.

docs.title: Response bodies are harder
docs.text:
Reading the response body requires swapping the stream entirely, because responses have no EnableBuffering:

var original = context.Response.Body;
using var buffer = new MemoryStream();
context.Response.Body = buffer;

await next(context);

buffer.Position = 0;
var responseText = await new StreamReader(buffer).ReadToEndAsync();

buffer.Position = 0;
await buffer.CopyToAsync(original);        // MUST copy it back
context.Response.Body = original;

⚠️ This buffers the entire response in memory, which breaks streaming endpoints and file downloads — a 500 MB file download becomes 500 MB of RAM. Response logging is worth avoiding unless you genuinely need it and can scope it tightly.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why does reading the request body in middleware break model binding?

Because Request.Body is a forward-only stream reading directly from the network socket, so nothing is retained. Once your middleware reads it, the bytes are gone, and when model binding runs later it finds an empty stream — so the action's parameter is null. With [ApiController] that surfaces as an automatic 400 saying the body is required; without it you get a null reference somewhere deeper. What makes it a nasty bug is that the middleware itself works perfectly and only breaks something else.

Q: How do you read the body without breaking things?

Call Request.EnableBuffering() first, which swaps in a FileBufferingReadStream that retains what it reads and is therefore seekable. Then read it, and critically set Body.Position = 0 afterwards to rewind, because EnableBuffering only makes rewinding possible — it does not do it for you. You also need leaveOpen: true on the StreamReader, otherwise disposing the reader closes the body stream and model binding throws ObjectDisposedException.

Q: What does buffering cost?

Memory, or disk. FileBufferingReadStream keeps up to a threshold in memory — 30 KB by default — and spills beyond that to a temporary file. So buffering every request means holding every request body in memory concurrently, which at a few hundred requests per second is significant GC pressure, and larger bodies mean disk IO on every request. There is also a denial-of-service angle: without a bufferLimit, an attacker can send large bodies to force allocation. So I would buffer selectively — by path, content type and size — rather than globally.

Q: Would you log request bodies in production?

Reluctantly and narrowly. Bodies contain passwords, card numbers, tokens and personal data, and logging them writes all of that to an aggregator that is widely readable and retained for months. If I needed it I would gate it behind a configuration flag so it can be switched on to investigate and off again, cap the size, log only when the response indicates a failure, and redact known sensitive fields — falling back to logging nothing rather than raw bytes if the body will not parse. Often the better answer is to log the bound model from an action filter instead, since that is typed and the framework has already parsed it.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Reading the body without EnableBuffering breaks model binding, and the middleware itself looks fine.
  • Forgetting Body.Position = 0 produces the exact same symptom as not buffering at all.
  • Forgetting leaveOpen: true disposes the stream and causes ObjectDisposedException later.
  • Buffering every request costs memory or disk on every request.
  • No bufferLimit is a denial-of-service vector.
  • Logging bodies leaks credentials and personal data into your log system.
  • Buffering the response breaks streaming and large downloads.
  • Reading the body of a GET is pointless — there usually is not one; check ContentLength.

docs.title: 5.10 — Tour of the Built-in Middleware
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.9 Request body buffering · Next: 5.11 Exception middleware

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core ships with roughly twenty middleware components. None of them are on by default — you add the ones you need.

  • The ones almost every app uses: exception handling, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, endpoints.
  • Several need a matching builder.Services.Add... call, and forgetting it throws at startup.
  • Knowing what exists saves you writing middleware that already ships in the box.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Built-in middleware framework components Middleware shipped with ASP.NET Core, added via Use... methods. Use... method an extension method Adds middleware to the pipeline. Phase 2 of Program.cs. Add... method an extension method Registers the services that middleware needs. Phase 1. UseExceptionHandler middleware Catches unhandled exceptions from below and produces a clean response. UseHsts middleware Sends Strict-Transport-Security, telling browsers to always use HTTPS. UseHttpsRedirection middleware Redirects HTTP requests to the HTTPS equivalent. UseStaticFiles middleware Serves files from wwwroot. Short-circuits on a match. UseRouting middleware Matches the request to an endpoint. Does not execute it. UseCors middleware Applies a cross-origin policy and answers preflight requests. UseAuthentication middleware Establishes who the caller is; populates context.User. UseAuthorization middleware Decides whether the caller may proceed. UseResponseCompression middleware Compresses responses with gzip or Brotli. UseRateLimiter middleware (.NET 7+) Rejects requests over a configured limit with 429. UseOutputCache middleware (.NET 7+) Caches whole responses server-side.

docs.title: Nothing is on by default
docs.text:
This follows from ASP.NET Core's opt-in design (4.1). A new minimal API project has a nearly empty pipeline. You add what you need.

The benefit is that you pay only for what you use, and the whole application's behaviour is visible in Program.cs. The cost is that forgetting something produces silent misbehaviour rather than an error — no UseAuthentication means User is never populated and every [Authorize] endpoint returns 401 with no explanation.

docs.title: The two-call pattern
docs.text:
Many middleware need services registered before the pipeline is built:

builder.Services.AddCors();              // phase 1 — register services
var app = builder.Build();
app.UseCors();                           // phase 2 — add to the pipeline

Forget the Add and you get a startup exception like "Unable to find the required services. Please add all the required services by calling IServiceCollection.AddCors" — which is at least a clear message pointing at the fix.

Which need both:

Middleware Needs an Add call? UseCors ✅ AddCors() UseAuthentication ✅ AddAuthentication() UseAuthorization ✅ AddAuthorization() UseResponseCaching ✅ AddResponseCaching() UseResponseCompression ✅ AddResponseCompression() UseRateLimiter ✅ AddRateLimiter(...) UseOutputCache ✅ AddOutputCache() UseSession ✅ AddSession() + a distributed cache UseHealthChecks / MapHealthChecks ✅ AddHealthChecks() UseStaticFiles ❌ UseHttpsRedirection ❌ UseExceptionHandler ❌ (but AddProblemDetails() improves it) UseRouting ❌

docs.title: The simple version — the ones you will actually use
docs.text:
Error handling

app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();      // dev only — full stack trace in the browser
app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");    // production — clean response, nothing leaked
app.UseStatusCodePages();             // adds a body to bare 404s and 401s

UseStatusCodePages is underused. Without it a 404 from routing has an empty body, which confuses API clients expecting JSON. UseStatusCodePages() gives them something. See 5.11.

HTTPS and security headers

app.UseHttpsRedirection();            // 307 redirect HTTP → HTTPS
app.UseHsts();                        // Strict-Transport-Security header

⚠️ UseHsts should be production-only. It tells browsers to refuse HTTP for this host for months, and browsers cache that aggressively. Enable it locally and you can lock yourself out of http://localhost across every project on that port. See 17.5.

⚠️ UseHttpsRedirection behind a TLS-terminating proxy causes an infinite loop — the app sees http, redirects, the proxy forwards http again (4.2).

Static files

app.UseStaticFiles();                 // serve wwwroot
app.UseDefaultFiles();                // serve index.html for a directory — BEFORE UseStaticFiles
app.MapStaticAssets();                // .NET 9+ — fingerprinting and precompression

See 4.10.

Routing, CORS, auth

app.UseRouting();
app.UseCors("Default");
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

The order here is the canonical one and matters enormously — 5.2.

docs.title: How it actually works — the performance ones
docs.text:
Response compression

builder.Services.AddResponseCompression(options =>
{
    options.EnableForHttps = true;                 // off by default — see below
    options.Providers.Add<BrotliCompressionProvider>();
    options.Providers.Add<GzipCompressionProvider>();
});

app.UseResponseCompression();

⚠️ EnableForHttps is false by default because of the BREACH and CRIME attacks, where an attacker who can inject content and observe compressed sizes can extract secrets. Turning it on is usually fine for JSON APIs with no reflected secrets, and genuinely risky for pages echoing tokens back.

⚠️ Do not compress in the app if your reverse proxy already does. Nginx and most CDNs compress better and it costs your app nothing. Doing both wastes CPU.

Rate limiting (.NET 7+)

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
    options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("api", limiter =>
    {
        limiter.PermitLimit = 100;
        limiter.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
        limiter.QueueLimit = 0;
    });

    options.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
});

app.UseRateLimiter();

⚠️ Register it after UseForwardedHeaders, or every request appears to come from the proxy and shares one bucket. See 17.10.

Output caching (.NET 7+)

builder.Services.AddOutputCache(options =>
{
    options.AddBasePolicy(p => p.Expire(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)));
});

app.UseOutputCache();

app.MapGet("/products", GetProducts).CacheOutput();

Different from response caching: output caching stores the response on the server and can be invalidated by tag, whereas response caching only sets HTTP headers and relies on the client or a proxy to honour them. See 19.6.

docs.title: The deeper detail — ones worth knowing exist
docs.text:
app.UseForwardedHeaders();       // real client IP behind a proxy — see 4.2
app.UseRequestLocalization();    // culture from Accept-Language — see 21.8
app.UseSession();                // server-side session. Makes your app stateful.
app.UseWebSockets();             // raw WebSocket support
app.UseRequestTimeouts();        // .NET 8+ — per-endpoint timeouts
app.UseRequestDecompression();   // .NET 7+ — accept compressed request bodies
app.UseAntiforgery();            // CSRF tokens — see 17.4
app.UseW3CLogging();             // W3C-format access logs
app.UseHttpLogging();            // structured request/response logging — see 5.14

⚠️ UseSession deserves a warning. It makes your application stateful, which breaks horizontal scaling unless you back it with a distributed cache (24.12). For APIs it is almost always the wrong choice — a token carries the state instead.

⚠️ UseRequestTimeouts is a genuinely useful addition most people have not noticed. It cancels the request's CancellationToken after a deadline, so a slow dependency cannot tie up a request indefinitely.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A complete production pipeline using the common set:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// ── phase 1: services the middleware needs ──
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();
builder.Services.AddCors(o => o.AddDefaultPolicy(p => p
    .WithOrigins("https://app.example.com")
    .AllowAnyHeader()
    .AllowAnyMethod()));
builder.Services.AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();
builder.Services.AddResponseCompression(o => o.EnableForHttps = true);
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(o => o.AddFixedWindowLimiter("api", l =>
{
    l.PermitLimit = 100;
    l.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
}));
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks();
builder.Services.AddControllers();

var app = builder.Build();

// ── phase 2: the pipeline, in canonical order ──
app.UseExceptionHandler();          // outermost — wraps everything below

app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
{
    ForwardedHeaders = ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto
});

if (!app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    app.UseHsts();                  // production only

app.UseResponseCompression();
app.UseStaticFiles();               // early — assets skip everything below

app.UseRouting();

app.UseCors();                      // before auth, so preflight is answered
app.UseRateLimiter();               // after forwarded headers, so it sees real IPs

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers().RequireRateLimiting("api");
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz").ShortCircuit();

app.Run();

Every ordering decision in that pipeline has a reason, and they are all covered in 5.2.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Which middleware does a typical ASP.NET Core API use?

Exception handling first so it wraps everything, then forwarded headers if behind a proxy, HSTS and HTTPS redirection, static files if the app serves any, routing, CORS, rate limiting, authentication, authorization, and finally endpoint mapping. None of them are enabled by default — ASP.NET Core is opt-in, so a new project starts with an almost empty pipeline and you add what you need. That makes the whole application's behaviour readable in Program.cs, at the cost of silent misbehaviour when you forget something.

Q: Why do some middleware need a matching Add call?

Because they depend on services that must be registered before the container is built. UseCors needs the policy configuration from AddCors, UseAuthentication needs the registered schemes and handlers. Since builder.Build() freezes the service collection, those registrations have to happen in the first phase of Program.cs. Forgetting produces a startup exception that names the missing Add method, so it is at least a clear failure.

Q: What is the difference between response caching and output caching?

Response caching only sets HTTP cache headers and relies on the client or an intermediate proxy to honour them — you are asking someone else to cache. Output caching, added in .NET 7, stores the response on the server, so you control it: it works regardless of client behaviour, applies to authenticated requests, and supports invalidation by tag. For server-side caching that you actually control, output caching is the one you want.

Q: Why is EnableForHttps off by default for response compression?

Because of the BREACH and CRIME attack class, where an attacker who can inject content into a response and observe its compressed size can infer secrets in that same response. Compressing over HTTPS is generally fine for JSON APIs that do not reflect secrets back, and genuinely risky for pages that echo tokens. Worth adding that if a reverse proxy or CDN is already compressing, doing it in the application as well is just wasted CPU.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting the matching Add call throws at startup — but only for middleware that needs one.
  • UseHsts in development can lock you out of http://localhost for months, across projects.
  • UseHttpsRedirection behind a TLS proxy causes an infinite redirect loop.
  • UseRateLimiter before UseForwardedHeaders rate-limits the proxy, so all clients share one bucket.
  • UseSession makes the app stateful, breaking horizontal scaling without a distributed cache.
  • Compressing in both the app and the proxy wastes CPU for no benefit.
  • A bare 404 has an empty body unless you add UseStatusCodePages.
  • Nothing is on by default. Missing UseAuthentication means every [Authorize] returns 401 silently.

docs.title: 5.11 — Global Exception-Handling Middleware
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.10 Built-in middleware · Next: 5.12 IExceptionHandler

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Global exception handling means catching unhandled exceptions in one place — the outermost middleware — instead of wrapping every controller action in try/catch.

  • It works because the pipeline is nested: middleware at the top wraps everything below it, exactly like a try/catch around the rest.
  • It must be registered first, or it only protects what comes after it.
  • Never send exception details to the client. Log the detail; return something generic.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Global exception handling a pattern One place catching unhandled exceptions from the whole application. UseExceptionHandler a middleware method The built-in handler. Catches exceptions from below and produces a response. UseDeveloperExceptionPage a middleware method Full stack trace in the browser. Development only. ProblemDetails a class The RFC 7807 standard error shape for HTTP APIs. See 10.8. AddProblemDetails() a registration method Makes the framework produce ProblemDetails bodies automatically. IExceptionHandlerFeature an interface How the error handler retrieves the exception that occurred. UseStatusCodePages a middleware method Adds a body to bare status-code responses like a 404 with no content. Re-execute pipeline a behaviour UseExceptionHandler("/error") re-runs the pipeline against that path. IExceptionHandler an interface (.NET 8+) The modern, typed way to handle exceptions. See 5.12. Information disclosure a vulnerability class Leaking internal detail — stack traces, table names, file paths — to a caller.

docs.title: Why one place, not many
docs.text:
Without global handling, every action needs its own try/catch:

[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Get(Guid id)
{
    try
    {
        return Ok(await _service.GetAsync(id));
    }
    catch (NotFoundException)
    {
        return NotFound();
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Failed");
        return StatusCode(500);
    }
}

Repeated across forty actions, that is forty chances to format an error differently, forty chances to forget logging, and a lot of noise around three lines of actual work.

Global handling collapses it to one place, and the actions get to be honest about what they do:

[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Get(Guid id)
    => Ok(await _service.GetAsync(id));      // exceptions handled elsewhere

docs.title: Why it works — the nesting
docs.text:
From 5.1: each middleware wraps everything below it, structurally identical to nested try/finally blocks.

So a middleware near the top that wraps await next() in a try/catch catches exceptions thrown anywhere downstream — in another middleware, in a filter, in a controller, in a repository, in EF Core.

flowchart TD
    A["Exception handler<br/>try { ... } catch { ... }"] --> B["Auth middleware"]
    B --> C["Controller action"]
    C --> D["Service"]
    D --> E["Repository throws 💥"]
    E -.->|"exception propagates UP"| A

This is also why registration order is not optional. An exception handler registered last sits below everything, so nothing above it is protected.

A picture: a safety net under a trapeze. It has to be under the whole act, not under the last three metres.

docs.title: The simple version — the built-in handler
docs.text:
var app = builder.Build();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();     // full detail, locally only
}
else
{
    app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");   // generic response
    app.UseHsts();
}

UseExceptionHandler("/error") catches the exception, then re-executes the pipeline against /error, so an endpoint at that path produces the response:

app.Map("/error", (HttpContext context) =>
{
    var feature = context.Features.Get<IExceptionHandlerFeature>();
    var exception = feature?.Error;

    // Log the detail — this goes to YOUR logs, not the client
    // ...

    return Results.Problem(
        title: "An unexpected error occurred",
        statusCode: StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError);
        // deliberately NO detail, NO stack trace
});

Since .NET 8 there is a simpler form that produces ProblemDetails automatically:

builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();
// ...
app.UseExceptionHandler();      // no path needed

docs.title: ⚠️ The developer exception page is a production hazard
docs.text:
app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();

It renders the stack trace, source snippets, request headers, and all environment variables into the browser. Environment variables routinely hold connection strings and API keys.

So if anything accidentally sets ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development on a deployed system, any error hands an attacker your secrets. That happens through copied Dockerfiles and unset Helm values more often than people expect — 4.7.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
The built-in handler covers most cases. A custom one is worth it when you need to map specific exception types to specific status codes:

internal class ExceptionHandlingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware> logger,
    IHostEnvironment env)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        try
        {
            await next(context);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) when (context.RequestAborted.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            // The client went away. Normal traffic, not an error.
            logger.LogInformation("Request cancelled by client: {Path}", context.Request.Path);
            // No response — nobody is listening
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            await HandleAsync(context, ex);
        }
    }

    private async Task HandleAsync(HttpContext context, Exception ex)
    {
        // ⚠️ If the response already started we cannot change it
        if (context.Response.HasStarted)
        {
            logger.LogError(ex, "Exception after response started — cannot format it");
            throw ex;          // let the server abort the connection
        }

        var (status, title) = ex switch
        {
            NotFoundException            => (StatusCodes.Status404NotFound, "Resource not found"),
            ValidationException          => (StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest, "Validation failed"),
            UnauthorizedAccessException  => (StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden, "Forbidden"),
            ConcurrencyException         => (StatusCodes.Status409Conflict, "Conflict"),
            _                            => (StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError,
                                             "An unexpected error occurred")
        };

        // Log at the right level — 4xx is client error, 5xx is ours
        if (status >= 500)
            logger.LogError(ex, "Unhandled exception on {Path}", context.Request.Path);
        else
            logger.LogWarning(ex, "Handled {Type} on {Path}",
                ex.GetType().Name, context.Request.Path);

        var problem = new ProblemDetails
        {
            Status   = status,
            Title    = title,
            Instance = context.Request.Path,
            // Only include real detail outside production
            Detail   = env.IsDevelopment() ? ex.ToString() : null
        };

        // Always give the client something to quote in a support ticket
        problem.Extensions["traceId"] = Activity.Current?.Id ?? context.TraceIdentifier;

        context.Response.Clear();
        context.Response.StatusCode = status;
        context.Response.ContentType = "application/problem+json";

        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(problem, context.RequestAborted);
    }
}

Five decisions in that code worth explaining in an interview:

Cancellation is handled separately. A user closing a tab produces OperationCanceledException. Logging that at error level fills your dashboards with noise that hides real failures (2.14).

HasStarted is checked. If bytes have already gone out, the status code and headers are on the wire and cannot be changed (5.8). The honest response is to let the connection abort rather than produce a corrupted body.

Log level depends on status. A 404 is the client asking for something that does not exist — a warning at most. A 500 is your bug and belongs at error level.

Detail is environment-gated. Stack traces never reach a production client.

A trace ID is always included. The client cannot see what went wrong, but they can quote an ID that lets you find it in your logs immediately. That single field turns "the site is broken" into a searchable incident.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what it cannot catch
docs.text:
Middleware only catches exceptions from inside the pipeline. Not:

Where Why not What to do Startup, before app.Run() The pipeline does not exist yet try/catch in Program.cs; log and exit Background services Separate execution path try/catch inside ExecuteAsync (21.1) Fire-and-forget tasks Nobody awaits them Do not use them (2.15) Middleware registered above it Not wrapped by it Register the handler first After the response started Cannot change what is sent Check HasStarted

For startup:

try
{
    var app = builder.Build();
    // ... pipeline ...
    app.Run();
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    Log.Fatal(ex, "Application failed to start");
    throw;
}
finally
{
    Log.CloseAndFlush();      // ensure buffered logs are written before exit
}

That CloseAndFlush matters with Serilog and similar — a crash during startup otherwise loses the log entry explaining why.

docs.title: Do not forget UseStatusCodePages
docs.text:
Exception handling covers thrown exceptions. It does not cover a bare 404 from routing, which has an empty body:

app.UseStatusCodePages();      // gives 404s and 401s a body

Without it, an API client requesting a non-existent route gets a 404 with nothing in it, which breaks clients expecting JSON.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The complete production setup:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();      // standard error shape everywhere
builder.Services.AddControllers();

var app = builder.Build();

// FIRST — wraps everything below
if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
}
else
{
    app.UseMiddleware<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware>();
    app.UseHsts();
}

app.UseStatusCodePages();                  // bodies for bare 404s
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Controllers can now be honest:

[HttpGet("{id:guid}")]
public async Task<ActionResult<OrderDto>> Get(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Throws NotFoundException if missing. The middleware turns it into a 404.
    var order = await _orders.GetAsync(id, ct);
    return Ok(order);
}

No try/catch, no repeated error formatting, and every error in the application comes out the same shape.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you handle exceptions globally in ASP.NET Core?

With middleware registered at the top of the pipeline that wraps await next() in a try/catch. Because the pipeline is nested — each middleware wraps everything below it — a handler at the top catches exceptions thrown anywhere downstream, in other middleware, filters, controllers or data access. You either use the built-in UseExceptionHandler, or write your own when you need to map specific exception types to specific status codes. The critical part is that it must be registered first, since it can only protect what comes after it.

Q: What should the response contain?

Nothing internal. Stack traces, exception messages, table names and file paths all help an attacker and mean nothing to a legitimate client. I log the full detail server-side and return a generic ProblemDetails body with a status code and a title. The one thing I always include is a trace identifier, so a user reporting a problem can quote an ID that lets me find the exact request in the logs — that turns "the site is broken" into something searchable. In development I include the full detail, gated on the environment check.

Q: What can global exception middleware not catch?

Anything outside the request pipeline. Exceptions during startup, before app.Run(), because the pipeline does not exist yet — those need a try/catch in Program.cs with a flush of the logger before exit. Exceptions in background services, which run on a separate path and need their own handling inside ExecuteAsync. Fire-and-forget tasks, since nobody observes them. And anything thrown by middleware registered above the handler. There is also the case where the response has already started, at which point the status code is on the wire and cannot be changed.

Q: Why treat OperationCanceledException specially?

Because it usually is not an error. When a user navigates away or closes a tab, the request is cancelled and that exception propagates. Logging it at error level fills your dashboards with noise that hides real failures, and there is no point writing a response because nobody is listening. I catch it separately, with a filter checking that the request was actually aborted, and log it at information level — while letting cancellations from our own internal timeouts still surface as genuine problems.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Registering the handler late leaves everything above it unprotected.
  • The developer exception page in production leaks environment variables including secrets.
  • Returning ex.Message to the client discloses internals — messages often contain table names and file paths.
  • Not checking HasStarted produces a second exception while handling the first.
  • Logging OperationCanceledException as an error buries real failures in noise.
  • Exception middleware does not cover startup or background services.
  • A bare 404 has an empty body without UseStatusCodePages.
  • Logging everything at error level makes the level meaningless — 4xx is usually a warning.
  • Not flushing the logger on startup failure loses the entry explaining the crash.

docs.title: 5.12 — IExceptionHandler and the Developer Exception Page
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.11 Exception middleware · Next: 5.13 Middleware vs filters

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
IExceptionHandler (.NET 8+) is the modern way to handle exceptions — a typed interface you implement and register in DI, instead of writing raw middleware.

  • You can register several handlers. They run in registration order until one returns true.
  • Returning true means "I handled it, stop". Returning false means "not mine, try the next one".
  • It plugs into UseExceptionHandler(), so ordering rules from 5.11 still apply.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means IExceptionHandler an interface (.NET 8+) One method: TryHandleAsync(HttpContext, Exception, CancellationToken) returning ValueTask<bool>. TryHandleAsync a method Where you handle the exception. Returns whether you handled it. true / false the return value true = handled, stop. false = pass to the next handler. AddExceptionHandler<T>() a registration method Registers a handler. Call order determines execution order. UseExceptionHandler() a middleware method Runs the registered handlers. Still required. AddProblemDetails() a registration method Provides the default ProblemDetails fallback when no handler claims the exception. IProblemDetailsService an interface Writes a ProblemDetails response with the configured conventions. Chain of responsibility a design pattern Several handlers offered the same item until one takes it. See 22.5. Developer exception page middleware Full diagnostics in the browser. Development only.

docs.title: Why it was added
docs.text:
Custom exception middleware (5.11) works, but it has drawbacks:

  • One class ends up handling every exception type, so it grows into a large switch.
  • It is raw middleware, so it does not participate in DI as a normal service.
  • Everyone writes their own slightly differently.

IExceptionHandler makes it a first-class, typed concept. You implement an interface, register it, and can split handling across several small classes — one per concern.

A picture: a lost-property desk with several specialists. The first asks "is it a phone?" and takes it if so. Otherwise it passes down the line. The last one accepts anything so nothing is left unhandled.

That is the chain of responsibility pattern, and it is exactly how the handler list works.

docs.title: The simple version
docs.text:
internal sealed class NotFoundExceptionHandler(ILogger<NotFoundExceptionHandler> logger)
    : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(
        HttpContext context,
        Exception exception,
        CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Not my type — let someone else deal with it
        if (exception is not NotFoundException notFound)
            return false;

        logger.LogWarning("Not found: {Message}", notFound.Message);

        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound;
        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new ProblemDetails
        {
            Status = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound,
            Title  = "Resource not found",
            Detail = notFound.Message          // safe — this message is ours
        }, ct);

        return true;                            // handled — stop here
    }
}

Registration takes two calls, and both are required:

builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<NotFoundExceptionHandler>();
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();          // the fallback

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseExceptionHandler();                     // still needed — runs the handlers

⚠️ Forgetting app.UseExceptionHandler() is the classic mistake. Registering handlers in DI does nothing on its own — the middleware is what invokes them. There is no warning; exceptions simply go unhandled.

docs.title: How it actually works — the chain
docs.text:
Register several and they run in order:

builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<ValidationExceptionHandler>();   // 1st
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<NotFoundExceptionHandler>();     // 2nd
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<ConcurrencyExceptionHandler>();  // 3rd
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<FallbackExceptionHandler>();     // last
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();

flowchart TD
    E["Exception thrown"] --> H1{"Validation handler<br/>mine?"}
    H1 -->|"true — handled"| D["Response sent"]
    H1 -->|"false"| H2{"NotFound handler<br/>mine?"}
    H2 -->|"true — handled"| D
    H2 -->|"false"| H3{"Fallback handler<br/>takes anything"}
    H3 -->|"true"| D

Order matters, and specific must come before general. A fallback handler that returns true for everything must be registered last, or nothing after it ever runs.

If every handler returns false, AddProblemDetails() provides a default ProblemDetails response — which is why registering it is worth doing even with a fallback handler of your own.

docs.title: IExceptionHandler vs custom middleware
docs.text:
Custom middleware IExceptionHandler Shape try/catch around next Implement an interface Typed No Yes Several handlers One class, big switch Several small classes Registered in DI No Yes — constructor injection works Testable in isolation Yes Yes, more easily Available since Always .NET 8

For a new .NET 8+ application, IExceptionHandler is the better default. Custom middleware remains correct for older versions and for cases needing control over the whole pipeline rather than just the exception.

docs.title: ⚠️ The developer exception page
docs.text:
The other half of this topic, and the security-critical half.

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();

It renders into the browser:

  • The full stack trace with source code snippets
  • Every request header, including Authorization
  • Query string and route values
  • Every environment variable

That last one is the problem. Environment variables in a deployed app hold connection strings, API keys and signing secrets — so any error on a system accidentally running as Development hands them to whoever triggered it.

That happens more often than people expect: a copied Dockerfile, a Helm value never overridden, a base image with the variable baked in (4.7).

Defence in depth — make production refuse to start if it detects the wrong environment:

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment() &&
    builder.Configuration["DeploymentRing"] is "production")
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "Development environment detected on a production deployment. Refusing to start.");
}

Failing loudly at startup beats running with full diagnostics exposed.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what IExceptionHandler does not do
docs.text:
It does not run for non-exception errors. A bare 404 from routing throws nothing, so no handler runs. You still need UseStatusCodePages() (5.11).

It cannot help once the response has started. If bytes are already on the wire the status code is fixed. Check HasStarted in your handler and return false so the framework aborts the connection rather than producing a corrupted body.

It does not catch exceptions outside the pipeline — startup, background services, fire-and-forget. Same limits as any exception middleware.

Cancellation still needs care. OperationCanceledException from a client disconnect will reach your handlers. Handle it explicitly and log at information level, or your dashboards fill with false errors (2.14).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A complete, production-shaped setup.

A specific handler:

internal sealed class ValidationExceptionHandler(
    ILogger<ValidationExceptionHandler> logger) : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(
        HttpContext context, Exception exception, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (exception is not ValidationException validation)
            return false;

        logger.LogInformation("Validation failed on {Path}", context.Request.Path);

        var problem = new ValidationProblemDetails(validation.Errors)
        {
            Status = StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest,
            Title  = "One or more validation errors occurred",
            Instance = context.Request.Path
        };

        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest;
        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(problem, ct);
        return true;
    }
}

The fallback, registered last:

internal sealed class FallbackExceptionHandler(
    ILogger<FallbackExceptionHandler> logger,
    IProblemDetailsService problemDetails,
    IHostEnvironment env) : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(
        HttpContext context, Exception exception, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Client went away — normal, and nobody is listening for a response
        if (exception is OperationCanceledException &&
            context.RequestAborted.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            logger.LogInformation("Request cancelled: {Path}", context.Request.Path);
            return true;
        }

        // Too late to change the response
        if (context.Response.HasStarted)
        {
            logger.LogError(exception, "Exception after response started");
            return false;                     // let the connection abort
        }

        logger.LogError(exception, "Unhandled exception on {Path}", context.Request.Path);

        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError;

        return await problemDetails.TryWriteAsync(new ProblemDetailsContext
        {
            HttpContext = context,
            Exception = exception,
            ProblemDetails =
            {
                Status = StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError,
                Title  = "An unexpected error occurred",
                Detail = env.IsDevelopment() ? exception.ToString() : null
            }
        });
    }
}

Wiring it up:

builder.Services.AddProblemDetails(options =>
{
    // Add a trace id to EVERY problem response, however it was produced
    options.CustomizeProblemDetails = ctx =>
    {
        ctx.ProblemDetails.Extensions["traceId"] =
            Activity.Current?.Id ?? ctx.HttpContext.TraceIdentifier;
    };
});

// Order matters — specific first, fallback last
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<ValidationExceptionHandler>();
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<NotFoundExceptionHandler>();
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<FallbackExceptionHandler>();

var app = builder.Build();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
else
    app.UseExceptionHandler();        // ← without this, none of the above runs

app.UseStatusCodePages();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();

That CustomizeProblemDetails callback is worth knowing. It applies to every problem response — including automatic 400s from model validation — so every error your API produces carries a trace ID with no per-handler code.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is IExceptionHandler and how does it differ from custom exception middleware?

It is an interface added in .NET 8 with a single TryHandleAsync method that returns a bool saying whether it handled the exception. You implement it, register it with AddExceptionHandler, and UseExceptionHandler() invokes the registered handlers in order until one returns true. The advantages over raw middleware are that it is typed rather than a try/catch you write yourself, it is a normal DI service so constructor injection works, and you can split handling across several small classes — one per exception category — instead of one class with a growing switch statement.

Q: How does the chain work?

Handlers run in registration order. Each is offered the exception and returns true if it handled it, which stops the chain, or false to pass it along. It is the chain of responsibility pattern. The important consequence is that specific handlers must be registered before general ones — a fallback that returns true for everything has to be last, or nothing after it ever executes. If every handler returns false, AddProblemDetails supplies a default response, which is why registering it is worthwhile even when you have your own fallback.

Q: What is the most common mistake when using it?

Registering the handlers but forgetting app.UseExceptionHandler(). The handlers exist in the container and are never invoked, because that middleware is what runs them, and there is no warning — exceptions simply go unhandled and you get raw 500s. The second most common is getting the registration order wrong, putting a catch-all handler before the specific ones.

Q: Why is the developer exception page dangerous?

Because it renders far more than a stack trace — it includes every request header including Authorization, and every environment variable. In a deployed application those variables hold connection strings, API keys and signing secrets, so any error on a system accidentally running as Development hands them to whoever triggered it. That misconfiguration happens through copied Dockerfiles and unset Helm values more often than people expect, so beyond gating it on the environment check I would have production refuse to start if it detects a Development environment name.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting app.UseExceptionHandler(). Handlers registered in DI do nothing without it.
  • Registering a catch-all handler before specific ones makes the specific ones unreachable.
  • Returning true without writing a response produces an empty 200.
  • The developer exception page leaks environment variables, which contain secrets.
  • It does not run for non-exception errors like a bare 404. Add UseStatusCodePages.
  • It cannot help after the response has started. Check HasStarted and return false.
  • Cancellation reaches your handlers and will be logged as an error unless you handle it.
  • `.NET 8+ only. Older projects need custom middleware (5.11).
