docs.title: 5.13 — Middleware vs Filters
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.12 IExceptionHandler · Next: 5.14 Logging middleware

Markers: 🔥 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Both wrap a request and both can run code before and after. The difference is where they sit and what they know.

  • Middleware runs for every request, including static files and 404s. It knows nothing about which action was selected.
  • Filters run inside MVC, only for matched actions. They know the action, its arguments and its return value.
  • The rule: if you need to know which action ran, use a filter. Otherwise use middleware.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Middleware a pipeline component Runs for every request that reaches it. See 5.1. Filter an MVC component Runs inside the endpoint, around action execution. See 12.1. Filter pipeline a nested pipeline Authorization → Resource → Action → Result filters, inside the endpoint. ActionExecutingContext a class Given to action filters. Exposes the bound arguments and the controller. ActionExecutedContext a class Exposes the result the action returned, and any exception. Model binding a framework step Converts the raw request into typed action parameters. Happens after middleware. Endpoint the matched handler The controller action or minimal API delegate selected by routing. Endpoint filter a minimal API concept (.NET 7+) The minimal API equivalent of an action filter. See 12.7. Cross-cutting concern a design term Something needed across many places — logging, auth, caching.

docs.title: Where each one sits
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    R["Request arrives"] --> M1["Middleware: exception handler"]
    M1 --> M2["Middleware: static files"]
    M2 --> M3["Middleware: routing — endpoint selected"]
    M3 --> M4["Middleware: authentication / authorization"]
    M4 --> E["ENDPOINT begins"]
    E --> F1["Filter: authorization"]
    F1 --> F2["Filter: resource"]
    F2 --> MB["Model binding"]
    MB --> F3["Filter: action"]
    F3 --> A["YOUR ACTION METHOD"]
    A --> F4["Filter: result"]
    F4 --> E2["endpoint ends"]
    E2 --> M4

Filters live inside the endpoint step of the middleware pipeline. So the entire filter pipeline is nested inside the last middleware.

That single fact explains every difference between them.

docs.title: What each one knows
docs.text:
Middleware Filters Runs for static files ✅ ❌ Runs for a 404 (no route matched) ✅ ❌ Runs for every request ✅ Only matched actions Knows the selected action ❌ ✅ Sees bound arguments ❌ ✅ Sees the action's return value ❌ ✅ Can apply per-controller or per-action ❌ (only by path) ✅ by attribute Works with minimal APIs ✅ Endpoint filters instead Works outside MVC ✅ ❌

The two that matter most in practice: middleware runs for everything but knows nothing about your action, and filters know everything about your action but only run when one matched.

A picture: middleware is building security at the front door. Everyone entering passes through, and they have no idea which office you are visiting. Filters are the receptionist on your specific floor — they know exactly who you came to see, what appointment you have, and what you left with.

docs.title: The simple version — the decision
docs.text:
Ask one question: do I need to know which action was selected, or see its arguments or result?

Yes → filter:

  • Validating an action's bound model
  • Caching based on the action's return value
  • Auditing which action a user invoked, with parameters
  • Applying behaviour to some controllers but not others
  • Wrapping the action in a database transaction

No → middleware:

  • Logging every request, including static files and 404s
  • Global exception handling
  • Security headers
  • Correlation IDs
  • Compression, CORS, HTTPS redirection
  • Rate limiting by IP

docs.title: The most common wrong choice
docs.text:
Trying to validate a model in middleware. It cannot be done properly, because model binding has not happened yet:

// ✗ Middleware — the model does not exist yet
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    // You would have to read and parse the raw body yourself,
    // which also breaks model binding downstream — see 5.9
    await next();
});

// ✓ Filter — the model is already bound and validated
public class ValidationFilter : IActionFilter
{
    public void OnActionExecuting(ActionExecutingContext context)
    {
        if (!context.ModelState.IsValid)
        {
            context.Result = new BadRequestObjectResult(context.ModelState);
            // Setting Result short-circuits — the action never runs
        }
    }

    public void OnActionExecuted(ActionExecutedContext context) { }
}

context.ActionArguments gives you the bound parameters by name. Nothing in middleware can do that.

docs.title: The other common wrong choice
docs.text:
Putting request logging in a filter, then wondering why 404s and static files never appear.

A filter only runs when routing matched an action. A request to a non-existent URL never reaches one, so a filter-based logger silently misses exactly the requests you most want to see when debugging.

Request logging belongs in middleware — 5.14.

docs.title: How it actually works — the ordering consequence
docs.text:
Because filters are nested inside middleware, the unwinding order is strict:

Middleware A: before
  Middleware B: before
    Filter X: before
      ACTION
    Filter X: after
  Middleware B: after
Middleware A: after

Two consequences worth knowing:

Middleware always sees the final response. Even if a filter short-circuits by setting context.Result, middleware above still runs its "after" half and sees what was produced.

Filters can catch exceptions middleware never sees — an exception filter can handle an error and set a result, so the exception never propagates up to your global handler. That is why an exception filter and global exception middleware can conflict: whichever is innermost wins. See 12.5.

docs.title: The deeper detail — minimal APIs
docs.text:
Minimal APIs have no MVC filter pipeline. The equivalent is endpoint filters (.NET 7+):

app.MapPost("/orders", CreateOrder)
   .AddEndpointFilter<ValidationFilter>();

public class ValidationFilter : IEndpointFilter
{
    public async ValueTask<object?> InvokeAsync(
        EndpointFilterInvocationContext context,
        EndpointFilterDelegate next)
    {
        // context.Arguments holds the bound parameters
        var request = context.GetArgument<CreateOrderRequest>(0);

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.CustomerName))
            return Results.BadRequest("Customer name is required");

        return await next(context);
    }
}

Same idea, different API: they run after binding and know the arguments, but they are attached per-endpoint or per-route-group rather than by attribute.

So the full decision becomes:

Need Controllers Minimal APIs Every request, no action knowledge Middleware Middleware Action-aware, per-endpoint Filter Endpoint filter

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The same concern — auditing — done both ways, showing what each can and cannot see.

Middleware version — every request, but only raw data:

internal class AuditMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, IAuditLog audit)
    {
        await next(context);

        // We know the path, method and status. That is all.
        await audit.RecordAsync(new AuditEntry
        {
            Path   = context.Request.Path,
            Method = context.Request.Method,
            Status = context.Response.StatusCode,
            User   = context.User.Identity?.Name
            // ✗ Cannot record WHICH action ran, or with what arguments
        });
    }
}

Filter version — only matched actions, but full detail:

public class AuditFilter(IAuditLog audit) : IAsyncActionFilter
{
    public async Task OnActionExecutingAsync(
        ActionExecutingContext context, ActionExecutionDelegate next)
    {
        var descriptor = (ControllerActionDescriptor)context.ActionDescriptor;

        var executed = await next();      // run the action

        await audit.RecordAsync(new AuditEntry
        {
            Controller = descriptor.ControllerName,
            Action     = descriptor.ActionName,           // ✓ we know the action
            Arguments  = context.ActionArguments,         // ✓ and its bound arguments
            Succeeded  = executed.Exception is null,
            User       = context.HttpContext.User.Identity?.Name
        });
    }
}

// Applied selectively — impossible with middleware
[Audit]
[HttpPost("transfer")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Transfer(TransferRequest request) { }

That selectivity is the other big difference. Middleware applies to a path prefix at best; a filter is an attribute you put exactly where you want it.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between middleware and filters?

Position and knowledge. Middleware sits in the request pipeline and runs for every request that reaches it — including static files, 404s and anything that never matched a route — but it runs before model binding, so it knows nothing about which action was selected or what its arguments are. Filters run inside MVC, around action execution, so they only execute when routing matched an action, but they have full access to the action descriptor, the bound arguments and the return value. Structurally the entire filter pipeline is nested inside the endpoint step of the middleware pipeline, and that nesting explains every other difference.

Q: How do you decide which to use?

One question: do I need to know which action was selected, or see its bound arguments or result? If yes, it has to be a filter — model validation, caching on the return value, auditing which action ran with what parameters, or applying behaviour to specific controllers by attribute. If no, middleware is the right place and usually the better one, because it also covers requests that never reach an action. Global exception handling, correlation IDs, security headers and request logging all belong in middleware.

Q: What goes wrong if you put request logging in a filter?

You silently miss the requests you most want to see. Filters only run when routing matched an action, so a request to a URL that does not exist never reaches one — meaning your logs contain no 404s. The same applies to static file requests and to anything rejected by middleware higher up, like a rate-limited request or a failed authentication. Request logging belongs in middleware, registered early enough to see everything.

Q: How does this work with minimal APIs?

Minimal APIs have no MVC filter pipeline, so the equivalent is endpoint filters, added in .NET 7. You implement IEndpointFilter and attach it with AddEndpointFilter on an endpoint or a route group. They serve the same purpose — they run after model binding and can see the bound arguments through the invocation context — but they are attached per endpoint or group rather than by attribute on a controller.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Trying to validate a bound model in middleware. Binding has not happened yet; reading the body yourself also breaks binding downstream.
  • Request logging in a filter misses 404s, static files and anything rejected upstream.
  • Assuming filters run for every request. They only run for matched actions.
  • An exception filter can swallow an exception before global exception middleware sees it — whichever is innermost wins.
  • Middleware cannot be applied per-controller. Path-based branching is the closest, via UseWhen (5.3).
  • Filters do not exist for minimal APIs. Use endpoint filters.
  • Filters cannot run before routing, so they cannot influence which endpoint is chosen.

docs.title: 5.14 — Request/Response Logging Middleware
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 5. Middleware and the Request Pipeline Prev: 5.13 Middleware vs filters · Next: 6.1 IoC and DI

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Request logging middleware records what came in and what went out — path, method, status, duration — for every request.

  • It belongs in middleware, not a filter, so it also sees 404s, static files and rejected requests.
  • ASP.NET Core has UseHttpLogging() built in. Try it before writing your own.
  • ⚠️ Logging bodies and headers leaks credentials. That is the real risk in this topic.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Request logging a cross-cutting concern Recording each request's method, path, status and duration. UseHttpLogging() a middleware method The built-in logger. Configurable via AddHttpLogging. HttpLoggingFields an enum, flags Which parts to log — request path, headers, body, response status, and so on. Structured logging a logging style Logging named fields rather than an interpolated string, so they can be queried. Message template a log format string "{Method} {Path}" with values passed separately. Keeps fields queryable. Log scope a logging feature Attaches properties to every log entry written inside a block. BeginScope. Correlation ID a tracing value An identifier shared across services for one logical operation. Sampling a volume-control technique Logging a percentage of requests rather than all of them. Redaction a safety technique Replacing sensitive values with a placeholder before logging. W3CLogger built-in middleware Writes access logs in the standard W3C format to a file.

docs.title: Why it is middleware, not a filter
docs.text:
A filter only runs when routing matched an action (5.13). So a filter-based logger silently misses:

  • 404s — no action matched, so no filter ran
  • Static files — served and short-circuited before the endpoint
  • Rejected requests — rate limited, failed authentication, blocked by CORS
  • Exceptions in earlier middleware

Those are exactly the requests you most want when investigating a problem. Request logging belongs in middleware, registered early.

docs.title: ⚠️ The thing that actually matters here
docs.text:
Before any of the mechanics: request logging is the most common way applications leak credentials into their logs.

Headers contain Authorization: Bearer eyJ... and Cookie: session=.... Bodies contain passwords, card numbers and personal data. Query strings contain API keys and reset tokens.

Log those wholesale and you have written every secret your application handles into a system that is widely readable inside your company and retained for months. It is also a data-protection problem — under GDPR and similar rules, personal data in logs is personal data you are processing and must justify, secure and eventually delete.

A picture: a security camera pointed at the keypad. Recording who enters is sensible. Recording the code they typed is a liability.

Default to logging metadata, not content.

docs.title: The simple version — use the built-in one first
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddHttpLogging(options =>
{
    options.LoggingFields =
        HttpLoggingFields.RequestMethod |
        HttpLoggingFields.RequestPath |
        HttpLoggingFields.RequestQuery |
        HttpLoggingFields.ResponseStatusCode |
        HttpLoggingFields.Duration;

    // Headers are NOT logged unless explicitly allowed — a good default
    options.RequestHeaders.Add("X-Correlation-Id");
    options.ResponseHeaders.Add("X-Correlation-Id");
});

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpLogging();      // early, so it sees everything

⚠️ Note what is absent: no RequestBody or ResponseBody. Those fields exist, and the framework deliberately makes you opt in per header and per body because of the leak risk.

By default UseHttpLogging logs at Information, which is very high volume on a busy service. Adjust it:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpLogging.HttpLoggingMiddleware": "Warning"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: How it actually works — writing your own
docs.text:
You write your own when you need a specific shape, sampling, or enrichment the built-in one does not provide:

internal class RequestLoggingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<RequestLoggingMiddleware> logger)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

        try
        {
            await next(context);
        }
        finally
        {
            // finally, so we log even when an exception propagates
            var elapsed = Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start);

            // Level depends on outcome — 5xx is our problem, 4xx is theirs
            var level = context.Response.StatusCode switch
            {
                >= 500 => LogLevel.Error,
                >= 400 => LogLevel.Warning,
                _ when elapsed.TotalMilliseconds > 1000 => LogLevel.Warning,   // slow
                _ => LogLevel.Information
            };

            logger.Log(level,
                "{Method} {Path} responded {StatusCode} in {ElapsedMs:0.0}ms",
                context.Request.Method,
                context.Request.Path,
                context.Response.StatusCode,
                elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
        }
    }
}

Three deliberate choices:

finally — so a request that throws is still logged. Without it, the requests that failed are exactly the ones missing from your logs.

Level varies by outcome — if everything logs at Information, the level conveys nothing and you cannot alert on errors. A slow request also gets promoted to Warning, which is how you notice degradation before users complain.

A message template, not interpolation:

// ✗ One opaque string. You cannot query or aggregate it.
logger.LogInformation($"{method} {path} took {ms}ms");

// ✓ Named fields, queryable in your log system
logger.LogInformation("{Method} {Path} took {Ms}ms", method, path, ms);

That difference is what makes structured logging useful — you can ask "show me all requests to /api/orders slower than 2 seconds", which is impossible with pre-formatted strings. See 18.1.

docs.title: Correlation IDs and scopes
docs.text:
Better than logging fields per entry: put them in a scope so everything downstream inherits them.

internal class RequestContextLoggingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<RequestContextLoggingMiddleware> logger)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var correlationId = context.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault()
                            ?? context.TraceIdentifier;

        using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
        {
            ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId,
            ["UserId"] = context.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value ?? "anonymous"
        }))
        {
            await next(context);
        }
    }
}

Now every log line written anywhere in that request — in a controller, a service, EF Core — carries the correlation ID and user, with no extra code. Searching one ID reconstructs the whole request, and if the ID came from an upstream service, across services too. See 18.4.

docs.title: The deeper detail — volume and cost
docs.text:
On a service handling 1,000 requests per second, logging every request at Information produces 86 million entries a day. That has real consequences: ingestion cost in your log platform, storage, and slower queries when you actually need to search.

Three ways to control it:

Sample the successful ones:

var shouldLog =
    context.Response.StatusCode >= 400 ||                    // always log failures
    elapsed.TotalMilliseconds > 500 ||                       // always log slow ones
    Random.Shared.Next(100) < 5;                             // 5% of the rest

Exclude noise:

if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/healthz"))
{
    await next(context);
    return;               // health probes every 5s would dominate your logs
}

Raise the level of the built-in loggers in configuration, so framework chatter does not drown your own entries:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning",
      "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command": "Warning"
    }
  }
}

That EF Core line is worth knowing — at Information it logs every SQL statement, which is useful in development and overwhelming in production.

docs.title: If you must log bodies
docs.text:
Covered fully in 5.9, but the safety rules:

private static readonly string[] SensitiveKeys =
    ["password", "token", "secret", "apiKey", "cardNumber", "ssn", "authorization"];
  • Buffer selectively — by path, content type and size, never globally
  • Cap the size, so a large upload cannot force a large allocation
  • Log only on failure, which keeps volume manageable and diagnostic value high
  • Redact known sensitive fields, and log nothing rather than raw bytes if parsing fails
  • Gate the whole thing behind a config flag so it can be turned on and off without a deploy

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A production-shaped logger combining the above:

internal class RequestLoggingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    ILogger<RequestLoggingMiddleware> logger)
{
    private static readonly PathString[] Excluded =
        [new("/healthz"), new("/ready"), new("/metrics")];

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        // Skip high-frequency infrastructure endpoints entirely
        if (Excluded.Any(p => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments(p)))
        {
            await next(context);
            return;
        }

        var correlationId = context.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault()
                            ?? context.TraceIdentifier;

        context.Response.OnStarting(() =>
        {
            context.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"] = correlationId;
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        });

        using var scope = logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
        {
            ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId,
            ["UserId"] = context.User.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value ?? "anonymous",
            ["ClientIp"] = context.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "unknown"
        });

        var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

        try
        {
            await next(context);
        }
        finally
        {
            var elapsed = Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start);
            var status = context.Response.StatusCode;

            var level = status switch
            {
                >= 500 => LogLevel.Error,
                >= 400 => LogLevel.Warning,
                _ when elapsed.TotalMilliseconds > 1000 => LogLevel.Warning,
                _ => LogLevel.Information
            };

            logger.Log(level,
                "HTTP {Method} {Path} → {StatusCode} in {ElapsedMs:0.0}ms",
                context.Request.Method,
                context.Request.Path,        // note: Path, NOT QueryString — see traps
                status,
                elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
        }
    }
}

⚠️ Request.Path is logged, not Request.QueryString. Query strings routinely carry API keys, password-reset tokens and email addresses. If you need query parameters, log a specific allow-list of them rather than the whole string.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Should request logging be middleware or a filter?

Middleware, registered early. A filter only runs when routing matched an action, so it silently misses 404s, static file requests, and anything rejected upstream by rate limiting or authentication — which are exactly the requests you want when investigating a problem. Middleware sees everything that reaches it, and putting it near the top of the pipeline means it covers the whole request.

Q: What is the main risk with request logging?

Leaking credentials and personal data. Headers carry Authorization and Cookie, bodies carry passwords and card numbers, and query strings often carry API keys and reset tokens. Logging those wholesale writes every secret the application handles into a system that is widely readable and retained for months, and under data-protection rules personal data in logs is data you are processing and must justify. So I default to logging metadata — method, path, status, duration — and treat headers and bodies as opt-in with redaction.

Q: Why use a message template instead of string interpolation?

Because structured logging keeps the values as named, queryable fields. Writing logger.LogInformation("{Method} {Path} took {Ms}ms", method, path, ms) lets your log platform index those properties, so you can ask for all requests to a specific path slower than two seconds. With interpolation you get one opaque string per entry and no way to aggregate. It also allows the logging framework to skip formatting entirely when that level is disabled.

Q: How do you control log volume?

Three things. Exclude high-frequency infrastructure endpoints like health probes, which otherwise dominate the output since orchestrators poll every few seconds. Sample the successful requests — always log failures and slow requests, and a small percentage of the rest. And raise the level of noisy framework loggers in configuration, particularly Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command, which logs every SQL statement at Information level. At a thousand requests a second, logging everything is around eighty-six million entries a day, which costs real money and makes searching slower when you need it.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Logging in a filter misses 404s, static files and rejected requests.
  • Logging headers leaks Authorization and Cookie values.
  • Logging query strings leaks API keys and reset tokens. Log Path, not QueryString.
  • Logging without finally means failed requests — the important ones — are missing.
  • Everything at Information makes the level meaningless and prevents alerting.
  • String interpolation instead of a message template destroys queryability.
  • Health check endpoints dominate the logs unless excluded.
  • EF Core logs every SQL statement at Information. Raise it in production.
  • Buffering bodies for every request costs memory or disk on every request (5.9).

docs.title: 6.1 — Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 5.14 Logging middleware · Next: 6.2 The built-in container

Markers: 🔥 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Dependency Injection means a class does not create the things it needs — it asks for them in its constructor, and someone else supplies them.

  • The problem it solves: a class that uses new to build its dependencies is welded to them and cannot be tested or changed.
  • Inversion of Control is the general principle; DI is the specific technique.
  • In ASP.NET Core it is built into the framework, not a library you add.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Dependency a thing a class needs Any other object your class uses to do its job — a repository, a logger, an HTTP client. Dependency Injection (DI) a technique Supplying a class's dependencies from outside rather than letting it create them. Inversion of Control (IoC) a principle The framework calls your code, rather than your code calling the framework. DI is one form of it. IoC container an object The thing that knows how to build your objects and their dependencies. Also called a DI container. Constructor injection the main style Dependencies arrive as constructor parameters. The default in ASP.NET Core. Registration a setup step Telling the container "when someone asks for IFoo, give them Foo". Resolution a runtime step The container building an object and everything it needs. Composition root a place in your app The single spot where everything is wired together. In ASP.NET Core that is Program.cs. Tight coupling a design problem A class that cannot work without one specific other class. Dependency Inversion Principle the "D" in SOLID Depend on abstractions, not concrete types. Related but not the same as DI. Service DI terminology Anything registered in the container. Not necessarily a "service class".

docs.title: The problem: new is glue
docs.text:
Consider a class that creates what it needs:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly SqlOrderRepository _repo = new SqlOrderRepository();
    private readonly SmtpEmailSender _email = new SmtpEmailSender();

    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id)
    {
        var order = await _repo.GetAsync(id);
        order.Complete();
        await _repo.SaveAsync(order);
        await _email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Order complete");
    }
}

This looks fine and is genuinely difficult to work with. Four problems:

You cannot test it. Creating an OrderService creates a real SQL connection and a real SMTP client. A unit test would hit your database and send actual emails.

You cannot change it. Switching from SMTP to SendGrid means editing this class — and every other class that does the same thing.

You cannot configure it. The connection string is buried inside SqlOrderRepository's constructor, wherever that is.

It hides its dependencies. Reading the constructor tells you nothing. You have to read the whole class to discover it sends email.

docs.title: The fix: ask, do not create
docs.text:
public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, IEmailSender email)
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct);
        order.Complete();
        await repo.SaveAsync(order, ct);
        await email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Order complete", ct);
    }
}

The class now declares what it needs and lets someone else provide it. All four problems disappear:

  • Testable — pass in fakes, and the test touches no database and sends no email.
  • Changeable — swap the registration in one place; this class never changes.
  • Configurable — whoever builds the repository supplies the connection string.
  • Honest — the constructor is a complete list of what this class depends on.

A picture: a chef who buys their own ingredients versus one who is handed them.

The first has to go shopping mid-service, always uses the same supplier, and you cannot test the recipe without a real trip to the market. The second declares "I need two eggs and flour", and you can hand over real ingredients or plastic ones for a photo shoot. The recipe does not change either way.

docs.title: IoC versus DI
docs.text:
These get used interchangeably. They are not the same.

Inversion of Control is the broad principle: the framework calls you, you do not call the framework. You do not write a loop that accepts TCP connections — ASP.NET Core does that and calls your controller. Event handlers, template methods and middleware are all IoC.

Dependency Injection is one specific application of it: inverting control over object creation. Instead of your class deciding what to construct, something else decides and hands it over.

So: all DI is IoC. Not all IoC is DI.

⚠️ And a third thing that sounds the same: the Dependency Inversion Principle — the "D" in SOLID — says depend on abstractions rather than concrete types. That is about what you depend on. DI is about how you get it. You can do DI badly by injecting concrete classes, and you can follow dependency inversion without a container at all.

Being able to separate those three cleanly is a good senior-level signal — 22.1.

docs.title: The simple version — three steps
docs.text:
1. Depend on an interface:

public interface IEmailSender
{
    Task SendAsync(string to, string subject, string body, CancellationToken ct);
}

2. Ask for it in the constructor:

public class OrderService(IEmailSender email)
{
    // 'email' is usable anywhere in this class
}

3. Register the real implementation once, in Program.cs:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();

That is the whole pattern. ASP.NET Core does the rest.

docs.title: How it actually works — the container builds the graph
docs.text:
When something needs an OrderService, the container:

  1. Looks at its constructor and sees it needs IOrderRepository and IEmailSender
  2. Looks up what is registered for each
  3. Builds those — recursively, since they have their own dependencies
  4. Constructs the OrderService with them
flowchart TD
    A["OrdersController"] --> B["IOrderService<br/>→ OrderService"]
    B --> C["IOrderRepository<br/>→ EfOrderRepository"]
    B --> D["IEmailSender<br/>→ SendGridEmailSender"]
    C --> E["AppDbContext"]
    D --> F["HttpClient"]
    E --> G["Configuration"]

You wrote none of that wiring. You declared what each class needs, and the container worked out the order.

That graph is the real payoff. Adding a dependency to a class three levels down requires no change to anything above it.

docs.title: The composition root
docs.text:
All registration happens in one place — Program.cs (4.3). That is the composition root: the single spot where the application decides which concrete types to use.

Why it matters: everywhere else in your codebase depends only on interfaces. Change the implementation and exactly one line changes.

// The only place SendGrid is mentioned
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();

// Swapping providers is one line. No other file changes.
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, PostmarkEmailSender>();

docs.title: The deeper detail — what DI is not for
docs.text:
DI is a genuinely good default, and it is possible to overuse it.

⚠️ Not every class needs an interface. An interface with exactly one implementation, no test double and no plans for a second is ceremony without benefit:

// Probably unnecessary
public interface IOrderMapper { OrderDto Map(Order order); }
public class OrderMapper : IOrderMapper { }

If it is a pure function with no dependencies, a static method or a plain class is clearer. Add the interface when you actually need to substitute it.

⚠️ Do not inject value types or configuration primitives. Use the options pattern instead:

// ✗ awkward
public class Service(string connectionString) { }

// ✓ typed, validated, reloadable — see 7.6
public class Service(IOptions<DatabaseOptions> options) { }

⚠️ Too many constructor parameters is a design smell, not a DI problem. A class needing eight dependencies is doing eight things. The fix is splitting the class, not hiding the parameters behind a service locator (6.9).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The full picture, and why it pays off.

Production wiring:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

The same class in a test, with no database and no email:

[Fact]
public async Task CompleteAsync_sends_confirmation_email()
{
    var repo  = Substitute.For<IOrderRepository>();
    var email = Substitute.For<IEmailSender>();

    var order = new Order(Guid.NewGuid()) { CustomerEmail = "a@b.com" };
    repo.GetAsync(order.Id, Arg.Any<CancellationToken>()).Returns(order);

    var service = new OrderService(repo, email);

    await service.CompleteAsync(order.Id, CancellationToken.None);

    await email.Received(1).SendAsync("a@b.com", "Order complete",
        Arg.Any<string>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
}

That test runs in milliseconds and touches nothing external. With the new-everything version it would be impossible — you would need a real database and a real mail server, and the test would send an actual email every run.

That is the practical argument for DI, and the one worth giving in an interview.

And swapping an implementation for one environment:

if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, ConsoleEmailSender>();   // just logs
else
    builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();

No application code changes. OrderService has no idea which one it got.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is dependency injection and what problem does it solve?

It means a class declares what it needs in its constructor rather than creating it with new, and something else supplies those dependencies. The problem it solves is coupling. A class that constructs its own dependencies is welded to those specific implementations — you cannot unit test it without hitting a real database, you cannot swap an implementation without editing the class, and its constructor tells you nothing about what it actually uses. With injection the constructor becomes an honest list of requirements, and the decision about concrete types moves to one place.

Q: What is the difference between IoC and DI?

Inversion of Control is the broad principle that the framework calls your code rather than the other way round — middleware, event handlers and template methods are all examples. Dependency Injection is one specific application of it, where the thing being inverted is control over object creation. So all DI is IoC, but not all IoC is DI. Worth separating out a third term that sounds similar: the Dependency Inversion Principle from SOLID says depend on abstractions rather than concrete types, which is about what you depend on, whereas DI is about how you receive it.

Q: How does the container know how to build a class with several dependencies?

It inspects the constructor, sees the parameter types, looks up what is registered for each, and builds them recursively — so a controller needing a service that needs a repository that needs a DbContext is resolved as a whole graph. You never write that wiring; you declare each class's requirements and register the implementations once in Program.cs. The practical benefit is that adding a dependency to a class deep in the graph requires no change to anything above it.

Q: Does every class need an interface?

No, and adding one reflexively is a common overcorrection. An interface with a single implementation, no test double and no realistic second implementation is ceremony that adds a file and an indirection without buying anything. I add one when I actually need to substitute it in tests, when there genuinely are multiple implementations, or when I want a compiler-enforced boundary between layers. A pure mapping function with no dependencies is usually clearer as a plain class or a static method.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Confusing DI with the Dependency Inversion Principle. One is a technique, the other is a design rule about what you depend on.
  • Creating an interface for every class. One implementation and no test double means no benefit.
  • Injecting concrete classes technically works but loses most of the value.
  • Eight constructor parameters is a design smell, not a reason to switch to a service locator.
  • Injecting configuration as strings. Use IOptions<T> (7.6).
  • Registration must happen before builder.Build() (4.3).
  • DI does not make code good on its own. A badly designed class injected properly is still badly designed.

docs.title: 6.2 — The Built-in Container: IServiceCollection and IServiceProvider
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.1 IoC and DI · Next: 6.3 Service lifetimes

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core has a DI container built in. It has two halves, split by builder.Build().

  • IServiceCollection — the shopping list. You add registrations to it, before Build().
  • IServiceProvider — the built container. You resolve objects from it, after Build().
  • Once Build() runs, the collection is frozen. Adding more throws.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means IServiceCollection an interface The list of registrations. builder.Services is one. Write-only in practice. IServiceProvider an interface The built container. Resolves objects. app.Services is one. ServiceDescriptor a class One registration: service type, implementation type, and lifetime. Service type the key What you ask for — usually an interface, like IEmailSender. Implementation type the value What you get — the concrete class, like SendGridEmailSender. AddTransient<T> a method Register with transient lifetime — new instance every time. AddScoped<T> a method Register with scoped lifetime — one per request. AddSingleton<T> a method Register with singleton lifetime — one for the app. GetService<T>() a method Resolve, returning null if not registered. GetRequiredService<T>() a method Resolve, throwing if not registered. Preferred. builder.Build() a method Builds the provider from the collection and freezes it. Root provider the top-level IServiceProvider app.Services. Has no request scope.

docs.title: Two objects, two phases
docs.text:
Everything about the container follows from one split:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// ═══ PHASE 1 — IServiceCollection ═══
// "Here is what exists." Adding registrations.
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

var app = builder.Build();          // ← collection frozen, provider created

// ═══ PHASE 2 — IServiceProvider ═══
// "Give me one." Resolving objects.
var service = app.Services.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

A picture: a shopping list, then a kitchen.

IServiceCollection is the list — you write on it, you do not cook from it. IServiceProvider is the stocked kitchen — you take things out, you do not add to it.

builder.Build() is going shopping. After that, the list is done.

That is why adding a service after Build() throws with "Services cannot be added after the application is built". It is not an arbitrary restriction — the container has already been constructed from the registrations, and changing them afterwards would leave it inconsistent.

docs.title: The simple version — registering
docs.text:
Three lifetimes, three methods (6.3):

builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailFormatter, EmailFormatter>();   // new every time
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();    // one per request
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPriceCache, PriceCache>();           // one per app

Each has several overloads:

// Interface → implementation. The common case.
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

// Concrete type only — register a class as itself
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();

// A factory — when construction needs logic
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService>(sp =>
{
    var repo = sp.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();
    return new OrderService(repo, enableCache: true);
});

// An instance you already made. ⚠️ Singleton only, and YOU own disposal — see 6.10.
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IClock>(new SystemClock());

docs.title: Resolving
docs.text:
// Preferred — throws a clear exception if not registered
var service = provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

// Returns null if not registered — for genuinely optional dependencies
var optional = provider.GetService<IFeatureFlag>();

// All registrations for one type — see 6.7
var validators = provider.GetServices<IValidator>();

⚠️ Prefer GetRequiredService. GetService returning null means a missing registration surfaces later as a NullReferenceException somewhere unrelated, whereas GetRequiredService fails immediately and names the missing type.

docs.title: ⚠️ You rarely call these at all
docs.text:
This is worth stating plainly: in normal application code you do not touch IServiceProvider. You put dependencies in a constructor and the container supplies them.

// ✓ Normal — the container resolves the graph for you
public class OrdersController(IOrderService orders) : ControllerBase { }

// ✗ Reaching into the container manually — the service locator anti-pattern
public class OrdersController(IServiceProvider provider) : ControllerBase
{
    public IActionResult Get()
    {
        var orders = provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();   // don't
    }
}

The second hides dependencies — the constructor no longer tells you what the class needs — and turns a missing registration from a startup error into a runtime one. See 6.9.

Legitimate reasons to touch the provider directly: creating a scope in a background service (6.5), startup tasks in Program.cs, and writing a factory registration.

docs.title: How it actually works — what a registration is
docs.text:
Each call adds a ServiceDescriptor — a small record of three things:

public class ServiceDescriptor
{
    public Type ServiceType { get; }              // IOrderService
    public Type? ImplementationType { get; }      // OrderService
    public ServiceLifetime Lifetime { get; }      // Scoped
    // ...plus factory and instance variants
}

The collection is literally an IList<ServiceDescriptor>, which has two consequences worth knowing.

Registering the same service type twice does not replace — it appends. Both descriptors are in the list:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SmtpEmailSender>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();

// Resolving IEmailSender gives you SendGridEmailSender — the LAST one wins
// Resolving IEnumerable<IEmailSender> gives you BOTH

Last-one-wins is the rule for a single resolve. That is deliberate and useful — it is how you override a framework default — but it also means an accidental duplicate registration silently changes behaviour with no warning. See 6.6 for TryAdd, which exists precisely to avoid that.

And you can inspect or modify the list before Build():

// Replace an existing registration
builder.Services.RemoveAll<IEmailSender>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, FakeEmailSender>();

// Or replace in one call
builder.Services.Replace(
    ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IEmailSender, FakeEmailSender>());

That is exactly how WebApplicationFactory swaps real services for fakes in integration tests — 20.7.

docs.title: The deeper detail — validation options
docs.text:
Two settings turn silent DI bugs into startup failures:

builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(options =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes = true;      // catch captive dependencies
    options.ValidateOnBuild = true;     // catch unresolvable registrations
});

ValidateScopes detects a scoped service injected into a singleton — the captive dependency problem (6.4).

ValidateOnBuild walks every registration at startup and confirms it can actually be resolved, so a missing dependency fails immediately rather than on the first request that needs it.

⚠️ Both are enabled by default in Development only. That is precisely why these bugs reach production — the environment that would have caught them is the one you do not deploy. Enabling them everywhere costs a little startup time and is almost always worth it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic Program.cs showing the range of registration styles:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Simple interface → implementation
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

// Framework helpers that register several things at once
builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>          // registers as SCOPED
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IPaymentGateway, StripeGateway>();

// A factory — construction needs a decision
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IStorageProvider>(sp =>
{
    var config = sp.GetRequiredService<IConfiguration>();
    return config["Storage:Provider"] switch
    {
        "azure" => new AzureBlobStorage(config["Storage:ConnectionString"]!),
        "s3"    => new S3Storage(config["Storage:Bucket"]!),
        _       => new LocalFileStorage(config["Storage:Path"]!)
    };
});

// Options — typed configuration, not raw strings
builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"));

// Fail fast on bad wiring, in every environment
builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(o =>
{
    o.ValidateScopes = true;
    o.ValidateOnBuild = true;
});

var app = builder.Build();

// Startup work — needs a scope, because there is no request scope here. See 6.5.
using (var scope = app.Services.CreateScope())
{
    var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
    await db.Database.MigrateAsync();
}

app.Run();

Two things in that file are worth calling out.

AddDbContext registers as scoped — you do not choose the lifetime, and that is deliberate (13.2).

The startup scope is not optional. AppDbContext is scoped and app.Services is the root provider with no ambient scope, so resolving it directly throws.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between IServiceCollection and IServiceProvider?

They are the two halves of the container, split by builder.Build(). IServiceCollection is the list of registrations — you add to it during the first phase of Program.cs, saying what exists and with what lifetime. IServiceProvider is the built container that actually resolves objects, available after Build(). Once Build() runs the collection is frozen, which is why adding a service afterwards throws — the provider has already been constructed from those registrations.

Q: What happens if you register the same interface twice?

Both registrations stay in the list, because the collection is genuinely a list of descriptors rather than a dictionary. Resolving the single service gives you the last one registered, which is how you deliberately override a framework default. Resolving IEnumerable<T> of that type gives you all of them. The risk is that an accidental duplicate silently changes which implementation you get, with no warning — which is why TryAdd exists, to register only if nothing is there already.

Q: When would you resolve from IServiceProvider directly?

Rarely, and it is worth being suspicious when you see it. In normal application code you put dependencies in the constructor and let the container build the graph. The legitimate cases are creating a scope in a background service or a singleton that needs scoped work, running startup tasks in Program.cs before the app starts, and writing a factory registration. Injecting IServiceProvider into a controller to pull services out on demand is the service locator anti-pattern — it hides what the class depends on and turns a missing registration from a startup error into a runtime one.

Q: What do ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild do?

ValidateScopes detects captive dependencies — a scoped service injected into a singleton, which pins one request-lifetime object for the life of the application. ValidateOnBuild walks every registration at startup and verifies it can actually be resolved, so a missing dependency fails immediately instead of on the first request that hits that code path. The important detail is that both are enabled by default only in Development, which is exactly why those bugs survive into production. Turning them on in all environments costs a little startup time and catches a genuinely painful class of error.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Adding services after builder.Build() throws. The collection is frozen.
  • Duplicate registrations silently change behaviour — last one wins for a single resolve.
  • GetService returns null, so a missing registration surfaces later as a null reference. Prefer GetRequiredService.
  • Resolving a scoped service from app.Services throws. Create a scope first (6.5).
  • Injecting IServiceProvider into your classes is the service locator anti-pattern (6.9).
  • ValidateScopes is Development-only by default, so captive dependencies reach production.
  • An instance passed to AddSingleton(instance) is not disposed by the container — you own it (6.10).

docs.title: 6.3 — Service Lifetimes: Transient, Scoped, Singleton
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.2 The built-in container · Next: 6.4 Captive dependencies

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A lifetime answers one question: when someone asks for this service, does the container build a new one or hand back one it made earlier?

  • Transient — a new instance every time it is injected.
  • Scoped — one per scope, which in a web app means one per HTTP request.
  • Singleton — one for the entire application, shared by every request.

The rule that catches people: the consumer's lifetime wins. A transient injected into a singleton lives as long as the singleton.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Lifetime a registration setting How long an instance lives and how often a new one is made. Transient a lifetime A new instance for every injection. Never reused. Scoped a lifetime One instance per scope. In ASP.NET Core, one per HTTP request. Singleton a lifetime One instance for the whole application, created on first use. Scope an IServiceScope A bounded container that disposes what it created when it ends. See 6.5. Root scope the application-level scope app.Services. Lives for the whole app. Singletons live here. AddTransient<T> a method Register with transient lifetime. AddScoped<T> a method Register with scoped lifetime. AddSingleton<T> a method Register with singleton lifetime. Captive dependency a bug A shorter-lived service captured by a longer-lived one. See 6.4. ValidateScopes a container option Detects captive dependencies. Development-only by default.

docs.title: The one question a lifetime answers
docs.text:
Every registration has to answer: when someone asks for this, do I build a fresh one or reuse one I already have?

That is the whole idea. The three lifetimes are three answers.

A picture: three ways a restaurant handles items.

  • Transient is a paper napkin. Everyone gets a fresh one, every time. Cheap, disposable, no sharing.
  • Scoped is the bill for a table. One per table, shared by everyone sitting at it, closed when they leave. Two tables never share a bill.
  • Singleton is the espresso machine. One for the whole restaurant, used by everyone all day. It had better be able to handle several orders at once.

That last point is the crux of singleton — shared means concurrent.

docs.title: Why choosing wrong is dangerous
docs.text:
The reason interviewers ask is that the wrong lifetime produces bugs that do not appear in development.

With one developer clicking through the app, requests happen one at a time. A DbContext registered as a singleton looks fine — there is never a second concurrent request to expose the problem.

Under production load, fifty requests hit that shared DbContext simultaneously. It is not thread-safe, so its internal state corrupts, and its change tracker accumulates every entity it has ever seen (3.5).

The bug is invisible until the exact conditions you cannot easily reproduce.

docs.title: The simple version
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailFormatter, EmailFormatter>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPriceCache, PriceCache>();
Lifetime New instance when Disposed when Needs thread safety? Transient Every injection The owning scope ends Usually not Scoped Once per scope / request The request ends Not usually Singleton Once, on first use App shuts down Yes

docs.title: Seeing the difference
docs.text:
public class LifetimeDemo(
    ITransientService a, ITransientService b,
    IScopedService    c, IScopedService    d,
    ISingletonService e, ISingletonService f)
{
    // Within ONE request:
    //   a.Id != b.Id   — two separate instances
    //   c.Id == d.Id   — same instance
    //   e.Id == f.Id   — same instance
    //
    // On the NEXT request:
    //   c.Id is DIFFERENT — new scope, new instance
    //   e.Id is THE SAME  — singletons survive
}

That table is the whole behaviour. Everything else is consequences of it.

docs.title: ⚠️ The rule people get wrong: the consumer's lifetime wins
docs.text:
This is the part that separates a memorised answer from an understood one.

Lifetime describes how often the container creates an instance — not how long the result survives. Survival is decided by whoever holds the reference.

builder.Services.AddTransient<IReportBuilder, ReportBuilder>();   // "transient"
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ReportCache>();                     // holds one

public class ReportCache(IReportBuilder builder)     // singleton constructor
{
    // 'builder' is resolved ONCE, when the singleton is created.
    // It now lives for the life of the application.
    // "Transient" described how it was created, not how long it lasts.
}

So a transient inside a singleton is effectively a singleton. The word describes the container's creation policy, not a guarantee about lifespan.

This is the mechanism behind the captive dependency problem, which is important enough to have its own note — 6.4.

docs.title: How it actually works — what a scope is in a web app
docs.text:
A scope is a bounded sub-container that disposes everything it created when it ends (6.5).

ASP.NET Core creates one scope per HTTP request and disposes it when the response completes. That is why "scoped" and "per request" are used interchangeably — but they are not the same thing, and the difference matters:

flowchart TD
    R["Root container (app lifetime)"] --> S1["Singleton instances<br/>live here"]
    R --> Q1["Request 1 scope"]
    R --> Q2["Request 2 scope"]
    Q1 --> A1["Scoped instance A"]
    Q1 --> T1["Transient x2"]
    Q2 --> A2["Scoped instance B — different object"]
    Q2 --> T2["Transient x1"]

Outside an HTTP request there is no ambient scope. A BackgroundService, a hosted service, or startup code in Program.cs has none — so resolving a scoped service directly throws, and you must create a scope yourself.

docs.title: The deeper detail — choosing
docs.text:
Singleton when the service is stateless, or holds state that is genuinely meant to be shared and is thread-safe:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPriceCalculator, PriceCalculator>();     // stateless
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IMemoryCache, MemoryCache>();             // designed for sharing

Scoped for anything representing work on behalf of one request — a unit of work, the current user's context, a DbContext:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(...);      // registers as SCOPED automatically

Transient for cheap, stateless helpers where sharing buys nothing:

builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailFormatter, EmailFormatter>();

⚠️ Scoped is the right default in a web application. It matches the natural unit of work, avoids thread-safety questions entirely, and cleans up automatically. Reach for singleton when you can justify it and transient when the object is genuinely trivial.

⚠️ Transient is not free. Every injection allocates. A transient injected into ten services in one request is ten objects. For a class with no state that is fine; for anything holding a buffer or a connection it is waste.

⚠️ And a subtlety about transient disposal: a transient implementing IDisposable is tracked by the scope that created it and disposed when that scope ends — not when you finish using it. In a long-lived scope, transient disposables accumulate (6.10).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The realistic registration set for an API:

// SINGLETON — stateless or genuinely shared, and thread-safe
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPriceCalculator, PriceCalculator>();
builder.Services.AddMemoryCache();

// SCOPED — per-request work. The default for most application services.
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<ICurrentUser, HttpCurrentUser>();

// TRANSIENT — cheap, stateless helpers
builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailFormatter, EmailFormatter>();

docs.title: The background service case
docs.text:
A BackgroundService is a singleton with no ambient scope, so this is the one place you create scopes by hand:

public class OrderCleanupService(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory,
    ILogger<OrderCleanupService> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            // A FRESH scope per iteration — see the warning below
            using (var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope())
            {
                var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

                await db.Orders
                    .Where(o => o.ExpiresAt < DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)
                    .ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);
            }
            // scope disposed here — DbContext released

            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

⚠️ The scope must be inside the loop. Creating it outside gives you one DbContext for the service's entire lifetime — which is a singleton DbContext wearing a disguise, with the change tracker growing on every iteration. See 21.2.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain the three service lifetimes.

Transient gives you a new instance every time it is injected, so it suits cheap stateless helpers. Scoped gives you one instance per scope, and in a web application the framework creates a scope per HTTP request — so it is one per request, which is what you want for a DbContext or anything representing a unit of work. Singleton gives you one instance for the whole application, which is right for caches and stateless calculators, but it means the instance is shared across concurrent requests, so any mutable state has to be thread-safe.

Q: Is a transient service ever effectively a singleton?

Yes, and this is the part people miss. Lifetime is a property of the object graph, not just the registration. If a singleton takes a transient in its constructor, that transient is resolved once when the singleton is created and lives as long as it does. So "transient" describes how often the container creates an instance, not how long the result survives — survival is decided by whoever holds the reference. That is exactly the mechanism behind captive dependencies.

Q: Why is DbContext scoped rather than transient or singleton?

Because it represents a unit of work. Scoped means every repository and service handling one request shares the same context, so change tracking and SaveChanges cover the whole operation as one transaction. Transient would give each consumer its own context and its own separate transaction, defeating the purpose. Singleton would be worse — DbContext is not thread-safe, so concurrent requests would corrupt its internal state, and its change tracker would accumulate every entity it had ever loaded, which is a memory leak.

Q: What should you use as the default in a web application?

Scoped, for most application services. It matches the natural unit of work — one request — so thread safety stops being a question, and everything is cleaned up when the request ends. I would use singleton when the service is genuinely stateless or is designed for sharing and is thread-safe, and transient for trivial helpers where sharing buys nothing. Worth remembering that transient is not free either — each injection allocates, so a transient consumed by ten services in a request is ten objects.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "Scoped means one per class." It means one per scope. In a web request that is per request; outside one there is no ambient scope at all.
  • The consumer's lifetime wins. A transient inside a singleton lives as long as the singleton.
  • Injecting a scoped service into a singleton captures it forever (6.4).
  • ValidateScopes is Development-only by default, so the app can start cleanly in production and fail under load.
  • Singletons are shared across concurrent requests, so mutable state needs thread safety (2.18).
  • Transient disposables are held until the scope ends, not when you stop using them.
  • Creating a scope outside a background loop turns a scoped service into an application-lifetime one.
  • AddDbContext registers as scoped — you do not pick the lifetime, and overriding it is a mistake.

docs.title: 6.4 — The Captive Dependency Problem
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.3 Service lifetimes · Next: 6.5 Scopes

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A captive dependency is a short-lived service trapped inside a long-lived one — most often a scoped service injected into a singleton.

  • The singleton resolves it once and holds it forever, so a per-request object becomes an application-lifetime object.
  • With a DbContext that means a thread-safety bug and a memory leak at the same time.
  • The container detects it — but only in Development by default, which is exactly why it reaches production.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Captive dependency a bug A service held by something longer-lived than itself, so it never gets released. Lifetime mismatch the cause Injecting a shorter lifetime into a longer one. The rule a guideline A service may only depend on services with an equal or longer lifetime. ValidateScopes a container option Detects lifetime mismatches at resolution time. On by default in Development only. InvalidOperationException what it throws "Cannot consume scoped service X from singleton Y." IServiceScopeFactory an interface The safe way for a singleton to get scoped services — create a scope per operation. IServiceProvider an interface The container. Injecting the root one into a singleton is the common workaround, and a trap. Change tracker an EF Core component Holds every entity a DbContext has loaded. Grows without limit if the context is never disposed.

docs.title: The rule in one line
docs.text:
A service may only depend on services with an equal or longer lifetime.

Consumer May inject May not inject Singleton Singleton ⚠️ Scoped, Transient* Scoped Singleton, Scoped ⚠️ Transient* Transient Anything —

* Injecting a transient is legal and does not throw, but it becomes captive — see below.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text:
From 6.3: the consumer's lifetime wins. The container resolves a constructor parameter once, when it builds the consumer. If the consumer is a singleton, that happens once for the application.

builder.Services.AddScoped<AppDbContext>();          // "one per request"
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CacheWarmer>();        // one for the app

public class CacheWarmer(AppDbContext db)     // ⚠️ CAPTIVE
{
    // 'db' was resolved ONCE, when CacheWarmer was created.
    // It is now held for the entire application lifetime.
}

The DbContext was registered as scoped, and the registration is honoured — the container did create it inside a scope. The problem is that the singleton kept a reference to it after that scope ended.

A picture: a library book borrowed by someone who never returns it. The lending rules are fine. The book was meant to circulate. One person putting it on their permanent shelf breaks the system for everyone else.

docs.title: What actually breaks
docs.text:
The abstract rule matters less than the concrete damage. With a DbContext, three things go wrong at once.

1. It is not thread-safe. A singleton is shared by every concurrent request, so fifty requests use one DbContext simultaneously. EF Core detects some of this and throws "A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed" — but not reliably, and corruption can occur silently.

2. The change tracker grows forever. A DbContext remembers every entity it has loaded so it can detect changes. Normally it is disposed at the end of the request and that memory is released. Held forever, it accumulates every entity the application has ever touched — a textbook memory leak (3.5).

3. You read stale data. Because the change tracker caches entities by key, a query that returns a row already tracked gives you the cached version, not the current database state. So an update made by another request is invisible.

⚠️ All three get worse over time and under load, which is why this bug is a production problem rather than a development one.

docs.title: The transient case, which does not throw
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddTransient<IReportBuilder, ReportBuilder>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ReportScheduler>();

public class ReportScheduler(IReportBuilder builder)
{
    // No exception. Ever. But 'builder' lives for the app's lifetime.
}

ValidateScopes does not catch this, because transient into singleton is technically legal — the container will happily create one and hand it over.

But the effect is the same: a service you declared "new every time" is now a de facto singleton. If it holds a buffer, a connection or any state, you have a leak with no warning at all.

This is the sneakier half of the problem, and worth mentioning in an interview because most people only know the scoped case.

docs.title: How it actually works — detection
docs.text:
The container can catch the scoped case:

builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(options =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes  = true;      // catch lifetime mismatches
    options.ValidateOnBuild = true;      // check at startup, not first use
});

With ValidateScopes on, resolving the singleton throws:

InvalidOperationException: Cannot consume scoped service 'AppDbContext' from singleton 'CacheWarmer'.

That message is clear and names both types.

⚠️ The critical detail: both options default to on in Development and off elsewhere.

So the environment that would have caught the bug is the one you never deploy. The app starts cleanly in production and misbehaves under concurrency.

Turn both on in every environment. ValidateOnBuild costs a little startup time and moves the failure from "the first request that happens to hit this path" to "the moment the app starts", which is a much better place to find out.

docs.title: Fix 1 — inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope ⭐
docs.text:
The correct answer when a singleton genuinely needs a scoped service:

public class CacheWarmer(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) : IHostedService
{
    public async Task StartAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // A scope for THIS operation only
        using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

        var prices = await db.Prices.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);
        // ...
    }   // scope disposed — DbContext released

    public Task StopAsync(CancellationToken ct) => Task.CompletedTask;
}

The singleton holds the factory — which is itself a singleton, so no mismatch — and creates a short-lived scope whenever it needs scoped work. See 6.5.

docs.title: Fix 2 — reconsider the lifetime
docs.text:
Often the singleton did not need to be one:

// If it has no expensive state, scoped is simpler and has no mismatch
builder.Services.AddScoped<CacheWarmer>();

⚠️ Ask why it is a singleton at all. People reach for singleton believing it is faster, but scoped service creation is very cheap. Singleton earns its place when there is genuinely shared state — a cache, a connection pool — not by default.

docs.title: ⚠️ Fix 3 — the one that looks right and is not
docs.text:
// ✗ WRONG — injecting the root IServiceProvider
public class CacheWarmer(IServiceProvider provider)
{
    public async Task WarmAsync()
    {
        var db = provider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();   // ⚠️ from the ROOT
    }
}

This compiles, does not throw ValidateScopes, and is still broken. Resolving a scoped service from the root provider creates it in the root scope — which lives for the whole application. You have recreated exactly the same captive dependency, just later and less visibly.

IServiceProvider gives you the root. IServiceScopeFactory lets you make a real scope. That distinction is the point.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The realistic version — a background service, which is where this comes up most:

// ✗ BROKEN — DbContext captured for the life of the application
public class OrderCleanupService(AppDbContext db) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await db.Orders.Where(o => o.IsExpired).ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

BackgroundService is registered as a singleton, so this is a captive DbContext — and it runs for weeks.

// ✓ CORRECT — a fresh scope per iteration
public class OrderCleanupService(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory,
    ILogger<OrderCleanupService> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            try
            {
                using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();      // INSIDE the loop
                var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

                var removed = await db.Orders
                    .Where(o => o.ExpiresAt < DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)
                    .ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);

                logger.LogInformation("Removed {Count} expired orders", removed);
            }
            catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                break;                                             // shutting down — normal
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Cleanup failed, will retry");
            }

            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

⚠️ The scope goes inside the loop, not outside. A scope created once outside gives you a single DbContext for the service's entire life — the same bug, moved. Each iteration gets a fresh context that is disposed when the iteration ends. See 21.2.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a captive dependency?

It is a service held by something longer-lived than itself — most commonly a scoped service injected into a singleton. The container resolves constructor parameters once when it builds the consumer, so a singleton resolves its dependencies a single time and keeps them for the life of the application. A service registered as "one per request" becomes an application-lifetime object. The rule it violates is that a service should only depend on things with an equal or longer lifetime.

Q: What actually goes wrong with a captive DbContext?

Three things at once. It is not thread-safe, and a singleton is shared across concurrent requests, so simultaneous operations corrupt its state — sometimes surfacing as "a second operation was started on this context", sometimes silently. Its change tracker holds every entity it has ever loaded and is never disposed, so memory grows without limit. And because the tracker caches entities by key, queries return the cached version rather than current database state, so you read stale data. All three get worse under load, which is why it is a production bug rather than a development one.

Q: How do you fix it?

If the singleton genuinely needs scoped work, inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per operation — the factory is itself a singleton so there is no mismatch, and the scope is disposed when the operation finishes. Often the better answer is to question why the consumer is a singleton at all, since scoped service creation is very cheap and singleton should be reserved for genuinely shared state. The fix to avoid is injecting IServiceProvider and resolving from it, because that is the root provider — the scoped service is then created in the root scope and you have recreated the same problem less visibly.

Q: Why does this reach production so often?

Because the detection is enabled in Development only. ValidateScopes catches the mismatch and throws a clear exception naming both types, but it defaults to on in Development and off everywhere else — so the environment that would have caught it is the one you never deploy. The app starts cleanly in production and only misbehaves under concurrency. I would turn both ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild on in all environments; the startup cost is small and it moves the failure to a much better place.

Q: Can a transient be captive?

Yes, and this case is quieter because nothing throws. Injecting a transient into a singleton is technically legal, so ValidateScopes says nothing — but the transient is still resolved once and held for the application's lifetime. If it holds a buffer, a connection or any state, that is a leak with no warning at all. Most people only know the scoped case, so it is worth being aware of.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• ValidateScopes is Development-only by default. Turn it on everywhere.
  • Transient into singleton does not throw but is still captive.
  • Injecting IServiceProvider gives you the root scope, so resolving scoped services from it recreates the bug. Use IServiceScopeFactory.
  • Creating a scope outside a loop captures the service for the whole loop.
  • BackgroundService is a singleton, so this is the most common place it appears.
  • Conventional middleware is also a singleton — same problem, same fix (5.5).
  • IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, unlike IOptions<T>, so it cannot go in a singleton constructor (7.6).
