docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A scope is a temporary sub-container. Services resolved inside it are shared within it, and everything it created is disposed when the scope ends.

  • ASP.NET Core creates one scope per HTTP request automatically and disposes it when the response completes.
  • Outside a request there is no scope — background services, startup code and singletons have none.
  • Create one with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope(), and always wrap it in using.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Scope an IServiceScope A temporary sub-container. Disposable. Owns what it creates. IServiceScopeFactory an interface Creates scopes. Itself a singleton, so safe to inject anywhere. CreateScope() a method Creates a new IServiceScope. Must be disposed. CreateAsyncScope() a method Same, but supports IAsyncDisposable services. Use with await using. scope.ServiceProvider a property The scoped container. Resolve from this, not the root. Root scope the application container app.Services. Lives for the whole application. Ambient scope the one you are already in A request has one; a background service does not. RequestServices a property on HttpContext The current request's scope. Already exists — do not create another. ObjectDisposedException an exception What you get from using a service after its scope was disposed.

docs.title: What a scope actually is
docs.text:
A scope is a box with a lifetime. Ask it for a scoped service and it either builds one and remembers it, or hands back the one it already built. When the box is thrown away, everything disposable inside it is disposed.

That is the entire mechanism, and it explains both what "scoped" means and why disposal is automatic.

A picture: a hotel room key card. It works for the length of your stay, opens the same room every time, and stops working when you check out. Another guest's card opens a different room. The hotel — the root container — outlives every card.

docs.title: Where scopes come from
docs.text:
In a web application you almost never create one, because the framework does it for you:

Request arrives
  → framework creates a scope
    → middleware, filters and your action all resolve from it
      → one DbContext, one repository, shared by all of them
  → response completes
  → scope disposed → DbContext disposed

That is why "scoped" and "per request" are used interchangeably. But they are not the same thing, and the difference is the whole point of this note:

Scoped means per scope. A request happens to be a scope. Not everything is a request.

Background services, hosted services and startup code have no ambient scope. So resolving a scoped service there throws:

InvalidOperationException: Cannot resolve scoped service 'AppDbContext' from root provider.

docs.title: The simple version — creating one
docs.text:
public class ReportGenerator(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory)
{
    public async Task GenerateAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();

        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
        var orders = await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);

        // ... use them ...

    }   // scope disposed here → DbContext disposed
}

Three things must be right:

Inject IServiceScopeFactory, not IServiceProvider. The factory is a singleton, so no lifetime mismatch. IServiceProvider injected into a singleton gives you the root provider, and resolving scoped services from it recreates the captive dependency problem (6.4).

Resolve from scope.ServiceProvider, not the outer provider. That is the whole point of creating it.

using — without disposal the scope leaks, and so does everything it created.

docs.title: Async disposal
docs.text:
If any service implements IAsyncDisposable — DbContext does — use the async variant:

await using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope();

var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
// ...

⚠️ Disposing an IAsyncDisposable service synchronously throws in some cases, and blocks a thread in others. CreateAsyncScope was added because CreateScope could not dispose those correctly. Prefer it when the scope holds anything async-disposable — 1.21.

docs.title: ⚠️ Do not create a scope inside a request
docs.text:
A request already has one:

// ✗ WRONG — creates a SECOND scope inside a request that already has one
public class OrdersController(IServiceScopeFactory factory) : ControllerBase
{
    public async Task<IActionResult> Get()
    {
        using var scope = factory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
        // A DIFFERENT DbContext from the one the rest of the request is using
    }
}

That gives you two DbContext instances in one request, in separate change trackers and separate transactions. Saving in one does not see pending changes in the other, which produces genuinely confusing bugs.

// ✓ Just inject it — the request scope supplies it
public class OrdersController(AppDbContext db) : ControllerBase { }

The rule: create a scope only where there is not one already.

docs.title: How it actually works — the three places you do need one
docs.text:
1. Startup work in Program.cs:

var app = builder.Build();

using (var scope = app.Services.CreateScope())
{
    var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
    await db.Database.MigrateAsync();
}

app.Run();

Here app.Services is the root provider, and calling CreateScope() on it is correct — that is how you get a scope from the root.

2. Background services — the most common case (21.2):

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        using (var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope())      // INSIDE the loop
        {
            var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
            await ProcessBatchAsync(db, stoppingToken);
        }

        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), stoppingToken);
    }
}

⚠️ Inside the loop, not outside. A scope held for the whole loop is a DbContext that accumulates every entity from every iteration.

3. A singleton that occasionally needs scoped work:

public class PriceCache(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) : IPriceCache
{
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, decimal> _cache = new();

    public async Task RefreshAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

        foreach (var price in await db.Prices.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct))
            _cache[price.Sku] = price.Amount;
    }
}

docs.title: The deeper detail — what disposal actually covers
docs.text:
When a scope is disposed, it disposes every disposable service it created — including transients.

using (var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope())
{
    var a = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ITransientDisposable>();
    var b = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ITransientDisposable>();
    // two separate instances — BOTH tracked by this scope
}   // BOTH disposed here

⚠️ That has a consequence for long-lived scopes. Transient disposables are not released when you stop using them — they are held until the scope ends. In a long-running scope they accumulate, which is a real leak. See 6.10.

⚠️ And services resolved from the root are never disposed until shutdown, which is another reason not to resolve scoped things from app.Services.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The complete background service pattern, which is the case worth memorising:

public class OutboxProcessor(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory,
    ILogger<OutboxProcessor> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            try
            {
                // Fresh scope per iteration. Async, because DbContext is IAsyncDisposable.
                await using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope();

                var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
                var bus = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IMessageBus>();

                var pending = await db.OutboxMessages
                    .Where(m => m.SentAt == null)
                    .OrderBy(m => m.CreatedAt)
                    .Take(100)
                    .ToListAsync(stoppingToken);

                foreach (var message in pending)
                {
                    await bus.PublishAsync(message.Payload, stoppingToken);
                    message.SentAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
                }

                await db.SaveChangesAsync(stoppingToken);
            }
            catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                break;                                  // shutting down — normal
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Outbox processing failed, will retry");
            }

            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

Five decisions in that code, each worth being able to justify:

  • IServiceScopeFactory, not IServiceProvider — a real scope, not the root.
  • The scope is inside the loop, so each batch gets a fresh DbContext.
  • CreateAsyncScope with await using, because DbContext is IAsyncDisposable.
  • Cancellation is caught separately and treated as normal shutdown, not an error (2.14).
  • Other exceptions do not kill the loop — an unhandled exception in a BackgroundService stops it silently while the app keeps running and looks healthy.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a scope in ASP.NET Core dependency injection?

A scope is a temporary sub-container. Scoped services resolved from it are created once and shared within it, and when the scope is disposed everything disposable it created is disposed too. In a web application the framework creates a scope per HTTP request and disposes it when the response completes, which is why "scoped" and "per request" get used interchangeably. But they are not the same thing — scoped means per scope, and a request just happens to be one. Anything outside a request, like a background service or startup code, has no ambient scope at all.

Q: How do you use a scoped service in a background service?

Inject IServiceScopeFactory, call CreateScope — or CreateAsyncScope if anything is IAsyncDisposable — and resolve from that scope's provider, wrapped in a using. The critical detail is creating it inside the work loop rather than outside, because a scope held for the service's whole lifetime gives you a single DbContext whose change tracker grows on every iteration, which is the captive dependency problem moved rather than solved.

Q: Why inject IServiceScopeFactory rather than IServiceProvider?

Because IServiceProvider injected into a singleton is the root provider, and resolving a scoped service from the root creates it in the root scope — which lives for the whole application. You have recreated exactly the captive dependency you were trying to avoid, just less visibly, and scope validation will not catch it. IServiceScopeFactory is itself a singleton so there is no lifetime mismatch, and it gives you a genuine short-lived scope.

Q: Should you create a scope inside a controller?

No — the request already has one, and injecting a service directly gives you it. Creating another produces a second DbContext in the same request with its own change tracker and its own transaction, so saving through one does not see pending changes in the other. That leads to bugs that are very hard to reason about. The rule is to create a scope only where one does not already exist.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Creating a scope inside a request gives you a second DbContext with a separate transaction.
  • Creating a scope outside a loop holds one DbContext for the loop's entire lifetime.
  • Injecting IServiceProvider into a singleton gives the root, not a scope.
  • Forgetting using leaks the scope and everything it created.
  • CreateScope with IAsyncDisposable services can throw or block. Use CreateAsyncScope.
  • Using a service after its scope is disposed throws ObjectDisposedException — common when a scope is disposed before an async operation completes.
  • Transient disposables are held until the scope ends, not when you finish with them.
  • HttpContext.RequestServices is already the request scope — do not wrap it in another.

docs.title: 6.6 — Add vs TryAdd vs TryAddEnumerable, and Keyed Services
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.5 Scopes · Next: 6.7 Multiple implementations

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Add always appends. TryAdd only registers if nothing is there already. That difference matters most when writing libraries.

  • Add — always adds. Duplicates are allowed, and the last one wins on a single resolve.
  • TryAdd — adds only if the service type is unregistered. Lets consumers override your default.
  • AddKeyedSingleton (.NET 8+) — register several implementations under names, and ask for one by name.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Add{Lifetime} a method Always appends a registration. Duplicates allowed. TryAdd{Lifetime} a method Appends only if that service type has no registration yet. TryAddEnumerable a method Appends only if that exact service + implementation pair is absent. Replace a method Removes existing registrations for a type and adds a new one. RemoveAll<T> a method Removes every registration for a service type. Last-one-wins a resolution rule Resolving a single service gives the last registered implementation. Keyed service a registration (.NET 8+) Registered under a key, so several implementations coexist by name. [FromKeyedServices] an attribute Marks a constructor parameter to be resolved by key. GetRequiredKeyedService<T>(key) a method Resolve a keyed service explicitly. Default registration a library pattern A sensible implementation a library registers, expecting consumers may replace it.

docs.title: The problem TryAdd solves
docs.text:
builder.Services is genuinely a list (6.2), so Add appends rather than replaces:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SmtpEmailSender>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();

// Resolving IEmailSender → SendGridEmailSender (the LAST one)
// Resolving IEnumerable<IEmailSender> → BOTH

For your own application that is usually fine, and occasionally useful for deliberately overriding a framework default.

It becomes a real problem in libraries. Consider a library that registers a default:

// Inside SomeLibrary.AddSomeLibrary()
services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();

// The consumer wants their own
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IClock, TestClock>();
builder.Services.AddSomeLibrary();          // ⚠️ registered AFTER, so it wins

The consumer's deliberate choice is silently overridden, because the library ran last.

TryAdd fixes it:

// Inside the library
services.TryAddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();   // only if nobody registered one

Now the library provides a default without stomping on a caller's choice, regardless of call order.

A picture: Add is writing your name on the sign-up sheet. TryAdd is writing it only if the sheet is blank — you will take the job if nobody else has it, but you will not push someone else off.

docs.title: The simple version
docs.text:
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions;   // ← TryAdd lives here

services.TryAddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();
services.TryAddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
services.TryAddTransient<IEmailFormatter, EmailFormatter>();

⚠️ TryAdd requires a separate using. The methods are in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions, not the main namespace, so they will not appear in IntelliSense until you add it. That trips people up.

Method Adds when Add Always TryAdd The service type has no registration TryAddEnumerable That exact service + implementation pair is absent

docs.title: TryAddEnumerable — for collections
docs.text:
TryAdd is wrong when you deliberately want several implementations (6.7), because after the first registration it does nothing.

// ✗ Only the first is ever added
services.TryAddScoped<IValidator, EmailValidator>();
services.TryAddScoped<IValidator, PhoneValidator>();     // silently skipped

TryAddEnumerable compares the pair, so different implementations all register while duplicates of the same one do not:

services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IValidator, EmailValidator>());
services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IValidator, PhoneValidator>());
services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IValidator, EmailValidator>());  // skipped

// Resolving IEnumerable<IValidator> → EmailValidator, PhoneValidator

That is the point: an extension method called twice by accident does not double up. This is how the framework registers things like IConfigureOptions<T>.

docs.title: Replacing a registration
docs.text:
When you genuinely want to swap something out:

// Replace in one call
services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IEmailSender, FakeEmailSender>());

// Or remove then add
services.RemoveAll<IEmailSender>();
services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, FakeEmailSender>();

⚠️ Replace only replaces the first matching descriptor, so with several registrations for one type you may not get what you expect. RemoveAll followed by Add is unambiguous.

This is exactly what integration tests do to swap real dependencies for fakes — 20.7.

docs.title: How it actually works — keyed services (.NET 8+)
docs.text:
Before .NET 8, registering two implementations of one interface and choosing between them meant a factory or a marker interface. Keyed services made it first-class:

builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, AzureBlobStorage>("azure");
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, S3Storage>("s3");
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, LocalStorage>("local");

Resolve by key in a constructor:

public class BackupService(
    [FromKeyedServices("azure")] IStorage primary,
    [FromKeyedServices("s3")]    IStorage secondary)
{
    // Two different implementations of the same interface
}

Or explicitly from the provider:

var storage = provider.GetRequiredKeyedService<IStorage>("azure");

Keys can be any object, so an enum is often cleaner than a string:

public enum StorageKind { Azure, S3, Local }

builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, AzureBlobStorage>(StorageKind.Azure);

public class BackupService([FromKeyedServices(StorageKind.Azure)] IStorage storage) { }

⚠️ Keyed and non-keyed registrations are separate. Registering only keyed services means GetRequiredService<IStorage>() — without a key — throws. If you want both, register a default too:

builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, AzureBlobStorage>("azure");
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IStorage, AzureBlobStorage>();     // the default

docs.title: The deeper detail — keyed vs a factory
docs.text:
Keyed services are not always the answer. Two alternatives:

A factory, when the choice depends on runtime data:

public interface IStorageFactory { IStorage Create(string tenantId); }

Keys are fixed at registration time. If the decision depends on the current tenant or user, a factory is more appropriate.

Configuration-driven selection, when there is genuinely only one at runtime:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IStorage>(sp =>
{
    var config = sp.GetRequiredService<IConfiguration>();
    return config["Storage:Provider"] switch
    {
        "azure" => new AzureBlobStorage(...),
        "s3"    => new S3Storage(...),
        _       => new LocalStorage(...)
    };
});

If the app uses one storage provider chosen by configuration, this is simpler than keys — the consuming code just asks for IStorage and does not need to know which it got.

Keyed services earn their place when several implementations are used simultaneously — a primary and a secondary backup target, or a read and a write connection.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic library registration extension, using the right method for each case:

public static class PaymentModuleExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddPaymentModule(
        this IServiceCollection services,
        IConfiguration config)
    {
        // TryAdd — a sensible default the consumer may override
        services.TryAddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();

        // TryAddEnumerable — several handlers, and safe if called twice
        services.TryAddEnumerable(
            ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IPaymentValidator, AmountValidator>());
        services.TryAddEnumerable(
            ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IPaymentValidator, CurrencyValidator>());

        // Keyed — both gateways are used at once, so both must be reachable
        services.AddKeyedScoped<IPaymentGateway, StripeGateway>("stripe");
        services.AddKeyedScoped<IPaymentGateway, PayPalGateway>("paypal");

        // Add — our own type, no override expected
        services.AddScoped<IPaymentService, PaymentService>();

        services.Configure<PaymentOptions>(config.GetSection("Payments"));

        return services;
    }
}

public class PaymentService(
    [FromKeyedServices("stripe")] IPaymentGateway stripe,
    [FromKeyedServices("paypal")] IPaymentGateway paypal,
    IEnumerable<IPaymentValidator> validators)          // all of them — see 6.7
{
    public async Task<Receipt> PayAsync(Payment payment, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        foreach (var validator in validators)
            validator.Validate(payment);

        var gateway = payment.Method == PaymentMethod.PayPal ? paypal : stripe;
        return await gateway.ChargeAsync(payment, ct);
    }
}

Note the three different registration styles serving three different intents: a replaceable default, a collection of handlers, and named alternatives used side by side.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between Add and TryAdd?

Add always appends a registration, so calling it twice for the same interface leaves both in the list and a single resolve gives you the last one. TryAdd only registers if that service type has no registration at all. The distinction matters most in library code — a library registering a default with Add will silently override a consumer's deliberate choice if it happens to run afterwards, whereas TryAdd provides the default without stomping on anyone. Worth knowing that TryAdd lives in a separate namespace, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions, so it does not appear in IntelliSense until you add that using.

Q: When would you use TryAddEnumerable?

When you deliberately want several implementations of one interface and want to avoid accidental duplicates. TryAdd is wrong there, because after the first registration it does nothing — so a second, different implementation is silently skipped. TryAddEnumerable compares the service and implementation pair, so different implementations all register while a repeat of the same one is ignored. That makes a registration extension safe to call twice, which is how the framework registers things like options configuration.

Q: What are keyed services?

A .NET 8 feature letting you register several implementations of one interface under different keys and ask for a specific one — either with [FromKeyedServices("name")] on a constructor parameter or GetRequiredKeyedService on the provider. Before that you needed a factory or marker interfaces. The thing to watch is that keyed and non-keyed registrations are separate, so registering only keyed implementations means a plain GetRequiredService for that type throws.

Q: When would you use a factory instead of keyed services?

When the choice depends on runtime data rather than being fixed at registration. Keys are decided when you wire the container, so if the implementation depends on the current tenant or user, a factory that takes that value is more appropriate. And if the application genuinely uses only one implementation, selected by configuration, a factory registration with a switch is simpler than keys — consuming code just asks for the interface without needing to know which one it got. Keyed services earn their place when several implementations are genuinely used at the same time.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• TryAdd needs using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions. It will not appear in IntelliSense otherwise.
  • TryAdd with multiple implementations silently skips all but the first. Use TryAddEnumerable.
  • Add twice means last-one-wins for a single resolve, with no warning.
  • Replace only replaces the first matching descriptor. Use RemoveAll then Add when there could be several.
  • Keyed and non-keyed registrations are separate. Keyed-only means a plain resolve throws.
  • Keys are fixed at registration time. Runtime-dependent selection needs a factory.
  • A library using Add for defaults overrides consumer choices depending on call order.

docs.title: 6.7 — Multiple Implementations and IEnumerable<TService>
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.6 Registration APIs · Next: 6.8 Factories and open generics

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Register the same interface several times and the container keeps all of them. How you ask decides what you get.

  • Ask for IValidator → you get the last one registered.
  • Ask for IEnumerable<IValidator> → you get all of them, in registration order.
  • This is how you build a pipeline of handlers without writing any wiring code.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Multiple registration a container behaviour Several implementations registered for one service type. All are kept. IEnumerable<T> injection a resolution style Asking for the collection gives you every registered implementation. Last-one-wins a resolution rule A single-service resolve returns the last registration. Registration order the order of your Add calls Determines the order in the injected IEnumerable<T>. GetServices<T>() a method Resolves all implementations. The explicit form of IEnumerable<T>. TryAddEnumerable a method Registers only if that exact service+implementation pair is absent. See 6.6. Composite pattern a design pattern One implementation that wraps and delegates to a collection of others. Chain of responsibility a design pattern Handlers offered an item in turn until one takes it. See 22.5.

docs.title: One interface, many implementations
docs.text:
Some jobs are naturally plural. Validating an order means running several rules. Notifying a customer might mean email and SMS and a push notification.

You could write one class containing all of them, but then adding a rule means editing that class. Instead, register each as its own implementation:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator, AmountValidator>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator, StockValidator>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator, CustomerCreditValidator>();

And ask for all of them:

public class OrderService(IEnumerable<IOrderValidator> validators)
{
    public void Validate(Order order)
    {
        foreach (var validator in validators)
            validator.Validate(order);
    }
}

Adding a fourth rule is one registration line. OrderService never changes — which is the open/closed principle in practice (22.1).

A picture: a panel of inspectors rather than one inspector with a long checklist. Hiring another inspector does not mean rewriting anyone's job description.

docs.title: The two ways of asking
docs.text:
This is the part worth being precise about:

// Asking for ONE → the LAST registered
public class A(IOrderValidator validator) { }        // CustomerCreditValidator

// Asking for ALL → every one, in registration order
public class B(IEnumerable<IOrderValidator> validators) { }   // all three

⚠️ Last-one-wins for a single resolve is a deliberate feature — it is how you override a framework default — but it also means an accidental extra registration silently changes behaviour with no warning.

docs.title: The simple version
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationChannel, EmailChannel>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationChannel, SmsChannel>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationChannel, PushChannel>();

public class NotificationService(
    IEnumerable<INotificationChannel> channels,
    ILogger<NotificationService> logger)
{
    public async Task NotifyAsync(User user, string message, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        foreach (var channel in channels)
        {
            try
            {
                await channel.SendAsync(user, message, ct);
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                // One channel failing should not stop the others
                logger.LogError(ex, "Channel {Channel} failed", channel.GetType().Name);
            }
        }
    }
}

That try/catch inside the loop is a real design decision: if SMS is down, the email should still go. Letting the exception escape would abandon the remaining channels.

docs.title: Resolving explicitly
docs.text:
var validators = provider.GetServices<IOrderValidator>();      // IEnumerable<T>
var last       = provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderValidator>();  // just the last

GetServices<T>() returns an empty sequence if none are registered — it does not throw. That makes "zero or more handlers" easy to express, and it also means a missing registration is silent, which is occasionally a trap.

docs.title: ⚠️ TryAdd breaks this
docs.text:
// ✗ Only the first is ever registered
services.TryAddScoped<IOrderValidator, AmountValidator>();
services.TryAddScoped<IOrderValidator, StockValidator>();     // silently skipped

TryAdd checks whether the service type is registered, so after the first call it does nothing. Use TryAddEnumerable when you want several but no duplicates (6.6):

services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IOrderValidator, AmountValidator>());
services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IOrderValidator, StockValidator>());

docs.title: How it actually works — order matters
docs.text:
The IEnumerable<T> arrives in registration order, which matters when the handlers are not independent:

// Cheap checks first — fail fast before hitting the database
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator, AmountValidator>();        // in-memory
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator, StockValidator>();         // DB query
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator, CreditCheckValidator>();   // external API

If the amount is invalid, you never make the API call. That ordering is deliberate and invisible unless you know the rule.

⚠️ Relying on order is fragile though. Someone reorganising Program.cs can change behaviour with no obvious signal. If order genuinely matters, make it explicit:

public interface IOrderValidator
{
    int Order { get; }
    void Validate(Order order);
}

// Then sort, rather than trusting registration order
foreach (var validator in validators.OrderBy(v => v.Order))
    validator.Validate(order);

docs.title: The deeper detail — the composite pattern
docs.text:
Injecting IEnumerable<T> everywhere spreads the looping logic around. An alternative is one implementation that wraps the rest:

public class CompositeOrderValidator(IEnumerable<IOrderValidator> validators)
    : IOrderValidator
{
    public void Validate(Order order)
    {
        var errors = new List<string>();

        foreach (var validator in validators)
        {
            try { validator.Validate(order); }
            catch (ValidationException ex) { errors.Add(ex.Message); }
        }

        if (errors.Count > 0)
            throw new ValidationException(errors);      // report ALL failures, not just the first
    }
}

Consumers then inject the plain interface and know nothing about there being several:

public class OrderService(IOrderValidator validator)     // just one, apparently
{
    public void Process(Order order) => validator.Validate(order);
}

⚠️ Registering that needs care, because the composite implements the same interface it consumes — register it as itself and expose it via a factory:

builder.Services.AddScoped<AmountValidator>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<StockValidator>();

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderValidator>(sp => new CompositeOrderValidator(
[
    sp.GetRequiredService<AmountValidator>(),
    sp.GetRequiredService<StockValidator>()
]));

Registering the composite as IOrderValidator and injecting IEnumerable<IOrderValidator> into it would make it contain itself — infinite recursion and a stack overflow.

Collecting all errors rather than throwing on the first is the other real benefit of the composite. A user submitting a form wants every problem at once, not one per round trip. See 11.5.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic pipeline — several handlers, ordered, with one deliberately last:

public interface IOrderEnricher
{
    Task EnrichAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct);
}

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderEnricher, CustomerDetailsEnricher>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderEnricher, PricingEnricher>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderEnricher, ShippingEstimateEnricher>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderEnricher, AuditEnricher>();       // last on purpose

public class OrderQueryService(
    IOrderRepository repo,
    IEnumerable<IOrderEnricher> enrichers)
{
    public async Task<Order> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct)
                    ?? throw new NotFoundException(id);

        // Runs in registration order, so audit sees the fully enriched order
        foreach (var enricher in enrichers)
            await enricher.EnrichAsync(order, ct);

        return order;
    }
}

Adding a fifth enricher is one line in Program.cs. Nothing else in the codebase changes — that is the whole point of the pattern.

docs.title: Choosing between one and many
docs.text: You want Use One implementation, swappable A single registration One of several, chosen by name Keyed services (6.6) One of several, chosen at runtime A factory (6.8) All of them, every time IEnumerable<T> All of them, hidden behind one interface A composite

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens if you register two implementations of the same interface?

Both stay in the container, because the service collection is genuinely a list rather than a dictionary. Which you get depends on how you ask: resolving the interface directly gives you the last one registered, while injecting IEnumerable<T> of that interface gives you all of them in registration order. Last-one-wins is deliberate and useful for overriding a framework default, but it also means an accidental duplicate registration silently changes which implementation you get.

Q: When would you inject IEnumerable<T>?

When the job is naturally plural — running several validation rules, sending a notification through several channels, applying a set of enrichers. The benefit is that adding another implementation is a single registration line and the consuming class never changes, which is the open/closed principle in practice. I would also add a try/catch around each item where the handlers are independent, so one failing channel does not abandon the rest.

Q: Does the order of the injected collection matter?

It is registration order, and it often does matter — you typically want cheap in-memory checks before ones that hit a database or an external API, so you fail fast. The risk is that it is implicit: someone tidying Program.cs can change behaviour with no obvious signal. If the order is genuinely significant I would make it explicit, either with an Order property on the interface that you sort by, or by composing them deliberately rather than relying on the container.

Q: What is the composite pattern here?

One implementation of the interface that takes the collection of all the others and delegates to them. Consumers then inject the plain interface and have no idea there are several, which keeps the looping logic in one place rather than spread across every consumer. It also lets you collect all the failures rather than throwing on the first, which is what you want for validation. The thing to be careful about is registration — the composite implements the interface it consumes, so registering it as that interface while also injecting the collection into it would make it contain itself and recurse infinitely.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• TryAdd silently skips all but the first implementation. Use TryAddEnumerable.
  • Last-one-wins for a single resolve means a duplicate registration changes behaviour with no warning.
  • GetServices<T>() returns empty rather than throwing when nothing is registered, so a missing registration is silent.
  • Registration order is implicit. Reordering Program.cs can change behaviour.
  • A composite registered as the interface it consumes recurses infinitely.
  • An exception in one handler abandons the rest unless you catch per item.
  • Injecting both T and IEnumerable<T> gives you the last one plus all of them — including that same instance twice, if lifetimes allow.

docs.title: 6.8 — Factory Registrations and Open Generics
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.7 Multiple implementations · Next: 6.9 Injection styles

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Two registration techniques for when the simple AddScoped<IFoo, Foo>() form is not enough.

  • A factory registration gives you a lambda that builds the object, so construction can involve logic — reading config, choosing between implementations, passing a computed value.
  • An open generic registration registers IRepository<> once and serves IRepository<Order>, IRepository<Customer> and every other closed version.
  • Both are ways of saying "I cannot express this with a type pair alone".

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Factory registration a registration style You supply a lambda sp => new Thing(...) that builds the instance. IServiceProvider sp the lambda's parameter The container, so the factory can resolve other services. Open generic a generic type with no arguments IRepository<> — written with empty angle brackets. Closed generic a generic type with arguments IRepository<Order>. typeof(IRepository<>) the syntax How you refer to an open generic in C#. Generic type argument the filled-in type The Order in IRepository<Order>. ActivatorUtilities a static class Creates an object with DI-resolved dependencies plus extra arguments you supply. Decorator a design pattern Wrapping a service in another that adds behaviour. See 22.4. Lazy resolution a behaviour The factory runs when the service is first requested, not at registration.

docs.title: When a type pair is not enough
docs.text:
Most registrations are simple: "when someone asks for IFoo, give them Foo".

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

The container inspects OrderService's constructor and resolves everything itself. That covers the large majority of cases.

Two situations break it:

Construction needs a decision. Which storage provider? What connection string? A value from configuration that is not itself a service.

The type is generic and you do not want to register every version. IRepository<Order>, IRepository<Customer>, IRepository<Invoice> — twenty entities means twenty near-identical lines, and one more every time someone adds an entity.

Factory registrations solve the first; open generics solve the second.

docs.title: The simple version — a factory
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IStorageProvider>(sp =>
{
    var config = sp.GetRequiredService<IConfiguration>();

    return config["Storage:Provider"] switch
    {
        "azure" => new AzureBlobStorage(config["Storage:ConnectionString"]!),
        "s3"    => new S3Storage(config["Storage:Bucket"]!),
        _       => new LocalFileStorage(config["Storage:Path"]!)
    };
});

The lambda receives the IServiceProvider, so it can resolve anything already registered.

⚠️ The factory runs lazily — on first resolution, not at registration. So a configuration error inside it does not surface at startup; it surfaces on the first request that needs the service, potentially much later and in a confusing place.

If the failure should be loud and early, either validate at startup or enable ValidateOnBuild (6.2).

docs.title: ⚠️ Which provider does the factory get?
docs.text:
This catches people out. The sp passed to the factory is the provider for the scope the service is being created in:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IThing>(sp =>
{
    var db = sp.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();      // ✓ the REQUEST's DbContext
    return new Thing(db);
});

For a scoped registration that is the request scope, so resolving other scoped services is correct.

For a singleton registration it is the root provider — so resolving a scoped service there is a captive dependency (6.4):

// ✗ WRONG — a singleton factory resolving a scoped service
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IThing>(sp =>
{
    var db = sp.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();      // ⚠️ captured forever
    return new Thing(db);
});

The lifetime rules apply inside factories exactly as they do in constructors.

docs.title: Passing values a class needs
docs.text:
A common case — a constructor parameter that is not a service:

public class RetryPolicy(IHttpClientFactory factory, int maxAttempts) { }

builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp => new RetryPolicy(
    sp.GetRequiredService<IHttpClientFactory>(),
    maxAttempts: 3));

⚠️ But for anything configurable, use the options pattern instead. Hard-coding 3 in Program.cs means it cannot be changed per environment:

builder.Services.Configure<RetryOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Retry"));
builder.Services.AddSingleton<RetryPolicy>();     // takes IOptions<RetryOptions>

See 7.6.

ActivatorUtilities is the middle ground when you need DI plus runtime arguments:

var policy = ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<RetryPolicy>(provider, maxAttempts);
// Resolves IHttpClientFactory from DI, takes maxAttempts from you

docs.title: How it actually works — open generics
docs.text:
Registering a generic repository for every entity is unworkable:

// ✗ One line per entity, forever
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRepository<Order>, EfRepository<Order>>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRepository<Customer>, EfRepository<Customer>>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRepository<Invoice>, EfRepository<Invoice>>();

An open generic registration covers all of them:

builder.Services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));

Note the syntax: typeof(IRepository<>) with empty angle brackets. That is how C# refers to a generic type with its arguments unfilled.

Now anything can inject any closed version:

public class OrderService(IRepository<Order> orders) { }
public class CustomerService(IRepository<Customer> customers) { }

The container builds EfRepository<Order> when asked for IRepository<Order>. It substitutes the type argument automatically.

⚠️ The generic parameters must line up. IRepository<T> and EfRepository<T> need the same arity and compatible constraints, or you get a runtime error at resolution rather than a compile error:

public interface IRepository<T> where T : class, IEntity { }
public class EfRepository<T>(AppDbContext db) : IRepository<T> where T : class, IEntity { }

See 1.10.

This is how the framework registers ILogger<T>, which is why you can inject ILogger<AnyClassYouWrite> without registering anything.

docs.title: The deeper detail — decoration with factories
docs.text:
Factories let you wrap a service in another that adds behaviour:

builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderRepository>();          // the real one, as itself

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository>(sp =>
{
    var inner = sp.GetRequiredService<OrderRepository>();
    var cache = sp.GetRequiredService<IMemoryCache>();
    return new CachingOrderRepository(inner, cache);    // wrap it
});

Consumers inject IOrderRepository and get caching transparently.

⚠️ Register the inner one as its concrete type, not as the interface. Registering both as IOrderRepository and resolving the interface inside the factory would make the decorator wrap itself and recurse forever.

The library Scrutor makes this much cleaner:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.Decorate<IOrderRepository, CachingOrderRepository>();

See 6.11.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic set showing both techniques where they genuinely earn their place:

// ── Open generic: one line covers every entity ──
builder.Services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));

// ── Factory: the implementation depends on configuration ──
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IFeatureFlags>(sp =>
{
    var config = sp.GetRequiredService<IConfiguration>();
    var logger = sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<IFeatureFlags>>();

    var endpoint = config["FeatureFlags:Endpoint"];

    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(endpoint))
    {
        logger.LogWarning("No feature flag endpoint configured — using local defaults");
        return new LocalFeatureFlags(config.GetSection("FeatureFlags:Defaults"));
    }

    return new RemoteFeatureFlags(
        sp.GetRequiredService<IHttpClientFactory>(),
        endpoint);
});

// ── Factory: decoration ──
builder.Services.AddScoped<PriceCalculator>();                 // concrete
builder.Services.AddScoped<IPriceCalculator>(sp =>
    new LoggingPriceCalculator(
        sp.GetRequiredService<PriceCalculator>(),
        sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<LoggingPriceCalculator>>()));

And the generic repository that the open registration serves:

public interface IRepository<T> where T : class, IEntity
{
    Task<T?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<T>> ListAsync(CancellationToken ct);
    Task AddAsync(T entity, CancellationToken ct);
}

public class EfRepository<T>(AppDbContext db) : IRepository<T>
    where T : class, IEntity
{
    public Task<T?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
        => db.Set<T>().FirstOrDefaultAsync(e => e.Id == id, ct);

    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<T>> ListAsync(CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.Set<T>().AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);

    public async Task AddAsync(T entity, CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.Set<T>().AddAsync(entity, ct);
}

⚠️ Whether a generic repository is a good idea at all is a separate argument — EF Core's DbSet<T> already is one, and wrapping it often loses capability without gaining much. See 13.19.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you use a factory registration?

When construction needs logic rather than just picking a type — choosing an implementation based on configuration, passing a computed value, or wrapping one service in another. The lambda receives the IServiceProvider, so it can resolve whatever else it needs. Two things to watch: the factory runs lazily on first resolution rather than at startup, so a configuration error surfaces late; and the lifetime rules still apply inside it, so a singleton factory resolving a scoped service is a captive dependency exactly as it would be in a constructor.

Q: What is an open generic registration?

Registering a generic type without its type arguments filled in, using typeof(IRepository<>) with empty angle brackets. One registration then serves every closed version — IRepository<Order>, IRepository<Customer> and so on — with the container substituting the type argument when it builds the instance. It avoids one registration line per entity, and it is exactly how the framework registers ILogger<T>, which is why you can inject a logger for any class without registering anything.

Q: What provider does a factory lambda receive?

The one for the scope the service is being created in. For a scoped registration that is the request scope, so resolving other scoped services from it is correct. For a singleton registration it is the root provider, so resolving a scoped service there captures it for the application's lifetime — the same captive dependency problem you would get from constructor injection. The lifetime rules do not relax inside factories.

Q: How would you add caching to an existing repository without changing it?

Decoration. Register the real repository as its concrete type, then register the interface with a factory that resolves the concrete one and wraps it in a caching implementation. Consumers keep injecting the interface and get caching transparently. The thing to be careful about is registering the inner service as its concrete type rather than the interface — otherwise the decorator resolves the interface, finds itself, and recurses infinitely. Scrutor's Decorate method makes this a single line and handles that correctly.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Factories run lazily, so errors inside them surface on first use rather than at startup.
  • A singleton factory resolving a scoped service is a captive dependency.
  • A decorator registered as the interface it resolves wraps itself and recurses forever.
  • Open generic arity and constraints must match, or resolution fails at runtime rather than compile time.
  • typeof(IRepository<>) needs empty angle brackets. typeof(IRepository) will not compile for a generic type.
  • Hard-coding values in a factory makes them unconfigurable. Use IOptions<T>.
  • Factories bypass constructor inspection, so ValidateOnBuild cannot verify what happens inside them.

docs.title: 6.9 — Constructor Injection vs [FromServices] vs Service Locator
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.8 Factories and open generics · Next: 6.10 Disposal

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Three ways to get a dependency, in descending order of preference.

  • Constructor injection — the default. The constructor is an honest list of what the class needs.
  • [FromServices] — inject into a single action method. Useful when only one action needs it.
  • Service locator — injecting IServiceProvider and pulling services out. An anti-pattern, with narrow exceptions.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Constructor injection the main style Dependencies arrive as constructor parameters. Resolved when the object is built. Method injection a style Dependencies arrive as method parameters. Used by middleware's InvokeAsync. [FromServices] an attribute Marks an action parameter to come from DI rather than the request. Service locator an anti-pattern A class asks the container for what it needs, instead of declaring it. IServiceProvider an interface The container. Injecting it into your classes is the service locator smell. Hidden dependency a design problem A dependency not visible in the class's public surface. Explicit dependencies principle a design rule A class should state everything it needs in its constructor. ActivatorUtilities a static class Builds an object with DI plus runtime arguments. See 6.8.

docs.title: Why the constructor is the right place
docs.text:
public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository repo,
    IEmailSender email,
    ILogger<OrderService> logger)
{
    // ...
}

Read that constructor and you know everything this class depends on. Four benefits follow:

It is honest. Nothing is hidden. A reviewer sees the full list without reading the body.

It fails early. A missing registration throws when the object is built — and with ValidateOnBuild, at application startup (6.2).

It is testable. Construct it with fakes. No container involved.

It is a design signal. Eight parameters means the class does eight things. That pressure is useful — it pushes you to split the class.

A picture: a job application that lists your requirements up front, versus one where you turn up and start asking for things you forgot to mention.

docs.title: The alternative that looks convenient
docs.text:
public class OrderService(IServiceProvider provider)
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var repo  = provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();
        var email = provider.GetRequiredService<IEmailSender>();
        // ...
    }
}

This works. It is also worse in every way that matters:

Dependencies are invisible. The constructor says the class needs "the container", which is true of nothing useful. You have to read every method to discover what it actually uses.

Failures move to runtime. A missing registration no longer fails at startup — it fails on the first request that reaches that line, possibly in production, possibly months later.

Testing gets worse. You cannot pass two fakes; you have to build a container, or mock IServiceProvider and configure what it returns for each type.

The design smell is hidden. Eight dependencies no longer look like eight dependencies, so the pressure to split the class disappears.

⚠️ That last point is the real damage. Service locator does not just make one class worse — it removes the feedback that would have stopped the class growing.

docs.title: The simple version — the three styles
docs.text:
// 1. CONSTRUCTOR — the default
public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo) { }

// 2. [FromServices] — one action needs something the others do not
[HttpPost("export")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Export(
    ExportRequest request,
    [FromServices] IReportGenerator generator,      // ← from DI, not the request body
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    var report = await generator.CreateAsync(request, ct);
    return File(report, "application/pdf");
}

// 3. SERVICE LOCATOR — avoid
public class OrderService(IServiceProvider provider) { }

docs.title: When [FromServices] earns its place
docs.text:
A controller with twelve actions where one needs an expensive service:

// Without [FromServices] — every action pays for it
public class OrdersController(
    IOrderService orders,
    IReportGenerator generator) : ControllerBase      // only Export uses this
{
    public IActionResult Get() { }          // generator built anyway
    public IActionResult List() { }         // and here
    public IActionResult Export() { }       // only this one needs it
}

Constructor injection resolves every dependency when the controller is created, for every request — so a heavyweight service is built even for actions that never touch it.

[FromServices] defers it to the action that needs it.

⚠️ Do not over-apply this. Most services are cheap to construct, and scattering [FromServices] across a controller makes the dependencies harder to see. It is a targeted optimisation, not a style.

In .NET 7+ the attribute is often unnecessary for minimal APIs — the framework infers that a parameter whose type is registered in DI comes from services:

app.MapPost("/export", async (ExportRequest request, IReportGenerator generator) =>
{
    // 'generator' resolved from DI automatically — no attribute needed
});

For controllers you can enable the same inference:

builder.Services.Configure<ApiBehaviorOptions>(o =>
    o.DisableImplicitFromServicesParameters = false);   // the default in .NET 7+

docs.title: How it actually works — where the locator pattern is legitimate
docs.text:
Three cases where reaching into the container is correct:

1. A singleton needing scoped work — but use IServiceScopeFactory, not IServiceProvider (6.5):

public class Worker(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
    }
}

2. Startup code in Program.cs — there is no constructor to inject into:

using var scope = app.Services.CreateScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
await db.Database.MigrateAsync();

3. Factory registrations — the lambda receives the provider by design (6.8).

4. Inline middleware — there is no constructor, so context.RequestServices is the only option (5.4).

⚠️ The distinction: infrastructure code that composes the application may use the container. Application code that implements behaviour should not.

docs.title: The deeper detail — the "too many parameters" argument
docs.text:
The most common defence of service locator is that a class has too many constructor parameters.

public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository repo,
    IEmailSender email,
    ISmsSender sms,
    IPaymentGateway payments,
    IInventoryService inventory,
    IAuditLog audit,
    IPricingEngine pricing,
    ILogger<OrderService> logger)          // eight and counting
{ }

Switching to IServiceProvider makes the list disappear from view. It does not make the class simpler — it hides the complexity.

The real fixes:

Split the class. Eight dependencies usually means several responsibilities.

public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository repo,
    IOrderNotifier notifier,       // wraps email + SMS
    IOrderPricing pricing,         // wraps pricing + inventory
    ILogger<OrderService> logger)
{ }

Group related dependencies behind a facade. Notification is one concern whether it goes by email or SMS.

Use IEnumerable<T> where the dependencies are variations of one thing (6.7).

Question whether the class should exist. A service coordinating eight others is sometimes a sign the logic belongs in the domain model rather than a service layer (22.14).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The same class, three ways, with the consequences visible.

// ✓ CONSTRUCTOR — dependencies visible, fails at startup, trivially testable
public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository repo,
    IEmailSender email,
    ILogger<OrderService> logger) : IOrderService
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct) ?? throw new NotFoundException(id);
        order.Complete();
        await repo.SaveAsync(order, ct);
        await email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Order complete", ct);
        logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} completed", id);
    }
}

// The test needs no container
var service = new OrderService(fakeRepo, fakeEmail, NullLogger<OrderService>.Instance);

// ✗ SERVICE LOCATOR — dependencies hidden, fails at runtime, awkward to test
public class OrderService(IServiceProvider provider) : IOrderService
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var repo = provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();
        var email = provider.GetRequiredService<IEmailSender>();
        // ...
    }
}

// The test has to build a container or mock the provider
var provider = Substitute.For<IServiceProvider>();
provider.GetService(typeof(IOrderRepository)).Returns(fakeRepo);
provider.GetService(typeof(IEmailSender)).Returns(fakeEmail);
// ...and repeat for every dependency the method happens to use

That test setup is the argument. It is longer, it breaks whenever the method resolves something new, and nothing tells you what to configure until the test fails.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is constructor injection preferred?

Because the constructor becomes an honest, complete statement of what the class needs. That makes dependencies visible to anyone reading it, lets a missing registration fail at object creation — or at startup with ValidateOnBuild — and makes the class trivially testable by passing fakes with no container involved. It also preserves a useful design signal: a constructor with eight parameters obviously does too much, and that pressure pushes you to split the class.

Q: What is the service locator anti-pattern and why is it bad?

It is injecting IServiceProvider into a class and pulling services out on demand rather than declaring them. It works, but it hides the dependencies — the constructor tells you the class needs "the container", which is useless — so you have to read every method to find out what it actually uses. It moves failures from startup to runtime, since a missing registration only surfaces when that line executes. And it makes testing much worse, because you have to mock the provider and configure what it returns per type. The subtlest damage is that it hides the design smell, so nothing stops the class accumulating more dependencies.

Q: When is [FromServices] appropriate?

When one action on a controller needs a service the others do not, and that service is expensive to construct. Constructor injection resolves every dependency for every request regardless of which action runs, so a heavyweight report generator gets built even for a simple GET. [FromServices] defers it to the action that uses it. I would use it sparingly though — most services are cheap, and scattering the attribute makes the class's dependencies harder to see at a glance. In .NET 7 and later the attribute is often unnecessary anyway, since parameters whose types are registered in DI are inferred.

Q: A class has ten constructor parameters. Should you switch to IServiceProvider?

No — that hides the problem rather than solving it. Ten dependencies means the class has too many responsibilities, and making the list invisible removes the only signal telling you so. The real fixes are splitting the class, grouping related dependencies behind a facade — notification covering both email and SMS, for instance — or using IEnumerable<T> where they are variations of one thing. Occasionally it is a sign the logic belongs in the domain model rather than a coordinating service.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Injecting IServiceProvider into application code hides dependencies and defers failures to runtime.
  • Using service locator to hide too many parameters removes the design feedback you needed.
  • [FromServices] everywhere makes dependencies hard to see. It is a targeted optimisation.
  • Constructor injection resolves everything per request, so a heavy service costs you even on actions that never use it.
  • Injecting IServiceProvider into a singleton gives the root scope, which is a captive dependency waiting to happen (6.4).
  • Property injection is not supported by the built-in container. It requires a third-party one (6.11).
  • Mocking IServiceProvider in tests is brittle — it breaks whenever the method resolves something new.

docs.title: 6.10 — Disposal: Who Disposes What
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.9 Injection styles · Next: 6.11 Third-party containers

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The container disposes what it created. That single rule answers almost every question here.

  • Services the container constructed are disposed when their scope ends — scoped and transient at end of request, singletons at shutdown.
  • An instance you built yourself and passed to AddSingleton(instance) is not disposed. You own it.
  • Never dispose an injected service manually. The container will dispose it again, and the next request gets an ObjectDisposedException.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means IDisposable an interface Has Dispose(). Releases unmanaged resources. See 1.21. IAsyncDisposable an interface Has DisposeAsync(). For cleanup that needs to await. Container-created a service the container built Registered by type or factory. The container owns its disposal. Container-provided an instance you supplied Passed to AddSingleton(instance). You own its disposal. Disposal tracking a container behaviour The scope keeps a list of disposables it created, and disposes them in reverse order. ObjectDisposedException an exception Using a service after it was disposed. The symptom of double disposal. CreateAsyncScope() a method A scope that can dispose IAsyncDisposable services correctly. Transient disposable a leak risk A transient implementing IDisposable — held by the scope until it ends, not when you finish.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
The container disposes what it created. It does not dispose what you handed it.

Everything follows from that.

// Container CREATES it → container DISPOSES it
builder.Services.AddScoped<IFileStore, FileStore>();

// Container CREATES it (via your factory) → container DISPOSES it
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IFileStore>(sp => new FileStore("/data"));

// YOU created it → YOU dispose it. Container will not.
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IFileStore>(new FileStore("/data"));

Those last two look almost identical and behave differently. The factory version hands the container a recipe, so the container owns the result. The instance version hands over a finished object, and the container assumes you are managing it.

A picture: a restaurant washing the plates it owns. Bring your own plate and they will serve food on it, but they will not put it through the dishwasher — they assume you are taking it home.

docs.title: When disposal happens
docs.text:
Lifetime Disposed when Transient The scope that created it ends Scoped That scope ends — end of the HTTP request Singleton The application shuts down Instance you supplied Never — by the container

Disposal happens in reverse creation order, so a service is disposed before anything it depended on. Same logic as nested using blocks.

docs.title: The simple version — you do nothing
docs.text:
For the overwhelming majority of services, disposal is automatic and invisible:

builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(...);      // scoped, IAsyncDisposable

public class OrdersController(AppDbContext db) : ControllerBase
{
    public async Task<IActionResult> Get(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await db.Orders.FindAsync([id], ct);
        return Ok(order);
    }
    // No using, no Dispose. The request scope handles it.
}

docs.title: ⚠️ Never dispose an injected service
docs.text:
This is the trap:

// ✗ WRONG
public class OrderService(AppDbContext db) : IOrderService
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using (db)                             // ⚠️ don't
        {
            await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        }
    }
}

You did not create it, so it is not yours to dispose. Two things go wrong:

The rest of the request breaks. Other services sharing that scoped DbContext now get ObjectDisposedException.

The container disposes it again at end of scope. Dispose should be idempotent, so that usually does not throw — but you have introduced a real bug for a cleanup you never needed.

The rule: if it arrived through injection, you do not dispose it.

docs.title: How it actually works — transient disposables ⚠️
docs.text:
The genuinely surprising one.

A transient service implementing IDisposable is tracked by the scope that created it, and disposed when that scope ends — not when you finish using it:

builder.Services.AddTransient<IFileHandle, FileHandle>();      // IDisposable

public class BatchProcessor(IServiceProvider provider)
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(IEnumerable<string> paths, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        foreach (var path in paths)
        {
            var handle = provider.GetRequiredService<IFileHandle>();
            await handle.WriteAsync(path, ct);
            // ⚠️ NOT disposed here — held until the scope ends
        }
        // 10,000 files → 10,000 open file handles
    }
}

The container held every one, so the operating system handles stay open until the request completes. On a long-running scope — a background service loop — this is a real leak (3.5).

The fix is a scope per unit of work, so disposal happens when you expect:

foreach (var path in paths)
{
    using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
    var handle = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IFileHandle>();
    await handle.WriteAsync(path, ct);
}   // disposed here, every iteration

⚠️ The broader guidance: avoid registering disposable services as transient. If it holds a resource, scoped is usually more appropriate, because the disposal point is then clear.

docs.title: Async disposal
docs.text:
DbContext implements IAsyncDisposable. Disposing it synchronously can block a thread or throw:

// ✗ May not dispose async services correctly
using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();

// ✓ Handles IAsyncDisposable properly
await using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope();

CreateAsyncScope was added specifically because CreateScope could not dispose those services correctly. Prefer it whenever the scope might hold something async-disposable, which in practice means whenever a DbContext is involved. See 6.5.

docs.title: The deeper detail — HttpClient is the exception
docs.text:
The one service you must not dispose, and which the container deliberately does not either:

public class ApiClient(HttpClient http)         // from IHttpClientFactory
{
    public void Dispose() => http.Dispose();    // ✗ NEVER
}

IHttpClientFactory manages the underlying HttpClientHandler pool, rotating handlers on a schedule so DNS changes are picked up. Disposing the client defeats that mechanism entirely.

An HttpClient from the factory is safe to let go of — it is a lightweight wrapper. The handler underneath is pooled and reused. See 19.10.

docs.title: The captive disposal problem
docs.text:
A singleton holding a scoped disposable is a captive dependency (6.4) — and it is also a disposal problem, because the scoped service is never disposed until shutdown:

// ✗ The DbContext is never disposed until the app stops
public class CacheWarmer(AppDbContext db) { }

Beyond the thread-safety issue, the database connection and change tracker are held for the application's lifetime.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Getting it right in the cases that matter:

// ── 1. Normal service — do nothing. The container handles it. ──
public class OrderService(AppDbContext db, IEmailSender email) : IOrderService
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await db.Orders.FindAsync([id], ct);
        order!.Complete();
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        await email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Done", ct);
    }
    // No IDisposable. Nothing to clean up. Nothing was created here.
}

// ── 2. A service that creates something itself — it owns that ──
public class ReportService(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) : IReportService
{
    public async Task<byte[]> GenerateAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // WE created this stream, so WE dispose it
        await using var buffer = new MemoryStream();

        // The scope we created is also ours to dispose
        await using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

        var orders = await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);
        await WriteReportAsync(buffer, orders, ct);

        return buffer.ToArray();
    }   // buffer and scope disposed. The DbContext goes with the scope.
}

// ── 3. A disposable singleton — the container disposes at shutdown ──
public sealed class ConnectionPool(IOptions<PoolOptions> options) : IDisposable
{
    private readonly SemaphoreSlim _limit = new(options.Value.MaxConnections);

    public void Dispose() => _limit.Dispose();
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton<ConnectionPool>();     // container built it → disposes it

// ── 4. An instance you built — YOU own it ──
var pool = new ConnectionPool(Options.Create(new PoolOptions { MaxConnections = 10 }));
builder.Services.AddSingleton(pool);

// ⚠️ The container will NOT dispose this. If it holds a real resource,
// you must dispose it yourself on shutdown:
app.Lifetime.ApplicationStopped.Register(() => pool.Dispose());

That fourth case is the one worth remembering, because it looks identical to the third at the call site.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Who is responsible for disposing services in ASP.NET Core?

The container disposes what it created. If you register by type or with a factory, the container constructs the instance and disposes it when its scope ends — scoped and transient services at the end of the request, singletons at application shutdown. The exception is an instance you construct yourself and pass to AddSingleton, because the container did not create it and assumes you are managing its lifetime. So it will not dispose it, and if it holds a real resource you have to do that yourself, typically on the application-stopped lifetime event.

Q: Should you ever call Dispose on an injected service?

No. If it arrived through injection you did not create it, so it is not yours to dispose. Disposing a scoped DbContext inside one service breaks every other service in that request that shares it — they get ObjectDisposedException — and the container will dispose it again at the end of the scope. You only dispose what you created yourself, like a MemoryStream you opened or a scope you called CreateScope on.

Q: What is the problem with transient disposable services?

They are not disposed when you finish with them — they are tracked by the scope that created them and disposed when that scope ends. So resolving a transient disposable in a loop means every instance is held until the request or scope completes, which for something holding a file handle or a connection is a genuine leak. The fix is a scope per unit of work so disposal happens at a predictable point, and the broader guidance is to avoid registering disposable services as transient at all — if it holds a resource, scoped usually makes the disposal point clearer.

Q: Why must you not dispose an HttpClient from IHttpClientFactory?

Because the factory manages the underlying HttpClientHandler pool, rotating handlers periodically so DNS changes are picked up while reusing connections. The HttpClient you receive is a lightweight wrapper over a pooled handler, so disposing it defeats the pooling and undermines the whole reason for using the factory. You just let it go out of scope.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Disposing an injected service breaks the rest of the request for anything sharing it.
  • AddSingleton(instance) is not disposed by the container. You own it.
  • Transient disposables are held until the scope ends, not when you finish with them.
  • CreateScope cannot dispose IAsyncDisposable services properly. Use CreateAsyncScope.
  • Never dispose an HttpClient from IHttpClientFactory.
  • A scoped disposable captured by a singleton is never disposed until shutdown.
  • Dispose must be safe to call twice, because double disposal does happen.
  • A long-lived scope accumulates every disposable it created, including transients.
