docs.title: 6.11 — Third-Party Containers: Autofac and Scrutor
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.10 Disposal · Next: 6.12 DI and testability

Markers: 🧠 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The built-in container is deliberately minimal. Two libraries fill the gaps.

  • Scrutor — not a container. It adds assembly scanning and decoration to the built-in one. Small, no lock-in.
  • Autofac — a full replacement container with property injection, interceptors and richer lifetimes.
  • The honest answer: most applications need neither. Reach for Scrutor first, and Autofac only for a specific missing feature.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Built-in container Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection The default. Deliberately minimal — "good enough for 80% of apps". Scrutor a NuGet package Extensions for the built-in container. Adds scanning and decoration. Not a replacement. Autofac a NuGet package A full alternative container that plugs into ASP.NET Core. Assembly scanning a technique Finding and registering types automatically by convention, rather than one line each. Decoration a pattern Wrapping a registered service in another that adds behaviour. See 22.4. Property injection an injection style Dependencies set via properties rather than the constructor. Not supported by the built-in container. Interception a technique Automatically wrapping method calls — for logging, caching, retries — without writing a decorator. IServiceProviderFactory<T> an interface The extension point a third-party container plugs into. UseServiceProviderFactory a method How you tell the host to use a different container.

docs.title: Why the built-in one is minimal on purpose
docs.text:
Microsoft designed Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection to be the lowest common denominator. It supports what every container supports — constructor injection, three lifetimes, generics — and nothing more.

The reason is compatibility. If the framework relied on advanced features, every third-party container would have to implement them to be usable with ASP.NET Core. Keeping the abstraction small means any container can plug in.

The trade-off: it lacks several things mature containers have.

Feature Built-in Scrutor Autofac Constructor injection ✅ ✅ ✅ Three lifetimes ✅ ✅ ✅ Open generics ✅ ✅ ✅ Keyed services ✅ (.NET 8+) ✅ ✅ Assembly scanning ❌ ✅ ✅ Decoration ❌ (manual) ✅ ✅ Property injection ❌ ❌ ✅ Interception ❌ ❌ ✅ Child lifetime scopes Limited — ✅

A picture: a hotel that provides a bed, a shower and a kettle. That covers most guests. If you need a kitchen, you book an apartment instead — but most people do not need one, and the apartment costs more.

docs.title: The simple version — Scrutor
docs.text:
Scrutor is not a container. It adds extension methods to IServiceCollection, so you keep the built-in container entirely.

Assembly scanning — register by convention instead of one line per service:

// Instead of forty lines like this...
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<ICustomerService, CustomerService>();
// ...

// ...scan for them
builder.Services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<OrderService>()
        .AddClasses(c => c.Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Service")))
        .AsImplementedInterfaces()
        .WithScopedLifetime());

That registers every class ending in "Service" against the interfaces it implements, as scoped.

⚠️ Scanning trades explicitness for brevity, and that trade is not free. With explicit registration you can search Program.cs for IOrderService and find where it is wired. With scanning, a service appears by convention, and the convention lives in a lambda somewhere. A typo in a class name silently means it is not registered, and the failure appears at runtime.

For a large codebase with a consistent convention it saves real effort. For a small one, explicit is clearer.

Decoration — the feature that genuinely fills a gap:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();

// Wrap it — consumers still inject IOrderRepository
builder.Services.Decorate<IOrderRepository, CachingOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.Decorate<IOrderRepository, LoggingOrderRepository>();

Compare with doing it by hand (6.8):

// The manual version — verbose, and easy to get wrong
builder.Services.AddScoped<EfOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository>(sp =>
    new LoggingOrderRepository(
        new CachingOrderRepository(
            sp.GetRequiredService<EfOrderRepository>(),
            sp.GetRequiredService<IMemoryCache>()),
        sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<LoggingOrderRepository>>()));

Scrutor handles the ordering and the resolution correctly. Decoration is the strongest reason to add it.

The decorator itself is an ordinary class:

public class CachingOrderRepository(
    IOrderRepository inner,                  // ← the wrapped one, injected
    IMemoryCache cache) : IOrderRepository
{
    public async Task<Order?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (cache.TryGetValue(id, out Order? cached))
            return cached;

        var order = await inner.GetAsync(id, ct);

        if (order is not null)
            cache.Set(id, order, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));

        return order;
    }
}

Note it takes IOrderRepository in its constructor — Scrutor supplies the previously registered implementation, not itself.

docs.title: How it actually works — Autofac
docs.text:
Autofac replaces the container. You plug it in at the host level:

builder.Host.UseServiceProviderFactory(new AutofacServiceProviderFactory());

builder.Host.ConfigureContainer<ContainerBuilder>(container =>
{
    container.RegisterType<OrderService>().As<IOrderService>().InstancePerLifetimeScope();

    // Property injection — not possible with the built-in container
    container.RegisterType<ReportService>().PropertiesAutowired();

    // Interception — wrap every call without writing a decorator
    container.RegisterType<PaymentService>()
        .As<IPaymentService>()
        .EnableInterfaceInterceptors()
        .InterceptedBy(typeof(LoggingInterceptor));
});

builder.Services.Add... still works — Autofac reads those registrations too — so framework registrations like AddControllers() are unaffected.

The two features worth switching for:

Property injection, when you cannot change a constructor — usually because a base class in a framework you do not control defines it.

Interception, which applies cross-cutting behaviour to every method of an interface without writing a decorator per service. If you want logging or retries on twenty services, twenty decorators is a lot of code; one interceptor is not.

⚠️ Both come at a cost. Property injection hides dependencies, which is the same objection as service locator (6.9). Interception uses dynamic proxies, which are harder to debug — the stack trace goes through generated types — and do not work with Native AOT (3.2).

docs.title: The deeper detail — should you?
docs.text:
The honest answer for most applications is no.

The built-in container covers constructor injection, three lifetimes, open generics and — since .NET 8 — keyed services. That is the large majority of what applications actually need.

Adding Scrutor is a small decision. It is a lightweight package that extends the existing container rather than replacing it, so there is no lock-in and no behaviour change to what you already have. If you need decoration, take it.

Replacing the container is a large decision:

  • Everyone on the team learns a second registration API
  • Debugging DI problems means understanding two systems
  • Some ASP.NET Core features assume the built-in container's behaviour
  • Container-specific registrations are hard to migrate away from later

⚠️ The question to ask: which specific feature do I need, and is there a simpler way? "More powerful" is not a reason. Needing interception across thirty services is.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Decoration with Scrutor, which is the realistic case:

// The real implementation
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();

// Layers applied inward-out: caching wraps EF, logging wraps caching
builder.Services.Decorate<IOrderRepository, CachingOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.Decorate<IOrderRepository, LoggingOrderRepository>();

// Resulting call order:
//   Logging → Caching → EfOrderRepository

public class LoggingOrderRepository(
    IOrderRepository inner,
    ILogger<LoggingOrderRepository> logger) : IOrderRepository
{
    public async Task<Order?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();
        try
        {
            return await inner.GetAsync(id, ct);
        }
        finally
        {
            logger.LogDebug("GetAsync({Id}) took {Ms}ms",
                id, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(sw).TotalMilliseconds);
        }
    }
}

Neither EfOrderRepository nor any consumer knows the decorators exist. That is the value — you added caching and timing without touching either end.

⚠️ Decoration order is registration order, applied outermost-last. Registering logging before caching would put caching outside logging, so cache hits would not be logged. That is easy to get backwards.

docs.title: Scanning, used carefully
docs.text:
builder.Services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<OrderService>()

        // Everything ending in "Service" → its interfaces, scoped
        .AddClasses(c => c.Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Service")), publicOnly: true)
            .AsImplementedInterfaces()
            .WithScopedLifetime()

        // Everything implementing IValidator<> → all of them, scoped
        .AddClasses(c => c.AssignableTo(typeof(IValidator<>)))
            .AsImplementedInterfaces()
            .WithScopedLifetime());

That second block is where scanning genuinely shines — registering every validator without one line each, which pairs with IEnumerable<T> injection (6.7).

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why would you replace the built-in DI container?

Usually you would not. The built-in one deliberately implements the lowest common denominator so that any third-party container can plug in, which means it covers constructor injection, the three lifetimes, open generics and keyed services — enough for most applications. You would replace it for a specific missing feature: property injection, when you cannot change a constructor because a framework base class defines it, or interception, when you want cross-cutting behaviour across many services without writing a decorator for each. "More powerful" is not a good enough reason, because you are asking the whole team to learn a second registration API and to debug two systems.

Q: What is Scrutor and how is it different from Autofac?

Scrutor is not a container at all — it is a small package of extension methods on IServiceCollection that adds two things the built-in container lacks: assembly scanning and decoration. You keep the built-in container entirely, so there is no lock-in and nothing about existing behaviour changes. Autofac is a full replacement container that plugs in through IServiceProviderFactory. So Scrutor is a small additive decision and Autofac is an architectural one.

Q: What is decoration and why does it need a library?

Decoration is wrapping a registered service in another implementing the same interface, so you can add caching or logging without changing the original or its consumers. The built-in container can do it, but only manually with factory registrations, and it is verbose and easy to get wrong — particularly the trap where registering the inner service as the interface makes the decorator wrap itself and recurse infinitely. Scrutor's Decorate handles the ordering and resolution correctly in one line, which is the strongest single reason to add it.

Q: What are the downsides of assembly scanning?

It trades explicitness for brevity. With explicit registration you can search for an interface and find exactly where it is wired; with scanning, services appear by convention and the convention is a lambda somewhere else. A class that does not match the naming pattern is silently not registered, and the failure appears at runtime rather than as a missing line you would notice in review. For a large codebase with a genuinely consistent convention it saves real effort, and for a smaller one explicit registration is clearer.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Scanning hides registrations, so a class not matching the convention is silently unregistered.
  • Decoration order is registration order, applied outermost-last. Easy to get backwards.
  • A decorator resolving the interface it implements recurses infinitely, unless the library handles it.
  • Property injection hides dependencies, the same objection as service locator.
  • Interception uses dynamic proxies, which complicate stack traces and break Native AOT.
  • Replacing the container is hard to reverse. Container-specific registrations do not port.
  • Scanning by name is fragile. Renaming a class can silently unregister it.

docs.title: 6.12 — Designing for Testability Through DI
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.11 Third-party containers · Next: 6.13 DI traps

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The practical payoff of DI is that a class can be built with fakes instead of the real thing, so tests run in milliseconds and touch nothing external.

  • A class using new to build its dependencies cannot be unit tested — the test hits the real database and sends real email.
  • Constructor injection means a unit test needs no container at all. Just new the class with test doubles.
  • The things that break testability are static access, DateTime.Now, and new inside a method.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Unit test a test Tests one class in isolation, with its dependencies replaced. Milliseconds. Integration test a test Tests several real components together, usually via WebApplicationFactory. Test double a stand-in Any fake object used in place of a real dependency. Stub a test double Returns canned answers. You do not assert on it. Mock a test double Records calls so you can assert they happened. Fake a test double A working but simplified implementation — an in-memory repository. Seam a design term A place where you can substitute behaviour without changing code. An interface is a seam. TimeProvider an abstract class (.NET 8+) The built-in abstraction over the clock. Makes time testable. WebApplicationFactory<T> a test class Boots the whole app in memory for integration tests. See 20.7. NullLogger<T> a class A logger that discards everything. For tests that do not care about logging.

docs.title: The argument in one comparison
docs.text:
Without DI:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly SqlOrderRepository _repo = new("Server=prod;...");
    private readonly SmtpEmailSender _email = new("smtp.company.com");

    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id) { /* ... */ }
}

To test CompleteAsync you need a real SQL Server, a real SMTP server, and you will send an actual email every time the test runs. In practice that means nobody tests it.

With DI:

public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, IEmailSender email)
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct) { /* ... */ }
}

var service = new OrderService(fakeRepo, fakeEmail);

No database, no mail server, no container. Milliseconds, and deterministic.

That is the whole argument, and it is the one to give in an interview — testability is the concrete, everyday benefit of DI, more than the "swap implementations" story people usually lead with.

A picture: a flight simulator. You cannot practise engine failure by breaking a real engine. A simulator lets you substitute the dangerous parts and test the pilot's response safely and repeatedly.

docs.title: The key insight: unit tests need no container
docs.text:
This surprises people who assume DI means "you need the DI framework in tests".

// No IServiceCollection, no IServiceProvider, no builder
var service = new OrderService(fakeRepo, fakeEmail, NullLogger<OrderService>.Instance);

The container is for composing the application. Tests compose one object by hand, which is simpler and faster. If a test needs a container, that is usually a sign it is an integration test rather than a unit test.

docs.title: The simple version — a real unit test
docs.text:
[Fact]
public async Task CompleteAsync_marks_order_complete_and_sends_email()
{
    // Arrange — fakes for both dependencies
    var repo  = Substitute.For<IOrderRepository>();
    var email = Substitute.For<IEmailSender>();

    var order = new Order(Guid.NewGuid()) { CustomerEmail = "ada@example.com" };
    repo.GetAsync(order.Id, Arg.Any<CancellationToken>()).Returns(order);

    var service = new OrderService(repo, email, NullLogger<OrderService>.Instance);

    // Act
    await service.CompleteAsync(order.Id, CancellationToken.None);

    // Assert — both the state change and the side effect
    Assert.Equal(OrderStatus.Complete, order.Status);

    await email.Received(1).SendAsync(
        "ada@example.com", "Order complete", Arg.Any<string>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
}

NullLogger<T>.Instance is worth knowing — a logger that discards everything, so you do not have to mock ILogger in every test.

docs.title: ⚠️ The three things that break testability
docs.text:
DI alone is not enough. Three habits defeat it.

1. Static access

public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo)
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct);
        EmailSender.Send(order.CustomerEmail, "Done");    // ⚠️ static — unsubstitutable
    }
}

The repository is injected and the email is not. You cannot replace a static call, so the test sends a real email. Anything static is a hard dependency (1.5).

2. new inside a method

public async Task ProcessAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    var client = new HttpClient();                        // ⚠️ real network call
    var response = await client.GetAsync("https://api.example.com", ct);
}

Injection in the constructor does not help if the method constructs its own dependencies. Inject IHttpClientFactory instead (19.10).

3. DateTime.Now — the sneakiest one

public bool IsExpired(Order order) => order.ExpiresAt < DateTime.UtcNow;    // ⚠️

You cannot test the boundary. A test for "expires in one second" would have to actually wait, and a test written at 23:59 may fail at midnight. Time-dependent logic becomes untestable or flaky.

The fix, since .NET 8, is TimeProvider:

public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, TimeProvider timeProvider)
{
    public bool IsExpired(Order order) => order.ExpiresAt < timeProvider.GetUtcNow();
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);       // production

// In a test — control time exactly
var time = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
var service = new OrderService(repo, time);

Assert.False(service.IsExpired(order));

time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(31));                      // move time forward instantly

Assert.True(service.IsExpired(order));

FakeTimeProvider comes from Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing. Before .NET 8 you hand-rolled an IClock interface, which is why so many codebases have one. See 20.12.

docs.title: How it actually works — designing the seams
docs.text:
A seam is somewhere you can substitute behaviour. Interfaces create seams; static calls and new destroy them.

The question to ask when designing a class: what does this touch that I cannot control in a test?

Touches Replace with Database IRepository or inject DbContext and use SQLite in-memory HTTP IHttpClientFactory, or a fake HttpMessageHandler File system IFileStore Current time TimeProvider Randomness Inject Random, or an IRandomProvider Environment variables IConfiguration The current user ICurrentUser rather than IHttpContextAccessor

⚠️ That last one matters. Injecting IHttpContextAccessor into a service couples it to the web (21.12). A small ICurrentUser abstraction is trivially fakeable and keeps the service usable from a background job too.

docs.title: The deeper detail — when not to abstract
docs.text:
⚠️ Not everything needs an interface (6.1). A pure function with no external dependencies is already testable:

public static class PriceCalculator
{
    public static decimal WithVat(decimal net, decimal rate) => net * (1 + rate);
}

There is nothing to substitute — the test just calls it. Wrapping it in IPriceCalculator adds a file and an indirection for no benefit.

The test for whether an abstraction is worth it: would I ever want to substitute this? If the answer is no, it is ceremony.

And there is a real cost to over-mocking:

// A test asserting on implementation details rather than behaviour
repo.Received(1).BeginTransaction();
repo.Received(1).GetAsync(Arg.Any<Guid>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
repo.Received(1).SaveAsync(Arg.Any<Order>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
repo.Received(1).Commit();

That test breaks whenever you refactor, even if the behaviour is unchanged. Assert on outcomes, not on the sequence of calls — see 20.4.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A service designed to be testable, with every seam deliberate:

public class SubscriptionService(
    ISubscriptionRepository repo,
    IPaymentGateway payments,
    IEmailSender email,
    TimeProvider time,                        // ← not DateTime.UtcNow
    ILogger<SubscriptionService> logger)
{
    public async Task<RenewalResult> RenewAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var subscription = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct)
                           ?? throw new NotFoundException(id);

        var now = time.GetUtcNow();

        if (subscription.ExpiresAt > now.AddDays(7))
            return RenewalResult.NotDue;

        var charge = await payments.ChargeAsync(
            subscription.CustomerId, subscription.Price, ct);

        if (!charge.Succeeded)
        {
            logger.LogWarning("Renewal declined for {SubscriptionId}", id);
            return RenewalResult.PaymentDeclined;
        }

        subscription.ExtendUntil(now.AddMonths(1));
        await repo.SaveAsync(subscription, ct);

        await email.SendAsync(subscription.CustomerEmail, "Renewed", "Thanks!", ct);

        return RenewalResult.Renewed;
    }
}

Every external interaction goes through an injected abstraction — including time. So:

[Fact]
public async Task RenewAsync_returns_NotDue_when_more_than_a_week_remains()
{
    var time = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));

    var subscription = new Subscription(Guid.NewGuid())
    {
        ExpiresAt = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)   // a month away
    };

    var repo = Substitute.For<ISubscriptionRepository>();
    repo.GetAsync(subscription.Id, Arg.Any<CancellationToken>()).Returns(subscription);

    var payments = Substitute.For<IPaymentGateway>();

    var service = new SubscriptionService(
        repo, payments, Substitute.For<IEmailSender>(),
        time, NullLogger<SubscriptionService>.Instance);

    var result = await service.RenewAsync(subscription.Id, CancellationToken.None);

    Assert.Equal(RenewalResult.NotDue, result);

    // And prove we did NOT charge them
    await payments.DidNotReceive().ChargeAsync(
        Arg.Any<Guid>(), Arg.Any<decimal>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
}

That test is deterministic and instant. It would run identically in 2030, which a DateTime.UtcNow version would not.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does dependency injection make code testable?

Because a class declares what it needs rather than constructing it, you can supply test doubles instead of the real implementations. A service that builds its own SQL repository and SMTP client cannot be unit tested at all — the test would need a real database and would send an actual email, so in practice nobody tests it. With constructor injection the test just news up the class with fakes and runs in milliseconds with no external dependencies. Worth noting that unit tests need no container at all — the container composes the application, but a test composes one object by hand.

Q: What breaks testability even when you are using DI?

Three things. Static access, because you cannot substitute a static call — so a service that injects a repository but calls a static EmailSender still sends real email in tests. Constructing dependencies inside a method with new, since constructor injection does not help if the method builds its own HttpClient. And DateTime.Now, which is the sneakiest, because time-dependent logic then either cannot be tested at boundaries or produces tests that fail at midnight. TimeProvider in .NET 8 is the built-in fix for the last one.

Q: What is TimeProvider and why does it matter?

It is an abstraction over the clock added in .NET 8. You inject it and call GetUtcNow instead of DateTime.UtcNow, register TimeProvider.System in production, and in tests use FakeTimeProvider, which lets you set the current time and advance it instantly. That makes expiry logic, scheduling and timeouts genuinely testable — you can assert behaviour a month later without waiting. Before .NET 8 everyone hand-rolled an IClock interface for the same reason, which is why so many codebases have one.

Q: Should every class have an interface so it can be mocked?

No, and doing it reflexively adds files and indirection for nothing. The test is whether you would ever want to substitute it — a pure calculation with no external dependencies is already testable by calling it directly. There is also a cost to over-mocking: tests that assert on the exact sequence of calls rather than on outcomes break whenever you refactor, even when the behaviour is unchanged. I would abstract the things a test cannot control — database, network, file system, time, randomness — and leave pure logic alone.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Static calls cannot be substituted. DI in the constructor does not help if a method calls a static.
  • new inside a method defeats constructor injection.
  • DateTime.Now makes time-dependent logic untestable or flaky. Use TimeProvider.
  • Injecting IHttpContextAccessor into a service couples it to the web. Use a small ICurrentUser abstraction.
  • Unit tests should not need a container. If yours does, it is probably an integration test.
  • Interfaces with one implementation and no test double are ceremony.
  • Asserting on call sequences rather than outcomes produces tests that break on every refactor.
  • Mocking IServiceProvider is brittle — a symptom of the service locator pattern (6.9).

docs.title: 6.13 — Classic DI Interview Traps
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.12 DI and testability · Next: 7.1 Configuration system

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The DI mistakes interviewers actually ask about, collected. Every one of them compiles, starts, and works in development — which is precisely why they get asked.

  • Scoped into singleton — the captive dependency. The single most-asked DI question.
  • Registering DbContext as a singleton — not thread-safe, and a memory leak.
  • Resolving scoped services in Program.cs or a background service without a scope.
  • The detection that would have caught most of these is Development-only by default.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Captive dependency a bug A short-lived service held by a longer-lived one. See 6.4. Root provider the app-level container app.Services. Has no request scope. Resolving scoped services from it is wrong. ValidateScopes a container option Detects lifetime mismatches. Development-only by default. ValidateOnBuild a container option Verifies every registration resolves, at startup. Development-only by default. Change tracker an EF Core component Holds every entity a DbContext has loaded. Never resets if the context is never disposed. IServiceScopeFactory an interface The correct way to create a scope from a singleton. IOptionsSnapshot<T> an interface Scoped, unlike IOptions<T>. Cannot go in a singleton constructor. Service locator an anti-pattern Injecting IServiceProvider to pull services out. See 6.9.

docs.title: Why these bugs survive to production
docs.text:
Every trap in this note shares one property: it works with one user.

In development you click through the app one request at a time. A singleton DbContext is never touched concurrently. A captive dependency never has a second scope to conflict with. A memory leak never runs long enough to matter.

Then production applies concurrency and uptime, and all three surface at once.

⚠️ Worse: the container's own detection is disabled in production by default. ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild default to on in Development and off elsewhere — so the environment that would have caught the bug is the one you never deploy.

That is the single most useful thing to say in an interview on this topic. It explains why these are production bugs rather than development ones, and the fix is one block of code:

builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(options =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes  = true;
    options.ValidateOnBuild = true;
});

docs.title: Trap 1 — Scoped into singleton ⭐ the most-asked
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(...);        // scoped
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CacheWarmer>();

public class CacheWarmer(AppDbContext db) { }            // ⚠️ CAPTIVE

The singleton resolves AppDbContext once and holds it forever. Three failures at once: it is not thread-safe across concurrent requests, its change tracker grows without limit, and it returns stale cached entities.

Fix: inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per operation (6.5). Full detail in 6.4.

docs.title: Trap 2 — DbContext as a singleton
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddSingleton<AppDbContext>();           // ✗ never

Usually done "for performance", on the assumption that creating one is expensive. It is not — DbContext creation is cheap, and AddDbContextPool exists if you want pooling (13.2).

Fix: AddDbContext registers it as scoped, which is correct. Do not override that.

docs.title: Trap 3 — Resolving scoped services at startup
docs.text:
var app = builder.Build();

var db = app.Services.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();   // ✗ throws
await db.Database.MigrateAsync();

InvalidOperationException: Cannot resolve scoped service from root provider.

app.Services is the root provider and there is no ambient scope during startup.

Fix:

using var scope = app.Services.CreateScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
await db.Database.MigrateAsync();

docs.title: Trap 4 — The scope outside the loop
docs.text:
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();         // ⚠️ outside
    var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        await ProcessBatchAsync(db, stoppingToken);
        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), stoppingToken);
    }
}

This looks correct — a scope was created. But it lives for the service's entire lifetime, so the change tracker accumulates every entity from every iteration. The captive dependency, moved rather than fixed.

Fix: the scope goes inside the loop (21.2).

docs.title: Trap 5 — IServiceProvider instead of IServiceScopeFactory
docs.text:
public class Worker(IServiceProvider provider) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var db = provider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();   // ⚠️ ROOT scope
    }
}

IServiceProvider injected into a singleton is the root provider. Resolving a scoped service from it creates it in the root scope — which lives for the whole application.

⚠️ And ValidateScopes does not catch this, because the resolution is explicit rather than a constructor mismatch. It is the quieter version of trap 1.

Fix: IServiceScopeFactory, then CreateScope().

docs.title: Trap 6 — Conventional middleware constructor
docs.text:
public class AuditMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, AppDbContext db)   // ⚠️
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context) { }
}

Conventional middleware is instantiated once, at pipeline construction — so it is a singleton (5.5).

Fix: scoped services go in the InvokeAsync parameters, which are resolved per request:

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, AppDbContext db) { }

docs.title: Trap 7 — IOptionsSnapshot<T> in a singleton
docs.text:
public class PriceService(IOptionsSnapshot<PriceOptions> options) { }   // ⚠️

IOptions<T> is a singleton and fine here. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, so injecting it into a singleton is a captive dependency.

Fix: use IOptions<T> if the value never changes, or IOptionsMonitor<T> — which is a singleton and still picks up changes (7.6).

docs.title: Trap 8 — Duplicate registration silently overriding
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SmtpEmailSender>();
// ... 200 lines later, in a different extension method ...
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();

Both register. Resolving IEmailSender gives you SendGrid — last one wins — with no warning.

Fix: TryAdd in library code, so a default does not override a deliberate choice (6.6).

docs.title: Trap 9 — Disposing an injected service
docs.text:
public async Task ProcessAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    using (db)                                            // ⚠️
    {
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    }
}

You did not create it. Disposing it breaks every other service in the request sharing that scoped context (6.10).

Fix: do not. The scope disposes it.

docs.title: Trap 10 — Transient disposables in a loop
docs.text:
foreach (var path in paths)
{
    var handle = provider.GetRequiredService<IFileHandle>();   // transient, IDisposable
    await handle.WriteAsync(path, ct);
}
// 10,000 file handles held until the scope ends

Transient disposables are tracked by the scope and disposed when it ends — not when you finish with them.

Fix: a scope per iteration, or do not register disposables as transient.

docs.title: The quick reference 🎯
docs.text: Trap Symptom Fix Scoped → singleton Corruption under load, growing memory IServiceScopeFactory Singleton DbContext "A second operation was started..." Keep it scoped Scoped at startup "Cannot resolve scoped service from root provider" CreateScope() Scope outside the loop Memory grows over hours Scope inside the loop IServiceProvider in a singleton Silent captive dependency IServiceScopeFactory Scoped in middleware constructor Captive DbContext Move to InvokeAsync params IOptionsSnapshot in a singleton Captive dependency IOptions or IOptionsMonitor Duplicate registration Wrong implementation, silently TryAdd Disposing an injected service ObjectDisposedException mid-request Do not dispose it Transient disposables in a loop Handle exhaustion Scope per iteration

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The defensive configuration that catches most of these at startup:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Turn the Development-only safety net on EVERYWHERE
builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(options =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes  = true;      // catches traps 1, 6, 7
    options.ValidateOnBuild = true;      // catches missing registrations at startup
});

⚠️ ValidateOnBuild adds startup time proportional to the number of registrations — a few hundred milliseconds on a large application. That is a good trade for turning a first-request failure in production into a startup failure in CI.

And the background service pattern that avoids traps 3, 4, 5 and 10 together:

public class OrderCleanupService(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory,                   // ✓ not IServiceProvider
    ILogger<OrderCleanupService> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            try
            {
                await using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope();   // ✓ inside the loop
                var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

                var removed = await db.Orders
                    .Where(o => o.ExpiresAt < DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)
                    .ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);

                logger.LogInformation("Removed {Count} expired orders", removed);
            }
            catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                break;
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Cleanup failed, will retry");
            }

            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

Four things right in that one method: the scope factory rather than the provider, the scope inside the loop, CreateAsyncScope because DbContext is IAsyncDisposable, and cancellation treated as normal shutdown rather than an error.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the most common DI mistake you see?

Injecting a scoped service into a singleton — the captive dependency. The singleton resolves it once at construction and holds it for the application's lifetime, so a DbContext meant to live one request ends up shared across every concurrent request. That is a thread-safety bug, a memory leak because the change tracker never resets, and a correctness bug because you read stale cached entities. The reason it reaches production is that the container's scope validation is enabled in Development only by default, so the environment that would catch it is the one you never deploy.

Q: Why does a background service need special handling for DbContext?

Because BackgroundService is registered as a singleton and there is no ambient scope outside an HTTP request, so injecting a scoped service into it is a captive dependency, and resolving one from app.Services throws. You inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work. The subtle part is that the scope has to go inside the work loop — creating it once outside looks correct and gives you a single DbContext for the service's entire lifetime, which is the same bug relocated rather than fixed.

Q: Why is injecting IServiceProvider into a singleton not a fix for that?

Because the provider you receive is the root one, so resolving a scoped service from it creates that service in the root scope, which lives for the whole application. You have recreated the captive dependency less visibly — and scope validation will not catch it, because the resolution is an explicit call rather than a constructor mismatch the container can inspect. IServiceScopeFactory is the right dependency, because it gives you a genuine short-lived scope.

Q: How would you make these bugs surface earlier?

Enable ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild in every environment rather than accepting the Development-only default. Scope validation turns a captive dependency into a startup exception naming both types, and build validation walks every registration and confirms it can actually be resolved, so a missing dependency fails at startup instead of on the first request that reaches that path. It costs some startup time on a large application, which is a good trade for finding the problem in CI rather than production.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild are Development-only by default. Enable them everywhere.
  • Transient into singleton does not throw but is still captive.
  • IServiceProvider in a singleton gives the root scope, and validation misses it.
  • A scope created outside a loop is a captive dependency in disguise.
  • IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, unlike IOptions<T>.
  • Conventional middleware is a singleton — scoped services go in InvokeAsync.
  • Duplicate registrations silently override, last one wins.
  • Never dispose an injected service.
  • All of these work fine with one user, which is why they reach production.

docs.title: 7.1 — The Configuration System: Providers and Precedence
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 6.13 DI traps · Next: 7.2 appsettings.json

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Configuration in ASP.NET Core is a set of key/value pairs, gathered from several providers and merged into one flat dictionary.

  • Providers are loaded in order, and later ones overwrite earlier ones with the same key.
  • The default order ends with environment variables and command-line arguments, which is how you override settings at deployment.
  • Everything becomes a string keyed by a colon-separated path — "Logging:LogLevel:Default".

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Configuration a key/value store A flat dictionary of string keys to string values, built at startup. Provider a source of settings Something that contributes key/value pairs — a JSON file, environment variables, Key Vault. IConfiguration an interface The merged result. Injectable. Read-only. IConfigurationBuilder an interface Assembles providers in order, then builds the IConfiguration. Precedence the override rule Later providers win. The last provider to supply a key decides its value. Key path a string Nested keys flattened with colons: "Logging:LogLevel:Default". Section an IConfigurationSection A subtree of the configuration, addressed by a key prefix. GetSection a method Returns a section. Never returns null — an absent section is an empty one. Double underscore an escape convention __ in an environment variable name becomes : in the key path. Reload a provider feature Re-reading a source when it changes. See 7.9.

docs.title: What replaced web.config
docs.text:
Classic ASP.NET had web.config — one XML file, on the machine, read at startup. Everything came from there, and changing it usually meant a deployment.

ASP.NET Core replaced it with something more flexible: many sources, merged in a defined order.

The reason is deployment. The same compiled application has to run on your laptop, in a test environment, and in production, with different connection strings and different secrets. You do not want three builds — you want one build and different configuration (4.7).

So configuration is layered:

appsettings.json                    ← shared defaults, in source control
appsettings.{Environment}.json      ← per-environment overrides, in source control
User Secrets                        ← local secrets, NOT in source control
Environment variables               ← deployment settings and secrets
Command-line arguments              ← last-minute overrides

Each layer only needs to specify what differs from the ones below it.

A picture: transparent sheets stacked on an overhead projector. The bottom sheet has the full picture. Each sheet above changes a few details. What you see is the combination, with the top sheet winning wherever they overlap.

docs.title: ⚠️ The rule that matters: later wins
docs.text:
This is the single most important thing to know:

Providers are loaded in order, and a later provider overwrites an earlier one with the same key.

That is why an environment variable beats appsettings.json, and why command-line arguments beat everything. It is also why setting a value in the wrong place silently does nothing — something later is overwriting it.

docs.title: The simple version — the default order
docs.text:
WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args) sets this up (4.3):

# Provider Notes 1 appsettings.json Always loaded 2 appsettings.{Environment}.json Only that environment's file 3 User Secrets Development only 4 Environment variables 5 Command-line arguments Highest priority

Higher number wins. So:

// appsettings.json
{ "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information" } } }

# This overrides it, because environment variables come later
Logging__LogLevel__Default=Warning

# And this overrides both
dotnet run --Logging:LogLevel:Default=Debug

docs.title: Keys are flat, nested by colon
docs.text:
Configuration is not a tree — it is a flat dictionary. Nested JSON gets flattened:

{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Default": "Server=localhost;Database=App"
  },
  "Orders": {
    "MaxItems": 100,
    "Notifications": { "Enabled": true }
  }
}

becomes:

"ConnectionStrings:Default"      = "Server=localhost;Database=App"
"Orders:MaxItems"                = "100"
"Orders:Notifications:Enabled"   = "true"

Two consequences worth noting.

Everything is a string. 100 and true are stored as "100" and "true". Conversion happens when you read them (7.5).

Arrays become indexed keys:

{ "AllowedHosts": ["a.com", "b.com"] }

"AllowedHosts:0" = "a.com"
"AllowedHosts:1" = "b.com"

⚠️ That array behaviour causes a real trap. Because merging happens key by key, overriding an array in a later provider does not replace it — it overwrites individual indices. A three-element array overridden by a one-element array leaves elements 1 and 2 from the original in place. See 7.2.

docs.title: ⚠️ Double underscores in environment variables
docs.text:
Environment variable names cannot contain colons on all platforms, so the convention is __:

# These are the same key
ConnectionStrings__Default="Server=prod;..."      # environment variable
"ConnectionStrings:Default"                       # configuration key

Getting this wrong is a very common deployment mistake — a single underscore does nothing, and there is no error. The setting is simply absent and you fall back to whatever appsettings.json said.

docs.title: How it actually works — building it yourself
docs.text:
The defaults cover almost everything, but you can add or reorder providers:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Added AFTER the defaults, so this wins over all of them
builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("appsettings.Local.json", optional: true, reloadOnChange: true);

// Or start from scratch
builder.Configuration.Sources.Clear();
builder.Configuration
    .AddJsonFile("appsettings.json", optional: false, reloadOnChange: true)
    .AddEnvironmentVariables()
    .AddCommandLine(args);

⚠️ Order of the Add calls is the precedence order. Adding AddEnvironmentVariables() before AddJsonFile(...) means the JSON file wins over environment variables — which is almost certainly not what you want, and is a genuinely confusing bug because everything looks configured correctly.

optional: false is worth using for the base file. It makes a missing appsettings.json fail at startup rather than silently producing an application with no configuration.

docs.title: Which provider supplied a value?
docs.text:
When a setting is not what you expect, this is how you find out:

var root = (IConfigurationRoot)builder.Configuration;
Console.WriteLine(root.GetDebugView());

That prints every key, its value, and which provider supplied it:

ConnectionStrings:
  Default=Server=prod;... (EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider)
Logging:
  LogLevel:
    Default=Warning (JsonConfigurationProvider for 'appsettings.Production.json')

⚠️ Never leave that in production code — it prints secrets. It is a debugging tool, and worth gating behind an environment check if you keep it at all.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what a provider actually is
docs.text:
A provider is anything that can produce key/value pairs. The built-in ones:

Provider Added by JSON file AddJsonFile Environment variables AddEnvironmentVariables Command line AddCommandLine User Secrets AddUserSecrets In-memory AddInMemoryCollection INI / XML AddIniFile / AddXmlFile Azure Key Vault AddAzureKeyVault AWS Secrets Manager AddSecretsManager

The in-memory one is genuinely useful in tests, because it lets you set configuration without files:

builder.Configuration.AddInMemoryCollection(new Dictionary<string, string?>
{
    ["ConnectionStrings:Default"] = "DataSource=:memory:",
    ["Features:EnableNewCheckout"] = "true"
});

See 20.7.

Writing your own provider is covered in 7.10.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic setup, with the reasoning inline:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// The defaults already gave us:
//   appsettings.json → appsettings.{Env}.json → User Secrets (dev) →
//   env vars → command line

// Add Key Vault in production only, AFTER the defaults so it wins over files
if (builder.Environment.IsProduction())
{
    builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
        new Uri($"https://{builder.Configuration["KeyVault:Name"]}.vault.azure.net/"),
        new DefaultAzureCredential());
}

// Fail fast if something essential is missing, rather than at first use
var connectionString = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "ConnectionStrings:Default is not configured.");

builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(connectionString));

var app = builder.Build();

That startup check is worth the two lines. Without it, a missing connection string surfaces as an obscure error on the first database call, potentially long after deployment.

docs.title: Where each thing belongs
docs.text:
Setting Belongs in Log levels, feature defaults appsettings.json Per-environment endpoints, log levels appsettings.{Environment}.json Local connection strings and API keys User Secrets — never in source control Production secrets Key Vault or the platform's secret store Deployment-specific values Environment variables One-off overrides while debugging Command-line arguments

⚠️ The line that matters: no real secret goes in any appsettings*.json file. Those are committed to source control, so anything in them is in your git history permanently and visible to everyone with repository access. See 17.7.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does configuration work in ASP.NET Core?

It is a flat dictionary of string keys to string values, built at startup by merging several providers. The defaults are appsettings.json, then the environment-specific file, then User Secrets in Development, then environment variables, then command-line arguments — and they are applied in that order, with later providers overwriting earlier ones for the same key. That layering is what lets one compiled build run in every environment with different settings, which is the whole point compared to web.config.

Q: What is the precedence order and why does it matter?

Later providers win. So an environment variable overrides appsettings.json, and a command-line argument overrides everything. It matters because that is how you supply deployment-specific values and secrets without changing files that are in source control. It also explains a common confusion — someone sets a value in appsettings.json, it has no effect, and the reason is that an environment variable set by the hosting platform is overwriting it. GetDebugView on the configuration root tells you which provider supplied each value, which is the fastest way to diagnose that.

Q: How do you express a nested configuration key as an environment variable?

With double underscores. Configuration keys are colon-separated paths like ConnectionStrings:Default, but environment variable names cannot reliably contain colons, so the convention is ConnectionStrings__Default. Using a single underscore is a common deployment mistake and there is no error — the variable simply is not recognised as that key, so the application silently falls back to whatever the JSON file said.

Q: What happens to arrays in configuration?

They are flattened into indexed keys, so a three-element array becomes Key:0, Key:1, Key:2. That causes a real trap when overriding: because merging happens per key, supplying a shorter array in a later provider overwrites only the indices it defines and leaves the rest of the original in place. So overriding a three-item list with a one-item list gives you the new first item and the original second and third. If you need to replace a list entirely you have to clear it explicitly or restructure the setting.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Later providers win. A value set in the wrong layer is silently overwritten.
  • Environment variables need __, not _. A single underscore silently does nothing.
  • Arrays merge by index, so a shorter override leaves the original tail elements in place.
  • The order of Add calls is the precedence order. Adding a JSON file after AddEnvironmentVariables makes the file win.
  • Everything is a string. "true" and "100" are converted when read, and a bad value throws at that point.
  • GetSection never returns null — an absent section is an empty one, so a typo produces silence rather than an error.
  • GetDebugView prints secrets. Never leave it in production code.
  • No secrets in appsettings*.json. Those files are in source control.

docs.title: 7.2 — appsettings.json and Environment Overrides
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.1 The configuration system · Next: 7.3 Environment variables and User Secrets

Markers: 🔥 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
appsettings.json holds your application's settings. appsettings.{Environment}.json is layered on top of it, overriding only the values that differ.

  • The environment file is chosen by ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT, so Production loads appsettings.Production.json.
  • Put only the differences in the environment file. Copying the whole base file causes drift.
  • ⚠️ These files are in source control. No real secrets go in either of them.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means appsettings.json a JSON file The base settings file. Always loaded. Shared defaults. appsettings.{Env}.json a JSON file Loaded on top of the base file for that environment only. Layering the merge behaviour The environment file's values overwrite the base file's for matching keys. ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT an environment variable Selects which environment file loads. See 4.7. optional a parameter on AddJsonFile Whether a missing file is an error. Base file false, environment file true. reloadOnChange a parameter on AddJsonFile Re-read the file when it changes on disk. See 7.9. ConnectionStrings a conventional section Read with GetConnectionString("Name"), which is shorthand for ["ConnectionStrings:Name"]. Copy to output a build setting These files are copied to the publish folder. That is why they deploy. $schema a JSON property Points at a schema so your editor offers IntelliSense and validation.

docs.title: Two files, one result
docs.text:
Every ASP.NET Core project starts with two:

appsettings.json                  ← always loaded
appsettings.Development.json      ← loaded only when the environment is Development

They are merged, not chosen between. The base file supplies everything, and the environment file overrides individual keys.

// appsettings.json — the shared baseline
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information", "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning" }
  },
  "ConnectionStrings": { "Default": "Server=localhost;Database=App;Trusted_Connection=true" },
  "Orders": { "MaxItems": 100, "AutoApproveUnder": 50.00 }
}

// appsettings.Development.json — ONLY what differs
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Default": "Debug" }
  }
}

Running in Development, the application sees:

  • Logging:LogLevel:Default = Debug — overridden
  • Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore = Warning — inherited from the base
  • ConnectionStrings:Default = localhost — inherited
  • Orders:MaxItems = 100 — inherited

Note that the override is per key, not per section. Supplying Logging:LogLevel:Default did not remove the sibling Microsoft.AspNetCore entry. That per-key merging is the behaviour to internalise.

A picture: a base recipe with a sticky note on top. The note says "use butter instead of oil". Everything else on the recipe still applies — you did not have to rewrite it.

docs.title: ⚠️ Do not copy the whole base file
docs.text:
The most common mistake:

// appsettings.Production.json — ✗ the entire base file, copied and edited
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Default": "Warning", "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning" }
  },
  "ConnectionStrings": { "Default": "Server=prod;..." },
  "Orders": { "MaxItems": 100, "AutoApproveUnder": 50.00 }
}

Now Orders:MaxItems exists in four files. Changing it means changing all four, someone forgets one, and environments drift apart in ways nobody notices until behaviour differs.

Override only what actually changes. If a value is the same everywhere, it belongs in the base file alone.

docs.title: The simple version — the file set
docs.text:
appsettings.json                  ← base, always
appsettings.Development.json      ← local machines
appsettings.Staging.json          ← staging
appsettings.Production.json       ← production

The environment name comes from ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT, and the file name must match it exactly (4.7).

⚠️ Case sensitivity is a real deployment trap. Environment name checks in code are case-insensitive, but file names on Linux are not. So appsettings.production.json is silently ignored when the environment is Production — the app starts, uses only the base file, and connects to the wrong database. On Windows it works, which is why this survives testing.

Match the case exactly.

docs.title: The ConnectionStrings convention
docs.text:
{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Default": "Server=localhost;Database=App",
    "ReadReplica": "Server=replica;Database=App"
  }
}

// These are identical
var cs = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default");
var cs = builder.Configuration["ConnectionStrings:Default"];

GetConnectionString is just shorthand. The section name is a convention rather than anything special — but following it means the shorthand works and other developers find it where they expect.

docs.title: How it actually works — the array merge trap ⚠️
docs.text:
Because merging happens key by key, arrays behave surprisingly.

// appsettings.json
{ "AllowedOrigins": [ "https://a.com", "https://b.com", "https://c.com" ] }

Flattened, that is:

AllowedOrigins:0 = "https://a.com"
AllowedOrigins:1 = "https://b.com"
AllowedOrigins:2 = "https://c.com"

Now override it:

// appsettings.Production.json — trying to allow only one origin
{ "AllowedOrigins": [ "https://prod.com" ] }

That sets AllowedOrigins:0 and nothing else. The result is:

AllowedOrigins:0 = "https://prod.com"     ← overridden
AllowedOrigins:1 = "https://b.com"        ← STILL THERE
AllowedOrigins:2 = "https://c.com"        ← STILL THERE

You intended one allowed origin and got three. For a CORS policy that is a security problem (10.10).

Three ways round it:

// 1. Do not put lists in the base file if they will be overridden
// appsettings.json — no AllowedOrigins at all
// appsettings.Production.json
{ "AllowedOrigins": [ "https://prod.com" ] }

// 2. Use a delimited string and split it yourself
{ "AllowedOrigins": "https://prod.com" }

// 3. Clear it explicitly before binding
var origins = config.GetSection("AllowedOrigins").Get<string[]>() ?? [];

Option 1 is usually cleanest. If a list varies by environment, it should live only in the environment files.

docs.title: The deeper detail — how these files reach production
docs.text:
appsettings*.json files are marked to copy to the output directory, so dotnet publish includes them (3.8).

That has two consequences.

All of them ship, including appsettings.Development.json. Only the matching one is loaded, so it does no harm functionally — but it is in the deployed artifact and readable by anyone with access to the container image. Do not treat "it is only for development" as protection.

Changes require a redeploy, unless reloadOnChange is enabled and something updates the file in place (7.9).

You can control the copy behaviour if needed:

<ItemGroup>
  <Content Update="appsettings.Development.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="Never" />
</ItemGroup>

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text:
Adding a schema reference gives you IntelliSense and validation in Visual Studio and VS Code:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/appsettings.json",
  "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information" } }
}

Small, and it catches typos in framework setting names — which otherwise fail silently, because an unrecognised key is simply an unused key.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic pair of files:

// appsettings.json — defaults that are true everywhere
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/appsettings.json",
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning",
      "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command": "Warning"
    }
  },
  "AllowedHosts": "*",
  "Orders": {
    "MaxItemsPerOrder": 100,
    "AutoApproveUnder": 50.00,
    "ReservationMinutes": 15
  },
  "Payments": {
    "TimeoutSeconds": 30,
    "MaxRetries": 3
    // NOTE: no ApiKey here — that is a secret. See 7.3 and 7.4.
  }
}

// appsettings.Development.json — ONLY the differences
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Debug",
      "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command": "Information"   // see the SQL locally
    }
  },
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Default": "Server=(localdb)\\mssqllocaldb;Database=AppDev;Trusted_Connection=true"
  }
}

// appsettings.Production.json — also only the differences
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Default": "Warning" }
  },
  "Orders": {
    "ReservationMinutes": 5      // shorter hold under real load
  }
  // No connection string — that comes from an environment variable or Key Vault
}

Three deliberate decisions there:

The production connection string is absent from the file. It arrives as an environment variable or from Key Vault, so the real credential is never in source control (7.4).

EF Core command logging is raised in development only. At Information it logs every SQL statement — invaluable locally, overwhelming in production (5.14).

Each environment file is short. Everything not mentioned is inherited.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do appsettings.json and appsettings.{Environment}.json work together?

They are merged rather than chosen between. The base file is always loaded and supplies the defaults; the environment file is loaded on top of it and overrides individual keys. The environment is selected by ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT, so a value of Production loads appsettings.Production.json. The merge is per key, not per section, so overriding one log level does not remove its siblings — which means each environment file should contain only the values that actually differ.

Q: What goes wrong if you copy the whole base file into each environment file?

Every setting then exists in several places, so changing one means changing all of them. Someone inevitably misses one and the environments drift apart in ways nobody notices until behaviour differs between staging and production. Since the merge is per key, there is no need — anything not mentioned in the environment file is inherited automatically.

Q: What is the trap with arrays in configuration?

Arrays are flattened into indexed keys, and merging happens per key, so overriding an array does not replace it. Supplying a one-element array over a three-element one sets index zero and leaves indices one and two from the original in place. That is genuinely dangerous for something like a CORS allowed-origins list, where you intended to restrict it to one origin and silently kept three. The cleanest fix is to keep lists that vary by environment out of the base file altogether.

Q: Should connection strings go in appsettings.json?

A local development one is fine, since it is not a real credential. A production connection string is not, because these files are in source control and anything in them is in the git history permanently and visible to everyone with repository access. Production connection strings belong in environment variables set by the hosting platform, or in a secret store like Key Vault. Worth also knowing that all the appsettings files ship in the published output, including the Development one, so "it is only for development" is not protection.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• File names are case-sensitive on Linux. appsettings.production.json is silently ignored when the environment is Production — and works fine on Windows.
  • Arrays merge by index, so a shorter override leaves the original tail elements behind.
  • Copying the whole base file into environment files causes configuration drift.
  • No real secrets in any appsettings*.json. They are in source control.
  • All the environment files ship in the published output, not just the active one.
  • An unrecognised key is silently ignored. Typos in framework setting names do nothing, with no warning. A $schema reference catches many of them.
  • Comments are allowed in these files by the .NET JSON reader, despite not being standard JSON — but some tooling will complain.

docs.title: 7.3 — Environment Variables, Command-Line Args, User Secrets
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.2 appsettings.json · Next: 7.4 Secret providers

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The three providers that sit above the JSON files, and the two that carry secrets.

  • User Secrets — local development secrets, stored outside the project folder so they cannot be committed. Development only.
  • Environment variables — how deployment platforms supply settings. Nested keys use double underscores.
  • Command-line arguments — highest precedence of all. For one-off overrides.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means User Secrets a development feature Settings stored in your user profile, outside the project, so git cannot see them. UserSecretsId a GUID in the .csproj Links the project to its secrets file. secrets.json a file Where User Secrets live, under your user profile directory. dotnet user-secrets a CLI command Sets, lists and removes secrets. Environment variable an OS-level setting A name/value pair the process reads at startup. __ an escape sequence Double underscore in a variable name becomes : in the key path. AddEnvironmentVariables(prefix) a method Loads only variables with a given prefix, stripping it. Command-line argument a startup argument --Key=Value or --Key Value. Highest precedence. Switch mapping an alias Maps a short argument like -e to a full key path. args the Main parameter Must be passed to CreateBuilder(args) or command-line config does not work.

docs.title: Why secrets cannot live in JSON
docs.text:
appsettings.json is committed to source control (7.2). Anything in it is:

  • In your git history permanently, even if you delete it later
  • Visible to everyone with repository access
  • Picked up by automated secret scanners, which is how leaked keys get found
  • Present in every clone, every fork, and every CI checkout

So a real API key in appsettings.json is effectively published.

But you still need those values to run the application locally. That is the problem User Secrets solves: settings that behave like configuration but live outside the project folder, where git cannot reach them.

A picture: your house keys versus the address on your business card. The address is fine to print and hand out. The keys stay in your pocket, and no amount of "I will remember to take them off the card later" makes printing them acceptable.

docs.title: The three, and where each fits
docs.text:
Provider Used for Available in User Secrets Local secrets during development Development only Environment variables Deployment settings and secrets Everywhere Command-line arguments Temporary overrides while debugging Everywhere

Precedence runs upward — command line beats environment variables, which beat User Secrets, which beat the JSON files (7.1).

docs.title: The simple version — User Secrets
docs.text:
# Once per project — adds a UserSecretsId to the .csproj
dotnet user-secrets init

# Set values. Note the COLON, not double underscore, in the CLI.
dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:Default" "Server=localhost;Database=Dev;..."
dotnet user-secrets set "Payments:ApiKey" "sk_test_abc123"

dotnet user-secrets list
dotnet user-secrets remove "Payments:ApiKey"
dotnet user-secrets clear

init adds one line to the project file:

<PropertyGroup>
  <UserSecretsId>a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890</UserSecretsId>
</PropertyGroup>

That GUID is the only link. The values themselves live at:

Windows:  %APPDATA%\Microsoft\UserSecrets\<UserSecretsId>\secrets.json
Linux:    ~/.microsoft/usersecrets/<UserSecretsId>/secrets.json
macOS:    ~/.microsoft/usersecrets/<UserSecretsId>/secrets.json

Outside the project folder, so git add . cannot pick them up. That is the entire mechanism — and it is the reason to prefer them over a gitignored file, which one careless git add -f can still commit.

Reading them needs no code — they are already in the provider chain:

var apiKey = builder.Configuration["Payments:ApiKey"];

⚠️ User Secrets load in Development only. In any other environment the provider is not added, so the value is simply absent. That is deliberate — they are not a deployment mechanism.

⚠️ And they are not encrypted. They are plain JSON in your profile directory. The protection is that they are outside source control, not that they are secure at rest. Anyone with access to your machine can read them.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
# Linux / macOS
export ConnectionStrings__Default="Server=prod;Database=App;..."
export Payments__ApiKey="sk_live_..."

# Windows PowerShell
$env:ConnectionStrings__Default = "Server=prod;..."

⚠️ Double underscore for nesting. ConnectionStrings__Default maps to the key ConnectionStrings:Default. A single underscore does not work, and there is no error — the value is silently absent and the app falls back to whatever the JSON said.

This is one of the most common deployment mistakes in ASP.NET Core.

In the places you actually set them:

ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
ENV ConnectionStrings__Default="Server=db;Database=App;..."

# Kubernetes — plain settings inline, secrets by reference
env:
  - name: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
    value: "Production"
  - name: ConnectionStrings__Default
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: app-secrets
        key: connection-string

Using a Kubernetes secret reference rather than a literal is the point. The manifest goes in source control; the secret does not.

Prefixed variables avoid collisions on shared machines:

builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables(prefix: "MYAPP_");

MYAPP_ConnectionStrings__Default="..."     # becomes ConnectionStrings:Default

The prefix is stripped, so your keys stay clean.

docs.title: Command-line arguments
docs.text:
dotnet run --Logging:LogLevel:Default=Debug
dotnet run --ConnectionStrings:Default="Server=test;..."
dotnet MyApp.dll --Orders:MaxItems=50

Note these use colons, not double underscores — the shell is not the constraint here.

⚠️ args must be passed through, or none of this works:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);      // ✓
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder();          // ✗ command-line config silently dead

The second compiles and runs. Command-line overrides just do nothing.

Switch mappings give you short aliases:

var switchMappings = new Dictionary<string, string>
{
    ["-e"] = "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT",
    ["--conn"] = "ConnectionStrings:Default"
};

builder.Configuration.AddCommandLine(args, switchMappings);

dotnet run --conn "Server=test;..."

docs.title: The deeper detail — which to use where
docs.text:
Local development
  └── User Secrets          ← real local secrets, outside source control

CI pipeline
  └── Environment variables ← from the CI system's secret store

Container / Kubernetes
  └── Environment variables ← from a Kubernetes Secret or the platform's store

Azure App Service
  └── Application settings  ← surface as environment variables automatically

Production, ideally
  └── Key Vault             ← see 7.4

⚠️ Environment variables are visible to the whole process and its children. Anything that can read /proc/self/environ, or crash and dump the environment, sees them. That includes the developer exception page, which renders every environment variable into the browser (4.7).

So they are better than committing secrets, and not as good as a dedicated secret store. For anything genuinely sensitive in production, Key Vault or its equivalent is the right answer — 7.4.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The realistic split for one application:

// appsettings.json — committed. Structure and non-secret defaults.
{
  "Payments": {
    "BaseUrl": "https://api.stripe.com",
    "TimeoutSeconds": 30,
    "MaxRetries": 3
    // ApiKey deliberately absent
  }
}

# Local development — User Secrets
dotnet user-secrets set "Payments:ApiKey" "sk_test_abc123"
dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:Default" "Server=(localdb)\\mssqllocaldb;Database=Dev;..."

# Production — Kubernetes, secret by reference
env:
  - name: Payments__ApiKey
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: { name: app-secrets, key: stripe-api-key }
  - name: ConnectionStrings__Default
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: { name: app-secrets, key: sql-connection }

// The application code is identical in both — it just reads configuration
builder.Services.Configure<PaymentOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Payments"));

The application never knows where the value came from. That is the point of the provider model — one build, and the source of each setting is a deployment concern.

docs.title: Failing fast on a missing secret
docs.text:
var apiKey = builder.Configuration["Payments:ApiKey"];

if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(apiKey))
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "Payments:ApiKey is not configured. Set it via User Secrets locally " +
        "or as the Payments__ApiKey environment variable in deployment.");
}

That message is worth writing properly. A missing secret otherwise surfaces as a 401 from the payment provider hours later, and the error tells whoever hits it exactly what to do. Better still, use options validation with ValidateOnStart — 7.8.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Where do you put secrets during local development?

User Secrets. You run dotnet user-secrets init, which adds a UserSecretsId GUID to the project file, and then set values with the CLI. The values are stored in a secrets.json under your user profile directory — outside the project folder entirely, so git cannot pick them up even accidentally. They are read automatically as a configuration provider in Development, so the application code is unchanged. Worth knowing they are not encrypted; the protection is that they are outside source control, not that they are secure at rest.

Q: How do you set a nested configuration key as an environment variable?

With double underscores. Configuration keys are colon-separated, like ConnectionStrings:Default, but environment variable names cannot reliably contain colons across platforms, so the convention is ConnectionStrings__Default. Using a single underscore is a very common deployment mistake and produces no error — the variable is simply not recognised as that key, so the application silently falls back to whatever the JSON file said, which usually means pointing at the wrong database.

Q: What is the precedence between these providers?

Command-line arguments beat environment variables, which beat User Secrets, which beat the environment-specific JSON file, which beats the base JSON file. That ordering is deliberate: the files supply defaults that are safe to commit, User Secrets supply local secrets, environment variables supply deployment values, and the command line lets you override anything temporarily. One thing to watch is that command-line configuration only works if args is passed to CreateBuilder — omitting it compiles fine and silently disables that provider.

Q: Are environment variables a good place for production secrets?

They are much better than committing them, and not as good as a dedicated secret store. The problem is exposure: environment variables are visible to the whole process and any child process, they appear in crash dumps, and the developer exception page renders every one of them into the browser — so a misconfigured environment turns them into an information disclosure. For production I would use Key Vault or the platform's secret manager, with environment variables used to supply the identity that reaches it rather than the secrets themselves.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Single underscore instead of double in an environment variable name silently does nothing.
  • User Secrets are Development-only. They are not a deployment mechanism.
  • User Secrets are not encrypted — just outside source control.
  • CreateBuilder() without args silently disables command-line configuration.
  • Environment variables are visible to the whole process, appear in dumps, and are rendered by the developer exception page.
  • Command-line args use colons; environment variables use double underscores. Mixing them up is common.
  • dotnet user-secrets must run from the project directory containing the .csproj, or it cannot find the UserSecretsId.
  • Deleting a secret from a JSON file does not remove it from git history. Once committed, rotate the credential.
