docs.title: 7.4 — Key Vault and Secrets Manager Providers
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.3 Environment variables and User Secrets · Next: 7.5 The IConfiguration API

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A secret store is a managed service that holds credentials, controls who can read them, and logs every access. Azure Key Vault and AWS Secrets Manager are the two you will meet.

  • They plug in as configuration providers, so your application code does not change — you still read config["Payments:ApiKey"].
  • The real win is not hiding the secret but auditing, rotation and access control.
  • The identity problem — how does the app authenticate to the vault? — is solved by managed identity, so there is no bootstrap secret.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Secret store a managed service Stores credentials with access control, auditing and versioning. Azure Key Vault a secret store Microsoft's. Holds secrets, keys and certificates. AWS Secrets Manager a secret store Amazon's equivalent. Adds built-in rotation. Managed identity an Azure feature An identity attached to the running resource, so no credential is needed to authenticate. DefaultAzureCredential a class Tries several authentication methods in order — managed identity in Azure, your developer login locally. AddAzureKeyVault a method Registers Key Vault as a configuration provider. Double dash a naming convention -- in a Key Vault secret name becomes : in the configuration key. Rotation a security practice Replacing a credential periodically, so a leaked one has a limited life. Bootstrap problem a chicken-and-egg issue Needing a secret in order to fetch your secrets. Managed identity solves it. Audit log a record Who read which secret, and when. The main reason to use a vault.

docs.title: What a vault actually buys you
docs.text:
The obvious answer is "it keeps secrets out of source control" — but environment variables do that too (7.3), and they are simpler.

The real reasons are the ones environment variables cannot provide:

Access control per secret. The payments service can read the Stripe key; the reporting service cannot. With environment variables, anyone who can read the deployment manifest or exec into the container sees everything.

An audit log. You can answer "who read the production database password, and when?" That question comes up during incidents and in compliance reviews, and environment variables have no answer to it.

Rotation without redeployment. Change the secret in the vault and applications pick it up — either on restart or on a refresh interval. With environment variables, rotating means editing manifests and redeploying every consumer.

Versioning. A bad rotation can be rolled back.

A picture: a hotel safe versus a drawer. Both keep things out of sight. The safe also records every opening, restricts who has the code, and lets you change the code without emptying the drawer.

docs.title: ⚠️ The bootstrap problem
docs.text:
If secrets live in a vault, how does the application authenticate to the vault? Storing a vault credential in configuration recreates exactly the problem you were solving.

Managed identity solves it. The cloud platform attaches an identity to the running resource — the App Service, the VM, the Kubernetes pod — and the platform itself vouches for it. There is no credential to store.

That is the piece that makes the whole approach work, and it is worth being able to explain, because it is the obvious objection to a vault.

docs.title: The simple version — Azure Key Vault
docs.text:
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

if (builder.Environment.IsProduction())
{
    builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
        new Uri($"https://{builder.Configuration["KeyVault:Name"]}.vault.azure.net/"),
        new DefaultAzureCredential());
}

Two details.

Added after the defaults, so it takes precedence over the JSON files (7.1). Order is precedence.

Production only. Locally you use User Secrets, so developers do not need vault access to run the application.

Reading the values needs no code change at all:

var apiKey = builder.Configuration["Payments:ApiKey"];      // may come from Key Vault

That is the point of the provider model. The application does not know or care where a setting came from.

docs.title: ⚠️ The naming convention
docs.text:
Key Vault secret names allow only alphanumerics and hyphens — no colons. So the convention is double hyphen:

Key Vault secret name Configuration key ConnectionStrings--Default ConnectionStrings:Default Payments--ApiKey Payments:ApiKey Payments--Stripe--WebhookSecret Payments:Stripe:WebhookSecret

Note this is a third escape convention, after : in JSON and __ in environment variables. Mixing them up is a genuinely common mistake:

JSON / CLI args     →  Payments:ApiKey
Environment vars    →  Payments__ApiKey        (double UNDERSCORE)
Key Vault           →  Payments--ApiKey        (double HYPHEN)

docs.title: How DefaultAzureCredential works
docs.text:
It tries authentication methods in order and uses the first that succeeds:

  1. Environment variables (a service principal, if configured)
  2. Managed identity — in Azure, this is the one that works
  3. Visual Studio / VS Code signed-in account
  4. Azure CLI (az login)
  5. Azure PowerShell

In production it lands on managed identity; on a developer machine it lands on your az login session. Same code, no configuration difference — which is why it is the recommended default.

⚠️ Because it tries several in order, failures are slow and the error is vague. A missing permission produces a long message listing every method it attempted. When diagnosing, specify the credential explicitly to get a clearer error:

new ManagedIdentityCredential(clientId: "...")     // one method, one clear failure

docs.title: AWS Secrets Manager
docs.text:
The same shape, different package:

builder.Configuration.AddSecretsManager(configurator: options =>
{
    options.SecretFilter = entry => entry.Name.StartsWith("myapp/");
    options.KeyGenerator = (entry, key) => key.Replace("myapp/", string.Empty)
                                              .Replace("__", ":");
    options.PollingInterval = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15);
});

Authentication uses the IAM role attached to the EC2 instance, ECS task or Lambda — the same idea as managed identity.

AWS Secrets Manager has built-in rotation with Lambda functions, including managed rotation for RDS credentials. Key Vault supports rotation but you wire the automation yourself.

docs.title: The deeper detail — refresh and caching
docs.text:
⚠️ By default, secrets are read once at startup. A rotated secret is not picked up until the application restarts.

For Key Vault you can enable periodic reloading:

builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
    vaultUri,
    new DefaultAzureCredential(),
    new AzureKeyVaultConfigurationOptions
    {
        ReloadInterval = TimeSpan.FromHours(1)
    });

⚠️ Do not set this too low. Key Vault is rate-limited and charged per operation, and every instance of your application polls independently. Fifty pods on a one-minute interval is 72,000 requests a day for values that change monthly.

⚠️ And reloading configuration does not update everything. Services holding IOptions<T> captured the value at startup — you need IOptionsMonitor<T> for it to change (7.6), and things like a DbContext connection string are fixed when the context is configured (7.9).

Restarting on rotation is often simpler and more predictable than chasing live refresh through every layer.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic production setup with a fallback and clear failure:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

if (!builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    var vaultName = builder.Configuration["KeyVault:Name"]
        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException(
            "KeyVault:Name must be configured outside Development.");

    builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
        new Uri($"https://{vaultName}.vault.azure.net/"),
        new DefaultAzureCredential(),
        new AzureKeyVaultConfigurationOptions
        {
            ReloadInterval = TimeSpan.FromHours(6)
        });
}

// Validate the secrets we need, at startup rather than at first use
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Payments"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();                    // fail at boot, not on the first payment

var app = builder.Build();

ValidateOnStart matters here. Without it, a missing secret produces a 500 on the first customer payment; with it, the deployment fails and never receives traffic (7.8).

docs.title: Setting the secrets
docs.text:
# Azure — note the DOUBLE HYPHEN
az keyvault secret set --vault-name myapp-kv \
    --name "Payments--ApiKey" --value "sk_live_..."

az keyvault secret set --vault-name myapp-kv \
    --name "ConnectionStrings--Default" --value "Server=prod;..."

# Grant the app's managed identity read access — and ONLY read
az role assignment create \
    --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
    --assignee <managed-identity-object-id> \
    --scope /subscriptions/.../vaults/myapp-kv

⚠️ "Key Vault Secrets User" is read-only, which is what an application needs. Granting a broader role like "Key Vault Administrator" means a compromised application can also write and delete secrets. Least privilege matters more here than almost anywhere else.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why use Key Vault rather than environment variables?

Environment variables keep secrets out of source control, which is the minimum, but a vault adds three things they cannot. Access control per secret, so one service can read the payment key and another cannot — whereas any process that can read the environment sees everything. An audit log, so you can answer who read the production database password and when, which comes up during incidents and compliance reviews. And rotation without redeployment, since changing the value in the vault does not require editing manifests and redeploying every consumer.

Q: How does the application authenticate to the vault without a secret?

Managed identity. The cloud platform attaches an identity to the running resource — the App Service, VM or pod — and vouches for it, so there is no credential to store. That solves the bootstrap problem, which is the obvious objection to using a vault: if secrets live in the vault, what protects the vault credential? DefaultAzureCredential tries several methods in order and lands on managed identity in Azure and your az login session locally, so the same code works in both without configuration differences. AWS uses IAM roles for the same purpose.

Q: What is the naming convention for Key Vault secrets?

Double hyphens, because secret names allow only alphanumerics and hyphens — no colons. So Payments--ApiKey becomes the configuration key Payments:ApiKey. It is worth being careful because that is the third escape convention in the same system: colons in JSON and command-line arguments, double underscores in environment variables, and double hyphens in Key Vault. Mixing them up produces a setting that is silently absent rather than an error.

Q: Do applications pick up a rotated secret automatically?

Not by default — secrets are read once at startup, so a rotation needs a restart. You can enable a reload interval on the Key Vault provider, but two caveats apply. The interval should not be short, because every instance polls independently and Key Vault is rate-limited and charged per operation. And reloading configuration does not automatically flow everywhere: a service holding IOptions<T> captured its value at startup, so you need IOptionsMonitor<T>, and some things like a configured connection string are fixed when the DbContext is set up. In practice restarting on rotation is often simpler and more predictable.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Key Vault uses --, environment variables use __, JSON uses :. Three conventions, easily confused.
  • Secrets are read once at startup unless you configure a reload interval.
  • A short reload interval hits rate limits and costs, multiplied by every instance.
  • Reloading configuration does not update IOptions<T> — that snapshot was taken at startup.
  • DefaultAzureCredential failures are slow and vague, because it tries several methods. Specify one explicitly when diagnosing.
  • Granting more than read access means a compromised app can delete your secrets.
  • Adding the provider before the defaults means JSON files override the vault.
  • Local developers should not need vault access. Use User Secrets in Development.

docs.title: 7.5 — The IConfiguration API
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.4 Secret providers · Next: 7.6 The options pattern

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
IConfiguration is the merged, read-only view of every provider. You read values from it by key path.

  • config["Key:Path"] returns a string or null. It never throws for a missing key.
  • GetValue<T>() converts to a type and lets you supply a default.
  • GetSection() never returns null — a missing section is an empty one, which is why typos fail silently.

⚠️ In application code you should mostly use IOptions<T> instead (7.6). IConfiguration is for Program.cs.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means IConfiguration an interface The merged key/value store. Read-only. Injectable. IConfigurationSection an interface A subtree, addressed by key prefix. Also an IConfiguration. IConfigurationRoot an interface The top-level configuration. Adds Reload() and GetDebugView(). Indexer config["Key"] Returns string?. Null when absent. Never throws. GetValue<T> an extension method Converts to T, with an optional default. GetSection a method Returns a section. Never null — absent means empty. GetChildren a method The immediate children of a section. Exists() an extension method Whether a section actually has a value or children. GetConnectionString an extension method Shorthand for ["ConnectionStrings:Name"]. Get<T> an extension method Binds a whole section to an object. See 7.7. GetRequiredSection a method (.NET 7+) Like GetSection but throws if absent.

docs.title: Everything is a string
docs.text:
Configuration is a flat dictionary of strings (7.1). Even this:

{ "Orders": { "MaxItems": 100, "Enabled": true } }

is stored as:

"Orders:MaxItems" = "100"      ← the string "100"
"Orders:Enabled"  = "true"     ← the string "true"

So reading is really two steps: look up a string, then convert it. The API gives you both.

docs.title: ⚠️ The silence problem
docs.text:
The single most important thing about this API is what it does when something is missing:

var value = config["Ordres:MaxItems"];        // typo — "Ordres"
// value is null. No exception. No warning.

var section = config.GetSection("Payments:Strpe");   // typo
// Returns an EMPTY section, not null. Reading from it gives you nulls.

Nothing tells you. A misspelled key produces a null, which becomes a default, which becomes wrong behaviour somewhere far away.

A picture: a filing cabinet that hands you an empty folder for any label you ask for. It never says "no such file" — you just get nothing and have to notice.

That silence is the argument for 7.6 and 7.8: bind to a typed class and validate it at startup, so a missing setting fails loudly at boot rather than quietly at runtime.

docs.title: The simple version — reading values
docs.text:
// String, by key path. Null if absent.
string? name = config["Orders:QueueName"];

// Typed, with conversion
int maxItems = config.GetValue<int>("Orders:MaxItems");

// Typed, with a default when absent
int timeout = config.GetValue("Orders:TimeoutSeconds", 30);

// Connection strings — shorthand for ConnectionStrings:Default
string? cs = config.GetConnectionString("Default");

⚠️ GetValue<int> on a missing key returns default(T) — zero — not an error. A missing MaxItems silently becomes 0, and your application processes nothing while looking healthy.

Always supply a default, or validate. The two-argument form makes the intent explicit:

int maxItems = config.GetValue("Orders:MaxItems", 100);     // clearly deliberate

⚠️ And a malformed value does throw, unlike a missing one:

// "Orders:MaxItems" = "abc"
config.GetValue<int>("Orders:MaxItems");
// InvalidOperationException: Failed to convert configuration value...

So missing is silent and invalid is loud — an inconsistency worth remembering.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
IConfigurationSection orders = config.GetSection("Orders");

// A section is itself an IConfiguration, so keys are now relative
int max = orders.GetValue<int>("MaxItems");
string? queue = orders["QueueName"];

// Nested
IConfigurationSection stripe = config.GetSection("Payments:Stripe");

GetSection never returns null. Checking for null is pointless:

// ✗ Never true
if (config.GetSection("Payments") is null) { }

// ✓ This is the check you want
if (!config.GetSection("Payments").Exists())
    throw new InvalidOperationException("The Payments section is missing.");

Since .NET 7 there is a stricter version:

var section = config.GetRequiredSection("Payments");   // throws if absent

Prefer GetRequiredSection for anything mandatory. It converts a silent failure into a clear one, at the point you ask.

docs.title: Enumerating
docs.text:
// Immediate children of a section
foreach (IConfigurationSection child in config.GetSection("Features").GetChildren())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{child.Key} = {child.Value}");
}

That is how you read a dictionary-shaped section whose keys you do not know in advance:

{
  "Features": {
    "NewCheckout": true,
    "BetaSearch": false,
    "DarkMode": true
  }
}

var features = config.GetSection("Features")
    .GetChildren()
    .ToDictionary(c => c.Key, c => bool.Parse(c.Value!));

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays are indexed keys (7.1), so:

{ "AllowedOrigins": [ "https://a.com", "https://b.com" ] }

// Bind the whole thing
string[] origins = config.GetSection("AllowedOrigins").Get<string[]>() ?? [];

// Or read one
string? first = config["AllowedOrigins:0"];

// Or enumerate
var all = config.GetSection("AllowedOrigins").GetChildren().Select(c => c.Value!);

docs.title: How it actually works — where to use it
docs.text:
⚠️ This is the part that matters for code review.

IConfiguration is injectable, so you can use it anywhere:

// ✗ Works, and is the wrong pattern
public class OrderService(IConfiguration config)
{
    public void Process()
    {
        var max = config.GetValue<int>("Orders:MaxItems");    // stringly-typed
    }
}

Three problems. The key is a magic string with no compile-time checking. There is no validation, so a missing value silently becomes zero. And the class's real dependency — a number — is hidden behind a general-purpose configuration object, which makes it awkward to test.

Bind to a typed options class instead:

// ✓ Typed, validated, and the dependency is explicit
public class OrderService(IOptions<OrderOptions> options)
{
    private readonly OrderOptions _options = options.Value;

    public void Process()
    {
        var max = _options.MaxItems;      // a real property
    }
}

The rule: IConfiguration belongs in Program.cs. Application services take IOptions<T>.

See 7.6 and 7.7.

docs.title: The deeper detail — debugging
docs.text:
When a value is not what you expect, this answers it immediately:

var root = (IConfigurationRoot)builder.Configuration;
Console.WriteLine(root.GetDebugView());

It prints every key, its value, and which provider supplied it:

Orders:
  MaxItems=100 (JsonConfigurationProvider for 'appsettings.json')
ConnectionStrings:
  Default=Server=prod;... (EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider)

That last column is what you actually need — the usual cause of a surprising value is a provider you forgot about overriding it.

⚠️ Never leave GetDebugView in production code. It prints secrets. Gate it behind a Development check, or use it only while diagnosing and remove it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Realistic use — all in Program.cs, none in services:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Required — fail at startup with a clear message
var connectionString = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "ConnectionStrings:Default is not configured. Set it via User Secrets " +
        "locally or the ConnectionStrings__Default environment variable.");

builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(connectionString));

// Optional with a sensible default
var maxConcurrency = builder.Configuration.GetValue("Processing:MaxConcurrency", 4);

// Conditional wiring based on configuration
if (builder.Configuration.GetValue<bool>("Features:UseRedisCache"))
{
    var redis = builder.Configuration.GetRequiredSection("Redis");   // throws if absent
    builder.Services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(o =>
        o.Configuration = redis["ConnectionString"]);
}
else
{
    builder.Services.AddDistributedMemoryCache();
}

// Everything else gets bound to typed options — services never see IConfiguration
builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"));
builder.Services.Configure<PaymentOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Payments"));

var app = builder.Build();

// Debugging aid — Development only, because it prints secrets
if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.Logger.LogDebug("Configuration:\n{Config}",
        ((IConfigurationRoot)builder.Configuration).GetDebugView());
}

Note the pattern: IConfiguration is used to wire things up, and every service receives typed options. No service in this application injects IConfiguration.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens when you read a configuration key that does not exist?

The indexer returns null, and GetValue<T> returns default(T) — so a missing integer silently becomes zero rather than throwing. GetSection never returns null either; an absent section comes back as an empty section, so a typo in a section name produces silence rather than an error. That is the main weakness of the API: mistakes are quiet. A malformed value does throw, though, so missing is silent and invalid is loud, which is a slightly awkward inconsistency.

Q: How do you check whether a section exists?

With Exists(), because comparing against null never works — GetSection always returns an object. Since .NET 7 there is also GetRequiredSection, which throws immediately if the section is absent, and I would prefer that for anything mandatory because it converts a silent failure into a clear one at the point you ask rather than somewhere downstream.

Q: Should services inject IConfiguration?

Generally no. It works, but it means magic-string keys with no compile-time checking, no validation so a missing value silently becomes a default, and the class's real dependency is hidden behind a general-purpose object that is awkward to fake in tests. The better pattern is to bind sections to typed options classes in Program.cs and have services take IOptions<T>, so the dependency is a real typed object and can be validated at startup. IConfiguration is for the composition root.

Q: How do you find out which provider supplied a value?

Cast the configuration to IConfigurationRoot and call GetDebugView, which prints every key, its value, and the provider it came from. That is usually the fastest way to diagnose a surprising setting, because the cause is almost always a provider later in the chain overriding the one you were looking at. The important caveat is that it prints secrets, so it must never run in production — gate it behind a Development check.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• A missing key returns null or default(T), silently. A missing int becomes zero.
  • A malformed value throws, unlike a missing one. Inconsistent, and worth remembering.
  • GetSection never returns null. Checking for null is dead code — use Exists().
  • Injecting IConfiguration into services gives you magic strings and no validation.
  • GetDebugView prints secrets. Development only.
  • Key lookup is case-insensitive, which is convenient but means orders:maxitems also works — so casing inconsistencies hide.
  • Arrays are indexed keys, so partial overrides leave the original tail elements (7.2).
  • GetValue<T> cannot bind complex objects. Use Get<T> or the options pattern.

docs.title: 7.6 — IOptions vs IOptionsSnapshot vs IOptionsMonitor
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.5 The IConfiguration API · Next: 7.7 Binding to POCOs

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The options pattern binds a configuration section to a typed class, which services then inject instead of reading strings. There are three interfaces, and choosing wrong causes real bugs.

  • IOptions<T> — singleton. Read once at startup, never changes. The default.
  • IOptionsSnapshot<T> — scoped. Re-read once per request, so it picks up changes.
  • IOptionsMonitor<T> — singleton, but with live values and a change callback.

⚠️ IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, so injecting it into a singleton is a captive dependency.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Options pattern a technique Binding a configuration section to a strongly-typed class. Options class a plain C# class Properties matching the configuration keys. No base class or interface needed. Configure<T> a method Binds a configuration section to T and registers the options interfaces. IOptions<T> an interface — singleton Value read once at startup. Never updates. IOptionsSnapshot<T> an interface — scoped Value re-read once per request. Picks up reloads. IOptionsMonitor<T> an interface — singleton Always current, plus OnChange notifications. .Value a property How you get the actual options object from IOptions or IOptionsSnapshot. .CurrentValue a property The equivalent on IOptionsMonitor. Re-read each time. OnChange a method Registers a callback fired when the underlying configuration reloads. Named options a feature Several configured instances of one options type, distinguished by name.

docs.title: Why not just read IConfiguration?
docs.text:
// ✗ The stringly-typed way
public class OrderService(IConfiguration config)
{
    public void Process()
    {
        var max = config.GetValue<int>("Orders:MaxItems");     // magic string
    }
}

Three problems (7.5): the key is a string with no compile-time checking, a missing value silently becomes zero, and the class's real dependency — a number — is hidden behind a general-purpose object.

The options pattern fixes all three:

public class OrderOptions
{
    public int MaxItems { get; set; } = 100;
    public decimal AutoApproveUnder { get; set; }
    public int ReservationMinutes { get; set; } = 15;
}

builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"));

// ✓ Typed, validatable, and the dependency is explicit
public class OrderService(IOptions<OrderOptions> options)
{
    private readonly OrderOptions _options = options.Value;

    public void Process()
    {
        var max = _options.MaxItems;      // a real property
    }
}

docs.title: ⚠️ The three interfaces
docs.text:
This is the part interviews focus on, because the lifetimes differ and that has consequences.

Lifetime Value read Sees config reloads? Named options? IOptions<T> Singleton Once, at first use ❌ No ❌ IOptionsSnapshot<T> Scoped Once per request ✅ Yes ✅ IOptionsMonitor<T> Singleton Every access ✅ Yes ✅

A picture: three ways of knowing today's exchange rate.

  • IOptions is a rate you wrote down when you opened the shop. Fast, and stale by evening.
  • IOptionsSnapshot is checking the board once when each customer walks in. Consistent for that customer, fresh per customer.
  • IOptionsMonitor is a live ticker on the wall. Always current, and it can change while you are mid-sentence.

That last point matters: with IOptionsMonitor, two reads of CurrentValue in one method can return different objects. If a method needs consistency, read it into a local variable once.

docs.title: The simple version — choosing
docs.text:
IOptions<T> is the right default. Most settings do not change while the application runs, and it is the only one usable everywhere, including in singletons.

public class OrderService(IOptions<OrderOptions> options)
{
    private readonly OrderOptions _options = options.Value;    // read once, cache it
}

IOptionsSnapshot<T> when a setting can change and you want it per request:

public class PricingService(IOptionsSnapshot<PricingOptions> options)
{
    // Fresh at the start of each request, consistent within it
    private readonly PricingOptions _options = options.Value;
}

IOptionsMonitor<T> in singletons and background services that need current values:

public class RateLimiter(IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitOptions> monitor)
{
    public bool IsAllowed(string clientId)
    {
        var limit = monitor.CurrentValue.RequestsPerMinute;    // current every time
        // ...
    }
}

docs.title: ⚠️ The captive dependency trap
docs.text:
IOptionsSnapshot<T> is registered as scoped. So this is a captive dependency (6.4):

// ✗ BROKEN — a singleton capturing a scoped service
public class PriceCache(IOptionsSnapshot<PriceOptions> options)     // singleton
{
    // The snapshot is resolved ONCE and held forever.
    // It never updates, and it holds a request-scoped object for the app's lifetime.
}

With ValidateScopes enabled you get a startup exception naming both types. But that is Development-only by default (6.13), so it starts cleanly in production and quietly stops updating.

The fix in a singleton is IOptionsMonitor<T>, which is itself a singleton and still sees changes:

// ✓ Singleton, and still current
public class PriceCache(IOptionsMonitor<PriceOptions> monitor)
{
    public decimal Markup => monitor.CurrentValue.Markup;
}

The rule: IOptionsSnapshot in scoped services and controllers; IOptionsMonitor in singletons.

Middleware is the case people forget — conventional middleware is a singleton (5.5), so it needs IOptionsMonitor, or IOptionsSnapshot as an InvokeAsync parameter.

docs.title: OnChange — reacting to reloads
docs.text:
public class CacheManager : IDisposable
{
    private readonly IDisposable? _subscription;

    public CacheManager(IOptionsMonitor<CacheOptions> monitor)
    {
        _subscription = monitor.OnChange(options =>
        {
            // Fires when the underlying configuration reloads
            ResizeCache(options.MaxSizeMb);
        });
    }

    public void Dispose() => _subscription?.Dispose();
}

⚠️ Two things to be careful about.

Dispose the subscription, or the monitor holds a reference to your object forever — a memory leak (3.5).

OnChange can fire more than once for a single edit. File watchers often report a save as two events, so the callback must be idempotent and cheap. Do not put expensive work directly inside it.

docs.title: How it actually works — named options
docs.text:
Several configured instances of one type, distinguished by name:

{
  "Storage": {
    "Primary":   { "ConnectionString": "...", "Container": "prod" },
    "Archive":   { "ConnectionString": "...", "Container": "archive" }
  }
}

builder.Services.Configure<StorageOptions>("Primary",
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Storage:Primary"));
builder.Services.Configure<StorageOptions>("Archive",
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Storage:Archive"));

public class BackupService(IOptionsSnapshot<StorageOptions> options)
{
    private readonly StorageOptions _primary = options.Get("Primary");
    private readonly StorageOptions _archive = options.Get("Archive");
}

⚠️ IOptions<T> does not support named options — it only ever gives you the default instance. You need IOptionsSnapshot<T> or IOptionsMonitor<T> for Get(name).

This is how IHttpClientFactory configures named clients, and how authentication configures multiple schemes.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what actually triggers a change
docs.text:
IOptionsSnapshot and IOptionsMonitor only see updates if the underlying provider reloads.

builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("appsettings.json",
    optional: false,
    reloadOnChange: true);          // ← without this, nothing ever changes

⚠️ In a container, editing the file is not a thing that happens. The image is immutable and config comes from environment variables, which do not reload. So in most deployments IOptionsSnapshot and IOptionsMonitor behave exactly like IOptions — the extra machinery buys nothing.

They earn their place with a mounted ConfigMap in Kubernetes, or a Key Vault provider with a reload interval (7.4).

Use IOptions<T> unless you have a specific reason. See 7.9 for what reloading actually reaches.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic set showing each in its right place:

// Program.cs
builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"));
builder.Services.Configure<RateLimitOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("RateLimit"));

// ✓ SCOPED service → IOptions is fine, since these settings do not change
public class OrderService(IOptions<OrderOptions> options) : IOrderService
{
    private readonly OrderOptions _options = options.Value;

    public bool CanAutoApprove(Order order)
        => order.Total < _options.AutoApproveUnder;
}

// ✓ SINGLETON that must see changes → IOptionsMonitor
public class RateLimitService(IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitOptions> monitor) : IRateLimitService
{
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, Counter> _counters = new();

    public bool IsAllowed(string clientId)
    {
        // Read ONCE into a local — CurrentValue could change between two reads
        var options = monitor.CurrentValue;

        var counter = _counters.GetOrAdd(clientId, _ => new Counter());
        return counter.Increment(options.Window) <= options.RequestsPerMinute;
    }
}

// ✓ Conventional middleware is a SINGLETON → IOptionsMonitor, not IOptionsSnapshot
internal class ApiKeyMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    IOptionsMonitor<SecurityOptions> monitor)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var options = monitor.CurrentValue;
        // ...
        await next(context);
    }
}

The comment in the middle example is the subtle one. CurrentValue re-reads on every access, so:

// ✗ These two reads can see DIFFERENT objects
if (monitor.CurrentValue.Enabled)
    Process(monitor.CurrentValue.BatchSize);     // config could have reloaded in between

// ✓ One read, consistent for this operation
var options = monitor.CurrentValue;
if (options.Enabled)
    Process(options.BatchSize);

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the options pattern and why use it over IConfiguration?

It binds a configuration section to a strongly-typed class that services inject, instead of reading string keys. That fixes three problems with using IConfiguration directly: the keys are magic strings with no compile-time checking, a missing value silently becomes a default rather than failing, and the class's real dependency is hidden behind a general-purpose configuration object that is awkward to fake in tests. With options the dependency is a plain typed class, and it can be validated at startup.

Q: What is the difference between the three options interfaces?

IOptions<T> is a singleton whose value is read once and never changes — the right default for settings that are fixed for the application's lifetime. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, so it is re-read once per request and picks up configuration reloads, staying consistent within a single request. IOptionsMonitor<T> is a singleton that reads the current value on every access and also exposes an OnChange callback. The critical detail is the lifetimes: because IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, injecting it into a singleton is a captive dependency, so singletons and conventional middleware need IOptionsMonitor instead.

Q: When would you actually need something other than IOptions<T>?

Only when the configuration genuinely reloads at runtime, which is rarer than people assume. It requires a provider with reloadOnChange enabled, and in most deployments configuration comes from environment variables that never change, or a container image that is immutable — so IOptionsSnapshot and IOptionsMonitor behave identically to IOptions and the extra machinery buys nothing. They earn their place with a mounted Kubernetes ConfigMap or a Key Vault provider configured with a reload interval.

Q: What is a subtlety of using IOptionsMonitor.CurrentValue?

It re-reads on every access, so two reads within the same method can return different objects if the configuration reloads in between. That produces genuinely confusing bugs — checking a flag and then using a related setting, and getting an inconsistent pair. So I read CurrentValue once into a local variable at the start of an operation and use that throughout. The other subtlety is that OnChange subscriptions must be disposed, or the monitor keeps a reference to your object forever, and the callback can fire twice for a single file save.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, so injecting it into a singleton or conventional middleware is a captive dependency.
  • ValidateScopes catches that in Development only, so it reaches production silently.
  • IOptions<T> does not support named options. Get(name) needs snapshot or monitor.
  • Nothing reloads without reloadOnChange: true on the provider — and environment variables never reload at all.
  • CurrentValue can change between two reads. Capture it once per operation.
  • OnChange subscriptions leak unless disposed, and can fire twice per edit.
  • IOptionsSnapshot in a background service throws — there is no scope (21.2).
  • Options classes need a parameterless constructor and settable properties, or binding silently produces defaults (7.7).

docs.title: 7.7 — Binding Configuration to POCOs
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.6 The options pattern · Next: 7.8 Options validation

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Binding is populating a plain C# class from a configuration section by matching property names to keys.

  • Three ways: Configure<T> (registers it in DI), Get<T> (returns a new object), Bind (fills an existing one).
  • The class needs a parameterless constructor and settable properties, or binding silently produces defaults.
  • ⚠️ Unmatched keys are ignored and unmatched properties keep their defaults. Nothing warns you about a typo.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Binding a process Populating an object's properties from configuration keys by name. POCO an acronym Plain Old CLR Object. A class with no base class, attributes or framework dependency. Configure<T> a method Binds a section to T and registers IOptions<T> and friends in DI. Get<T> an extension method Binds a section to a new T and returns it. Used in Program.cs. Bind an extension method Populates an existing object. BinderOptions a class Binding settings — ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration, BindNonPublicProperties. ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration a binder option Throw if a configuration key has no matching property. Off by default. Case-insensitive matching binder behaviour maxitems binds to MaxItems. Configuration binding source generator a build feature (.NET 8+) Generates binding code at compile time. Needed for Native AOT. required a C# keyword ⚠️ Not enforced by the binder. See traps.

docs.title: What binding does
docs.text:
Given this configuration:

{
  "Orders": {
    "MaxItems": 100,
    "AutoApproveUnder": 50.00,
    "QueueName": "orders-main",
    "EnableNotifications": true
  }
}

and this class:

public class OrderOptions
{
    public int MaxItems { get; set; } = 50;
    public decimal AutoApproveUnder { get; set; }
    public string QueueName { get; set; } = "default";
    public bool EnableNotifications { get; set; }
}

binding matches property names to keys, converts the strings to the right types, and sets each property.

builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"));

Matching is case-insensitive, so maxitems, MaxItems and MAXITEMS all bind to MaxItems.

A picture: a form and a filing system. Binding is a clerk reading the filing system and filling in the form, field by field, by matching labels. If a label on the form has no matching file, the clerk leaves the field as it was — and says nothing.

docs.title: ⚠️ The silence problem
docs.text:
That last part is the thing to internalise:

A configuration key with no matching property is ignored.

{ "Orders": { "MaxItem": 100 } }      // typo: "MaxItem", not "MaxItems"

No error. The key is simply unused.

A property with no matching key keeps its default.

public int MaxItems { get; set; } = 50;    // stays 50 — you get the default, not an error

So a typo in either direction produces an application that runs with the wrong values and tells you nothing. That is the argument for 7.8 — validation is what turns this silence into a startup failure.

docs.title: The simple version — the three methods
docs.text:
// 1. Configure<T> — bind AND register in DI. The normal choice.
builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"));
// Services then inject IOptions<OrderOptions>

// 2. Get<T> — bind to a new object, right now. For Program.cs.
var orderOptions = builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders").Get<OrderOptions>();

// 3. Bind — populate an object you already have
var options = new OrderOptions();
builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders").Bind(options);

Use Configure<T> for anything a service needs. Use Get<T> when you need a value during startup wiring:

// Needed while building the pipeline, before DI is available
var cacheOptions = builder.Configuration.GetSection("Cache").Get<CacheOptions>()
    ?? new CacheOptions();

if (cacheOptions.UseRedis)
    builder.Services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(o => o.Configuration = cacheOptions.ConnectionString);

⚠️ Get<T> returns null if the section does not exist, so the null-coalescing fallback there is not optional.

docs.title: What the class must look like
docs.text:
public class OrderOptions
{
    // ✓ Public settable property — binds
    public int MaxItems { get; set; }

    // ✓ Default used if the key is absent
    public string QueueName { get; set; } = "default";

    // ✗ Get-only — the binder cannot set it
    public int Computed => MaxItems * 2;

    // ✗ Private setter — not bound by default
    public string Secret { get; private set; } = "";

    // ✗ Field, not a property — ignored
    public int notAProperty;
}

Requirements: a public parameterless constructor, and public settable properties.

⚠️ init setters do work — the binder can set them during construction. But required does not:

public class OrderOptions
{
    public required string QueueName { get; init; }    // ⚠️ NOT enforced by binding
}

required is checked by the compiler at the call site (1.6). The binder constructs the object through reflection, bypassing that check entirely — so a missing key leaves it null despite the keyword promising otherwise.

Use [Required] from DataAnnotations plus validation instead (7.8).

⚠️ Records with positional parameters do not bind well either, because there is no parameterless constructor:

// ✗ Does not bind
public record OrderOptions(int MaxItems, string QueueName);

// ✓ Binds — a record with settable properties
public record OrderOptions
{
    public int MaxItems { get; set; }
    public string QueueName { get; set; } = "";
}

.NET 8 improved constructor binding, but a plain class with settable properties remains the reliable choice for options.

docs.title: How it actually works — nested objects and collections
docs.text:
Binding is recursive:

{
  "Payments": {
    "TimeoutSeconds": 30,
    "Stripe": {
      "BaseUrl": "https://api.stripe.com",
      "WebhookSecret": "whsec_..."
    },
    "AllowedCurrencies": [ "GBP", "USD", "EUR" ],
    "Limits": {
      "GBP": 10000,
      "USD": 12000
    }
  }
}

public class PaymentOptions
{
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; } = 30;
    public StripeOptions Stripe { get; set; } = new();              // nested object
    public List<string> AllowedCurrencies { get; set; } = [];       // array → list
    public Dictionary<string, decimal> Limits { get; set; } = [];   // section → dictionary
}

public class StripeOptions
{
    public string BaseUrl { get; set; } = "";
    public string WebhookSecret { get; set; } = "";
}

Three things bind here that people do not expect:

Nested classes bind automatically, as long as the property is initialised (= new()) or has a settable type the binder can construct.

Arrays bind to List<T> or T[] — the indexed keys become elements.

A section binds to Dictionary<string, T>, with the child keys becoming dictionary keys. That is genuinely useful for configuration that is a lookup rather than a fixed shape.

⚠️ Collections are added to, not replaced. If the property is initialised with items, the bound values are appended. Start collections empty.

docs.title: Catching typos with ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration
docs.text:
The binder can be told to complain about keys it does not recognise:

builder.Services.Configure<OrderOptions>(
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Orders"),
    binderOptions => binderOptions.ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration = true);

Now a key with no matching property throws at binding time, which catches the MaxItem typo.

⚠️ It only catches one direction. A property with no matching key still silently keeps its default — that needs validation (7.8).

⚠️ And it is strict. Any extra key in that section throws, including ones deliberately read elsewhere, so it works best on sections owned entirely by one options class.

docs.title: The deeper detail — the source generator
docs.text:
Binding uses reflection by default, which means it does not survive trimming and does not work with Native AOT (3.2).

.NET 8 added a configuration binding source generator that produces the binding code at compile time:

<PropertyGroup>
  <EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator>true</EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator>
</PropertyGroup>

No code changes — the same Configure<T> calls are intercepted and replaced with generated code. You get AOT compatibility and slightly faster startup.

This is part of the broader move from runtime reflection to compile-time generation across .NET (1.23).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic options class and its registration:

public class PaymentOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Payments";     // avoids a magic string at the call site

    public string BaseUrl { get; set; } = "";
    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = "";
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; } = 30;
    public int MaxRetries { get; set; } = 3;

    public List<string> AllowedCurrencies { get; set; } = [];
    public Dictionary<string, decimal> LimitsByCurrency { get; set; } = [];

    public StripeOptions Stripe { get; set; } = new();
}

public class StripeOptions
{
    public string WebhookSecret { get; set; } = "";
    public bool VerifySignatures { get; set; } = true;
}

// Program.cs
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(PaymentOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();                  // see 7.8

That SectionName constant is a small habit worth having. It keeps the string in one place, so renaming the section is one edit rather than a search-and-hope.

// The service — a plain typed dependency
public class PaymentService(IOptions<PaymentOptions> options, IHttpClientFactory factory)
{
    private readonly PaymentOptions _options = options.Value;

    public async Task<Receipt> ChargeAsync(decimal amount, string currency, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (!_options.AllowedCurrencies.Contains(currency))
            throw new NotSupportedException($"Currency {currency} is not enabled.");

        if (_options.LimitsByCurrency.TryGetValue(currency, out var limit) && amount > limit)
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"Amount exceeds the {currency} limit of {limit}.");

        // ...
    }
}

No configuration keys appear in the service at all. It receives a typed object, which is the whole point.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does configuration binding work?

It matches configuration keys to property names on a plain class, case-insensitively, converts the string values to the property types, and sets them. You either use Configure<T>, which binds a section and registers the options interfaces in DI, or Get<T> and Bind when you need the values during startup wiring. The class needs a public parameterless constructor and public settable properties — get-only and computed properties are skipped, as are fields. Binding is recursive, so nested objects, arrays and dictionaries all work.

Q: What happens if a key does not match any property, or vice versa?

Both are silently ignored by default. An unmatched configuration key is simply unused, and an unmatched property keeps whatever default the class gave it. So a typo in either direction produces an application running with the wrong values and no indication anything is wrong. You can set ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration to throw on unrecognised keys, but that only covers one direction — a property that never got a value still needs validation to be caught.

Q: Does required work on an options class?

No, and that is a genuine trap because it looks like it should. required is enforced by the compiler at the call site, but the binder constructs the object through reflection and sets properties afterwards, bypassing that check entirely. So a missing configuration key leaves the property null despite the keyword. The right tool is a [Required] DataAnnotations attribute combined with ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, which fails the application at startup rather than at first use.

Q: What is the configuration binding source generator?

A .NET 8 feature that generates the binding code at compile time instead of using reflection at runtime. You enable it with a property in the project file and your code does not change — the existing Configure<T> calls are intercepted and replaced. The reason it matters is that reflection-based binding does not survive trimming and does not work under Native AOT, since the trimmer removes the properties it cannot see being used. It is part of the same shift towards source generators that has happened for JSON serialization and logging.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Typos are silent in both directions. An unmatched key is ignored; an unmatched property keeps its default.
  • required is not enforced by the binder. Use [Required] plus validation.
  • Positional records do not bind — no parameterless constructor.
  • Get-only and computed properties are skipped, as are public fields.
  • Collections are appended to, not replaced. Initialise them empty.
  • Get<T> returns null when the section is absent.
  • Reflection-based binding breaks under trimming and AOT. Enable the source generator.
  • ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration is strict — any extra key in the section throws.

docs.title: 7.8 — Options Validation and ValidateOnStart
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.7 Binding to POCOs · Next: 7.9 Reload on change

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Options validation checks that a bound configuration class actually holds sensible values, and ValidateOnStart() makes that check run at application startup rather than at first use.

  • Without it, a missing setting is silent — binding leaves the default and you find out much later.
  • Three levels: DataAnnotations attributes, a Validate lambda, or a full IValidateOptions<T> class.
  • ⚠️ Validation is lazy by default. ValidateOnStart() is the part that actually matters.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Options validation a feature Checking a bound options object is valid before anything uses it. AddOptions<T>() a method Starts a fluent builder for configuring, binding and validating T. ValidateDataAnnotations() a method Validates [Required], [Range] and similar attributes on the class. Validate(...) a method Registers a lambda returning bool, with a failure message. IValidateOptions<T> an interface A full validation class. For anything needing dependencies or complex rules. ValidateOnStart() a method Runs validation at startup instead of first access. OptionsValidationException an exception Thrown when validation fails, listing every failure. Lazy validation the default behaviour Validation runs the first time .Value is read, not at startup. Fail fast a principle Detect a misconfiguration at boot, before the app serves traffic. ValidateComplexMembers a DataAnnotations option (.NET 8+) Validates nested options objects too.

docs.title: The problem: binding is silent
docs.text:
From 7.7: if a configuration key is missing, the property keeps its default. No error, no warning.

public class PaymentOptions
{
    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = "";       // key missing → stays ""
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; }        // key missing → stays 0
}

An application configured like that starts perfectly. Then:

  • The first payment fails with a 401 from Stripe, because the API key is empty
  • Or worse, TimeoutSeconds = 0 means every HTTP call times out instantly

And the error happens at the worst possible moment — during a customer transaction, hours after deployment, with a message that points at Stripe rather than at your configuration.

Validation moves that failure to application startup, where it fails the deployment and never receives traffic.

A picture: a pre-flight check versus discovering the fuel gauge is broken at 30,000 feet. Both find the problem. Only one of them is survivable.

docs.title: ⚠️ The part people miss
docs.text:
Validation on its own is lazy — it runs when someone first reads .Value:

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Payments"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations();          // ⚠️ runs on first ACCESS, not at startup

So the application still starts with broken configuration. The failure just moves from "Stripe returns 401" to "an exception on the first request that touches payments" — better, but still in production, still during a customer transaction.

ValidateOnStart() is the line that makes this worth doing:

    .ValidateOnStart();                  // ✓ fails at boot

Now the deployment fails, the orchestrator does not route traffic to it, and the previous version keeps running. That is the whole value.

docs.title: The simple version — DataAnnotations
docs.text:
public class PaymentOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Payments";

    [Required(AllowEmptyStrings = false)]
    [Url]
    public string BaseUrl { get; set; } = "";

    [Required(AllowEmptyStrings = false)]
    [MinLength(20)]
    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = "";

    [Range(1, 300)]
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; } = 30;

    [Range(0, 10)]
    public int MaxRetries { get; set; } = 3;
}

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(PaymentOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

Missing the API key now produces this at startup:

OptionsValidationException: DataAnnotation validation failed for 'PaymentOptions' members:
'ApiKey' with the error: 'The ApiKey field is required.'.

⚠️ [Required] on a string with a default of "" needs AllowEmptyStrings = false. By default [Required] treats an empty string as present, so the check passes and you are back to silence. That catches people out constantly.

⚠️ And [Required] on a value type is useless. An int is never null, so a missing key gives you 0 and [Required] is satisfied. Use [Range] with a sensible minimum instead:

[Range(1, 300)]              // ✓ catches the missing-key zero
public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; }

That is the more important of the two, because a zero timeout or a zero batch size fails in confusing ways.

docs.title: The Validate lambda — for rules attributes cannot express
docs.text:
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(PaymentOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .Validate(o => o.MaxRetries * o.TimeoutSeconds <= 300,
        "MaxRetries multiplied by TimeoutSeconds must not exceed 300 seconds total.")
    .Validate(o => !o.ApiKey.StartsWith("sk_test_") || o.AllowTestKeys,
        "A test API key is configured but AllowTestKeys is false.")
    .ValidateOnStart();

Each Validate takes a predicate and a message. Chain as many as you need.

That second rule is the kind of check worth writing. A test key in production is a real incident, and it is exactly the sort of thing nobody notices until money does not move.

⚠️ The lambda has no access to DI, so it cannot check anything requiring a service. For that you need the full interface.

docs.title: How it actually works — IValidateOptions<T>
docs.text:
When validation needs dependencies or produces several failures:

public class PaymentOptionsValidator(IHostEnvironment env) : IValidateOptions<PaymentOptions>
{
    public ValidateOptionsResult Validate(string? name, PaymentOptions options)
    {
        var failures = new List<string>();

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.ApiKey))
            failures.Add("Payments:ApiKey is required.");

        if (env.IsProduction() && options.ApiKey.StartsWith("sk_test_"))
            failures.Add("A test API key must not be used in Production.");

        if (options.TimeoutSeconds is < 1 or > 300)
            failures.Add($"Payments:TimeoutSeconds must be 1-300, but was {options.TimeoutSeconds}.");

        return failures.Count > 0
            ? ValidateOptionsResult.Fail(failures)      // ALL failures, not just the first
            : ValidateOptionsResult.Success;
    }
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IValidateOptions<PaymentOptions>, PaymentOptionsValidator>();

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(PaymentOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateOnStart();

Two advantages over the lambda: it can take dependencies through DI — IHostEnvironment here, so the rule differs by environment — and it can report every failure at once rather than stopping at the first.

Reporting all failures matters. Fixing configuration one error per deployment cycle is miserable; seeing all four at once takes one iteration.

docs.title: The deeper detail — nested options
docs.text:
⚠️ By default, DataAnnotations validation does not recurse into nested objects:

public class PaymentOptions
{
    [Required] public string ApiKey { get; set; } = "";

    public StripeOptions Stripe { get; set; } = new();     // ⚠️ NOT validated
}

public class StripeOptions
{
    [Required] public string WebhookSecret { get; set; } = "";   // never checked
}

.NET 8 added an option for it:

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Payments"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .Validate(o => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.Stripe.WebhookSecret),
        "Payments:Stripe:WebhookSecret is required.")          // explicit, works everywhere
    .ValidateOnStart();

Or use [ValidateObjectMembers] from the options validation source generator. The explicit Validate call is the most portable answer, and it is clearer about what is being checked.

docs.title: What ValidateOnStart actually does
docs.text:
It registers an IHostedService that resolves the options during startup (4.5). Resolving triggers binding and validation, and a failure throws before the server starts listening.

⚠️ Because it runs in StartAsync, it blocks startup — which is exactly what you want, but it means the failure appears in your startup logs rather than as an HTTP error. Make sure your logging is configured to capture startup output, or a failed deployment looks like a container that exited with no explanation.

Adding a top-level try/catch helps (4.6):

try
{
    app.Run();
}
catch (OptionsValidationException ex)
{
    Log.Fatal("Configuration is invalid:\n{Failures}", string.Join("\n", ex.Failures));
    throw;
}
finally
{
    Log.CloseAndFlush();        // ensure the message is written before the process dies
}

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The complete pattern, as it would appear in a real application:

public class PaymentOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Payments";

    [Required(AllowEmptyStrings = false), Url]
    public string BaseUrl { get; set; } = "";

    [Required(AllowEmptyStrings = false), MinLength(20)]
    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = "";

    [Range(1, 300)]
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; } = 30;

    [Range(0, 10)]
    public int MaxRetries { get; set; } = 3;

    public bool AllowTestKeys { get; set; }

    public StripeOptions Stripe { get; set; } = new();
}

// A registration extension keeps Program.cs readable — see 4.3
public static class PaymentModuleExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddPaymentModule(
        this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
    {
        services
            .AddOptions<PaymentOptions>()
            .Bind(config.GetSection(PaymentOptions.SectionName))
            .ValidateDataAnnotations()
            .Validate(o => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.Stripe.WebhookSecret),
                "Payments:Stripe:WebhookSecret is required.")
            .Validate(o => o.MaxRetries * o.TimeoutSeconds <= 300,
                "MaxRetries × TimeoutSeconds must not exceed 300 seconds.")
            .ValidateOnStart();

        // Environment-dependent rules need DI, so they go in a validator class
        services.AddSingleton<IValidateOptions<PaymentOptions>, PaymentOptionsValidator>();

        services.AddScoped<IPaymentService, PaymentService>();
        return services;
    }
}

// The service can now trust its options completely
public class PaymentService(IOptions<PaymentOptions> options, IHttpClientFactory factory)
{
    private readonly PaymentOptions _options = options.Value;

    // No null checks, no defensive defaults, no "if the API key is missing" branch.
    // Validation guaranteed all of that at startup.
}

That last comment is the real payoff. Validated options mean services stop defending against misconfiguration, which removes a whole layer of defensive code.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why do you need options validation?

Because binding is silent. If a configuration key is missing, the property keeps its default — an empty API key, or a timeout of zero — and the application starts perfectly. The failure then happens at the worst moment, during a real transaction, with an error that points at the downstream service rather than at your configuration. Validation moves that to startup, where a misconfigured deployment fails and never receives traffic.

Q: What does ValidateOnStart add?

It is the part that actually matters. Validation on its own is lazy — it runs the first time someone reads .Value, so the application still starts with broken configuration and fails later on some request. ValidateOnStart registers a hosted service that resolves the options during startup, so binding and validation happen before the server listens. A failure then aborts the boot, the orchestrator does not route traffic to the new instance, and the previous version keeps running.

Q: What are the ways to validate options?

Three levels. DataAnnotations attributes on the class with ValidateDataAnnotations, which covers Required, Range and similar. A Validate lambda with a message, for rules that span several properties. And an IValidateOptions<T> implementation for anything needing dependencies — checking that a test API key is not being used in Production requires IHostEnvironment, which the lambda cannot access. The interface also lets you report every failure at once instead of stopping at the first, which saves fixing configuration one error per deployment.

Q: What are the traps with DataAnnotations on options?

Two that catch people. [Required] on a string treats an empty string as present by default, and since a missing key leaves the property at its "" initialiser, the check passes — you need AllowEmptyStrings = false. And [Required] on a value type is meaningless, because an int is never null, so a missing key gives you zero and validation is satisfied. For numbers you want a [Range] with a sensible minimum, which catches the zero. There is also the fact that nested options objects are not validated by default.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Validation is lazy without ValidateOnStart(). The app starts broken and fails later.
  • [Required] on a string accepts empty strings unless you set AllowEmptyStrings = false.
  • [Required] on a value type does nothing. A missing key gives 0, which is "present". Use [Range].
  • Nested options objects are not validated by default.
  • The Validate lambda cannot use DI. Environment-dependent rules need IValidateOptions<T>.
  • DataAnnotations stops at the first failure per property, so returning all failures needs the validator interface.
  • Startup failures appear in startup logs, not as HTTP errors — configure logging to capture them, and flush before exit.
  • Validation runs per named option, so named options each need validating.

docs.title: 7.9 — Reloadable Configuration and Its Limits
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.8 Options validation · Next: 7.10 Custom providers

Markers: ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
reloadOnChange makes a configuration provider re-read its source when it changes, without restarting the application.

  • It works for file-based providers. Environment variables never reload — they are read once at process start.
  • ⚠️ A reload updates IConfiguration, but not everything that consumed it. Anything captured at startup keeps its old value.
  • In most deployments — immutable containers, environment-variable config — nothing ever reloads, so this machinery buys nothing.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means reloadOnChange a parameter on AddJsonFile Watch the file and re-read it when it changes. File watcher an OS mechanism Notifies the process when a file is modified. What reloadOnChange uses. IConfigurationRoot.Reload() a method Forces every provider to re-read its source. Change token an IChangeToken The notification primitive. Fires once, then must be re-registered. IOptionsMonitor<T> an interface The only options interface that sees changes in a singleton. See 7.6. OnChange a method Callback fired when configuration reloads. ConfigMap a Kubernetes object Configuration mounted into a pod as files. Can update in place. Captured value a stale reference A setting read once at startup and stored, so a reload never reaches it. Duplicate notification a file-watcher quirk One save often produces two change events.

docs.title: What reload actually does
docs.text:
Enable it on a file provider:

builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("appsettings.json",
    optional: false,
    reloadOnChange: true);        // ← the watcher

Edit the file, and the provider re-reads it. IConfiguration now returns the new values.

That is genuinely all it does — update the configuration object. What it does not do is push those values into everything that already read them.

A picture: updating the noticeboard in the staff room. The notice is now correct. Everyone who read it yesterday and wrote the number on their hand still has the old one.

docs.title: ⚠️ The limit that matters
docs.text:
This is the point of the note. A reload reaches:

Consumer Sees the change? IConfiguration read directly ✅ Yes IOptionsMonitor<T> ✅ Yes IOptionsSnapshot<T> ✅ Yes — on the next request IOptions<T> ❌ No — captured at startup A value read in Program.cs ❌ No — that was a one-off read A configured DbContext connection string ❌ No — set when the context was configured Kestrel endpoints and ports ❌ No — bound at startup Registered services ❌ No — the container is built once

Most of an application falls in the "no" column. So "we can change configuration without a restart" is only true for the small part of it that goes through IOptionsMonitor or IOptionsSnapshot.

That is worth being precise about in an interview, because the naive answer — "yes, it reloads automatically" — is wrong for most of the settings people care about.

docs.title: The simple version — what reloads
docs.text:
File providers, with the flag on:

builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("appsettings.json", optional: false, reloadOnChange: true);

The defaults from CreateBuilder already enable this for appsettings.json and the environment-specific file. So file reload is on unless you built the configuration manually.

Environment variables do not reload. Ever.

builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables();      // read once, at startup

A process reads its environment when it starts. Changing a variable afterwards has no effect on a running process — that is an operating system behaviour, not an ASP.NET Core limitation. Changing an environment variable requires restarting the process.

⚠️ This matters because most deployments configure through environment variables. In a container, in Kubernetes, in Azure App Service — the settings arrive as environment variables, so nothing reloads at all and the entire options-monitoring apparatus is inert.

Key Vault reloads only on a configured interval (7.4):

new AzureKeyVaultConfigurationOptions { ReloadInterval = TimeSpan.FromHours(6) }

docs.title: Consuming a change
docs.text:
The only two options interfaces that see it:

// Scoped service — fresh at the start of each request
public class PricingService(IOptionsSnapshot<PricingOptions> options)
{
    private readonly PricingOptions _options = options.Value;
}

// Singleton — read the current value each time
public class RateLimiter(IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitOptions> monitor)
{
    public bool IsAllowed(string client)
    {
        var options = monitor.CurrentValue;      // capture ONCE per operation
        // ...
    }
}

And reacting to a change:

public class CacheManager : IDisposable
{
    private readonly IDisposable? _subscription;

    public CacheManager(IOptionsMonitor<CacheOptions> monitor)
    {
        _subscription = monitor.OnChange(options => Resize(options.MaxSizeMb));
    }

    public void Dispose() => _subscription?.Dispose();     // ⚠️ not optional
}

⚠️ Dispose the subscription. The monitor holds a reference to your callback, and through it to your object, for the application's lifetime otherwise — a memory leak (3.5).

⚠️ OnChange often fires twice for one save. Editors write files in two steps — truncate, then write — and the watcher reports both. So the callback must be idempotent and cheap. Rebuilding an expensive cache directly inside it means doing that twice per edit.

A common mitigation is debouncing:

private DateTimeOffset _lastHandled = DateTimeOffset.MinValue;

_subscription = monitor.OnChange(options =>
{
    var now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
    if (now - _lastHandled < TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)) return;   // ignore the duplicate
    _lastHandled = now;

    Resize(options.MaxSizeMb);
});

docs.title: How it actually works — where reload is genuinely useful
docs.text:
Kubernetes ConfigMaps mounted as files. This is the main real case:

volumeMounts:
  - name: config
    mountPath: /app/config
volumes:
  - name: config
    configMap:
      name: app-settings

builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("/app/config/appsettings.json",
    optional: true, reloadOnChange: true);

Updating the ConfigMap updates the mounted file, and the application picks it up without a restart.

⚠️ Two caveats. ConfigMap updates propagate to the pod on a kubelet sync interval, often around a minute — so it is not instant. And ConfigMaps mounted via subPath do not update at all, which is a well-known trap; mount the whole directory instead.

Feature flags are the other genuine case, and there is a purpose-built system for them — 7.11.

docs.title: The deeper detail — why restarting is often better
docs.text:
⚠️ Live reload has real hazards:

Partial application. Half your settings update and half do not, so the application runs in a state that never existed in any config file. Debugging that is unpleasant.

Mid-request changes. With IOptionsMonitor, a value can change between two lines of the same method (7.6). One request sees an inconsistent pair of settings.

Validation is bypassed. ValidateOnStart runs at startup (7.8). A reload can introduce invalid values that never get checked — you can reload your way into a configuration the application would have refused to start with.

No rollback. A bad reload takes effect immediately, everywhere, with no deployment gate.

Against that, a rolling restart applies configuration atomically, runs validation, and rolls back automatically if the new pods fail their health checks (24.6).

The honest position: prefer a restart for configuration changes. Reserve live reload for things genuinely designed to change at runtime — feature flags, log levels — where the blast radius is small and the value is high.

Log levels are the best example, because turning on debug logging to diagnose a live incident without restarting the affected service is exactly when you need it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic setup that reloads only what should reload:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Defaults already watch appsettings.json and appsettings.{Env}.json.

// A separately mounted file for things that SHOULD change at runtime
builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("/app/config/runtime.json",
    optional: true, reloadOnChange: true);

// Fixed at startup — IOptions, so a reload deliberately does not affect it
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<DatabaseOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Database"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

// Designed to change — IOptionsMonitor consumers
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<RateLimitOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("RateLimit"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

var app = builder.Build();

// ✓ Reads the current value, safely
public class RateLimitService(
    IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitOptions> monitor,
    ILogger<RateLimitService> logger) : IDisposable
{
    private readonly IDisposable? _subscription;
    private DateTimeOffset _lastChange = DateTimeOffset.MinValue;

    public RateLimitService(/* ... */)
    {
        _subscription = monitor.OnChange(options =>
        {
            // Debounce the duplicate notification
            var now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
            if (now - _lastChange < TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)) return;
            _lastChange = now;

            logger.LogInformation(
                "Rate limit configuration reloaded: {Limit}/min", options.RequestsPerMinute);
        });
    }

    public bool IsAllowed(string clientId)
    {
        var options = monitor.CurrentValue;      // once per operation, not per line
        // ...
    }

    public void Dispose() => _subscription?.Dispose();
}

Four things right in that class: IOptionsMonitor because it is a singleton, CurrentValue captured once per operation, the change notification debounced, and the subscription disposed.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does configuration reloading work?

File-based providers can watch their source and re-read it when it changes, which is enabled with reloadOnChange: true — and the defaults already turn it on for appsettings.json. When the file changes, IConfiguration returns the new values. The important limitation is that a reload updates the configuration object but does not push values into anything that already consumed them, so most of an application does not see it.

Q: What does and does not see a reload?

IConfiguration read directly sees it, as do IOptionsMonitor<T> and IOptionsSnapshot<T>. What does not: IOptions<T>, because it captured the value at startup; anything read once in Program.cs; a DbContext connection string, which was fixed when the context was configured; Kestrel's endpoints, bound at startup; and the service registrations themselves, since the container is built once. So the claim "we can change configuration without a restart" only holds for the narrow part of the app going through monitor or snapshot.

Q: Do environment variables reload?

No, and this matters because most deployments use them. A process reads its environment when it starts, and changing a variable afterwards has no effect on a running process — that is an operating system behaviour, not a framework limitation. So in a container or a Kubernetes pod where configuration arrives as environment variables, nothing reloads at all and the whole options-monitoring apparatus is inert. It becomes useful with a ConfigMap mounted as files, or a Key Vault provider with a reload interval.

Q: Would you rely on live reload in production?

Sparingly. There are real hazards: a partial reload leaves the application in a state that never existed in any config file, IOptionsMonitor values can change between two lines of the same method so one request sees an inconsistent pair, and ValidateOnStart does not run on reload — so you can reload your way into a configuration the application would have refused to start with. A rolling restart applies changes atomically, runs validation, and rolls back automatically if health checks fail. I would reserve live reload for things designed to change at runtime, like log levels during an incident or feature flags, where the blast radius is small.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Environment variables never reload. Which means most deployments never reload at all.
  • IOptions<T> does not see changes. It captured the value at startup.
  • A DbContext connection string, Kestrel endpoints and DI registrations are fixed at startup.
  • OnChange fires twice for one save. Debounce, and keep the callback cheap.
  • OnChange subscriptions leak unless disposed.
  • ValidateOnStart does not run on reload. Invalid values can arrive unchecked.
  • Kubernetes ConfigMaps mounted with subPath do not update. Mount the directory.
  • ConfigMap updates take up to a kubelet sync interval, often around a minute.
  • CurrentValue can change mid-method. Capture it once per operation.
