docs.title: 7.10 — Writing a Custom Configuration Provider
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.9 Reload on change · Next: 7.11 Feature flags

Markers: 🧠 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A custom configuration provider lets you pull settings from a source ASP.NET Core does not support out of the box — a database table, an internal config service, a proprietary format.

  • Three pieces: a source (the recipe), a provider (does the loading), and an extension method (the friendly API).
  • Inherit ConfigurationProvider and override Load(), filling the inherited Data dictionary.
  • ⚠️ Ask whether you need one first. A database provider in particular has a startup-ordering problem worth understanding.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means IConfigurationSource an interface A factory. Its Build method creates the provider. IConfigurationProvider an interface Loads key/value pairs and answers lookups. ConfigurationProvider an abstract class Base implementation. Override Load() and fill Data. Data a protected property IDictionary<string, string?>. Where your provider puts its values. Load() a method Called at startup, and again on reload. Populates Data. OnReload() a method Signals that values changed, so IOptionsMonitor fires. ConfigurationKeyDelimiter a constant ":". Use it to build nested keys. AddXxx extension a method The friendly registration API, on IConfigurationBuilder. Startup ordering a constraint Providers load before DI exists, so a provider cannot inject services.

docs.title: When you would need one
docs.text:
The built-in providers cover JSON, XML, INI, environment variables, command line, User Secrets, Key Vault and Secrets Manager (7.1). That is most cases.

You write your own when configuration lives somewhere else:

  • A database table, so non-developers can change settings through an admin screen
  • An internal configuration service your company already runs
  • A proprietary or legacy format — a YAML file, or something bespoke
  • A remote store with no existing provider

A picture: a translator for a language the library does not speak. The library already reads English, French and German. If your settings are written in something else, you supply someone who can read it and dictate the contents in a form the library understands.

docs.title: ⚠️ Ask whether you need one
docs.text:
Before writing one, three questions:

Could environment variables do it? They cover most deployment-specific values and need no code (7.3).

Is this really configuration, or is it data? Settings that change per user, per tenant or during normal operation are application data, not configuration. They belong in a repository you query, not in IConfiguration — which is loaded once at startup and shared across every request.

Do you want feature flags? There is a purpose-built system for runtime toggles (7.11).

The database provider in particular is worth thinking twice about, for the reason below.

docs.title: The simple version — the three pieces
docs.text:
1. The source — a factory the builder holds:

public class DatabaseConfigurationSource : IConfigurationSource
{
    public required string ConnectionString { get; init; }
    public TimeSpan? ReloadInterval { get; init; }

    public IConfigurationProvider Build(IConfigurationBuilder builder)
        => new DatabaseConfigurationProvider(this);
}

2. The provider — does the work:

public class DatabaseConfigurationProvider : ConfigurationProvider
{
    private readonly DatabaseConfigurationSource _source;

    public DatabaseConfigurationProvider(DatabaseConfigurationSource source)
        => _source = source;

    // Called once at startup, and again whenever you decide to reload
    public override void Load()
    {
        var data = new Dictionary<string, string?>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

        using var connection = new SqlConnection(_source.ConnectionString);
        connection.Open();

        using var command = new SqlCommand("SELECT [Key], [Value] FROM AppSettings", connection);
        using var reader = command.ExecuteReader();

        while (reader.Read())
            data[reader.GetString(0)] = reader.IsDBNull(1) ? null : reader.GetString(1);

        Data = data;        // the inherited dictionary the framework reads from
    }
}

Three details in that:

StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase — configuration lookup is case-insensitive (7.5), so your dictionary must be too, or orders:maxitems will not find Orders:MaxItems.

Load() is synchronous. There is no async version, because it runs during builder.Build() before the host is running. Blocking here is expected.

Nested keys use colons, so a row with the key Orders:MaxItems becomes a nested setting automatically.

3. The extension method — so it reads like the built-in ones (1.14):

public static class DatabaseConfigurationExtensions
{
    public static IConfigurationBuilder AddDatabase(
        this IConfigurationBuilder builder,
        string connectionString,
        TimeSpan? reloadInterval = null)
    {
        return builder.Add(new DatabaseConfigurationSource
        {
            ConnectionString = connectionString,
            ReloadInterval = reloadInterval
        });
    }
}

// Program.cs — indistinguishable from a built-in provider
builder.Configuration.AddDatabase(
    builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Config")!,
    reloadInterval: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));

docs.title: ⚠️ The startup-ordering problem
docs.text:
This is the interesting constraint, and the reason a database provider needs care.

Configuration providers run before dependency injection exists. builder.Build() has not been called, so there is no container, no DbContext, no logger.

So a database provider cannot:

// ✗ Impossible — DI does not exist yet
public DatabaseConfigurationProvider(AppDbContext db) { }

It must open its own connection with a raw SqlConnection, using a connection string that came from an earlier provider — which is why the example above reads it from builder.Configuration before adding itself.

That creates a bootstrap chain: the database connection string must come from somewhere that loads first, usually an environment variable or appsettings.json.

⚠️ And there is a worse failure mode. If the database is unreachable at startup, Load() throws and the application does not start. A configuration source that is also a runtime dependency turns a transient database outage into a failure to boot.

Handle it deliberately:

public override void Load()
{
    try
    {
        // ... load from the database ...
    }
    catch (SqlException) when (_source.Optional)
    {
        Data = new Dictionary<string, string?>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        // Continue with no values rather than refusing to start.
        // The app then relies on defaults from earlier providers.
    }
}

That mirrors optional: true on AddJsonFile, and it is the right shape — but note the trade-off: starting with missing configuration may be worse than not starting. Options validation decides which (7.8).

docs.title: How it actually works — supporting reload
docs.text:
To make IOptionsMonitor see changes (7.6), call OnReload() after refreshing Data:

public class DatabaseConfigurationProvider : ConfigurationProvider, IDisposable
{
    private readonly DatabaseConfigurationSource _source;
    private readonly Timer? _timer;

    public DatabaseConfigurationProvider(DatabaseConfigurationSource source)
    {
        _source = source;

        if (source.ReloadInterval is { } interval)
        {
            _timer = new Timer(_ => ReloadFromDatabase(), null, interval, interval);
        }
    }

    private void ReloadFromDatabase()
    {
        try
        {
            var previous = Data;
            Load();

            // Only notify if something actually changed — OnReload is not free,
            // and every IOptionsMonitor subscriber runs its callback
            if (HasChanged(previous, Data))
                OnReload();
        }
        catch
        {
            // A failed refresh must NOT crash the app — keep the previous values
        }
    }

    public void Dispose() => _timer?.Dispose();
}

Three deliberate choices:

Only call OnReload when values changed. Every subscriber's callback fires otherwise, and those callbacks can be expensive (7.9).

Swallow refresh failures. A transient database blip should not take down a running application — keep serving the last known good values.

Dispose the timer, or it keeps the provider alive for the process lifetime.

docs.title: The deeper detail — a simpler alternative
docs.text:
⚠️ For database-backed settings, a repository is often the better design:

public interface ISettingsRepository
{
    Task<T?> GetAsync<T>(string key, CancellationToken ct);
}

Compared with a configuration provider, that gives you:

  • Async access, rather than blocking Load()
  • Per-request or per-tenant values, which IConfiguration cannot express
  • Normal DI, so it can use DbContext, caching and logging
  • No startup dependency — a database outage does not prevent booting
  • Ordinary error handling, rather than a provider that must not throw

Use a configuration provider when the values genuinely are application-wide configuration read at startup. Use a repository when they are data that changes during normal operation.

That distinction — configuration versus data — is the useful part of this topic, more than the mechanics.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A complete, minimal provider for a simpler case — a YAML file, where the ordering problem does not arise:

public class YamlConfigurationSource : FileConfigurationSource
{
    public override IConfigurationProvider Build(IConfigurationBuilder builder)
    {
        EnsureDefaults(builder);                      // sets the file provider and path
        return new YamlConfigurationProvider(this);
    }
}

public class YamlConfigurationProvider(YamlConfigurationSource source)
    : FileConfigurationProvider(source)
{
    // FileConfigurationProvider gives us file watching and reloadOnChange for free
    public override void Load(Stream stream)
    {
        var deserializer = new DeserializerBuilder().Build();
        var yaml = deserializer.Deserialize<Dictionary<string, object>>(new StreamReader(stream));

        var data = new Dictionary<string, string?>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        Flatten(yaml, prefix: "", data);
        Data = data;
    }

    private static void Flatten(
        Dictionary<string, object> source, string prefix, Dictionary<string, string?> target)
    {
        foreach (var (key, value) in source)
        {
            var path = string.IsNullOrEmpty(prefix)
                ? key
                : $"{prefix}{ConfigurationPath.KeyDelimiter}{key}";

            switch (value)
            {
                case Dictionary<string, object> nested:
                    Flatten(nested, path, target);                    // recurse
                    break;

                case IList<object> list:
                    for (var i = 0; i < list.Count; i++)              // arrays → indexed keys
                        target[$"{path}{ConfigurationPath.KeyDelimiter}{i}"] = list[i]?.ToString();
                    break;

                default:
                    target[path] = value?.ToString();
                    break;
            }
        }
    }
}

public static class YamlConfigurationExtensions
{
    public static IConfigurationBuilder AddYamlFile(
        this IConfigurationBuilder builder, string path, bool optional = false,
        bool reloadOnChange = false)
    {
        return builder.Add(new YamlConfigurationSource
        {
            Path = path,
            Optional = optional,
            ReloadOnChange = reloadOnChange
        });
    }
}

Inheriting FileConfigurationSource and FileConfigurationProvider is the shortcut worth knowing. They handle file resolution, the optional flag, and the file watcher for reloadOnChange — so you only implement the parsing.

builder.Configuration.AddYamlFile("appsettings.yaml", optional: true, reloadOnChange: true);

Note the flattening logic: nested maps become colon-separated keys and lists become indexed keys, matching how the JSON provider behaves (7.1). Getting that consistent is what makes your provider behave like the built-in ones.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you write a custom configuration provider?

Three pieces. An IConfigurationSource, which is a factory holding the settings and building the provider. A provider inheriting ConfigurationProvider, overriding Load() to populate the inherited Data dictionary with key/value pairs. And an extension method on IConfigurationBuilder so it registers like the built-in ones. For a file-based format you inherit FileConfigurationSource and FileConfigurationProvider instead, which give you file resolution and the reload watcher for free so you only write the parsing.

Q: What constraint does a custom provider have that other components do not?

It runs before dependency injection exists. Providers load during builder.Build(), so there is no container, no DbContext and no logger to inject. A database-backed provider has to open its own raw connection using a connection string that came from an earlier provider, which creates a bootstrap chain. It also means a failure in Load() prevents the application starting entirely — so a configuration source that is also a runtime dependency turns a transient database outage into a failure to boot, which needs handling deliberately.

Q: How do you support reloading in a custom provider?

Call the inherited OnReload() after refreshing Data, which raises the change token that IOptionsMonitor and IOptionsSnapshot listen to. For a polling source you would use a timer to re-run Load on an interval. Two things worth doing: only call OnReload when values actually changed, because every subscriber's callback fires and those can be expensive; and swallow failures during a refresh, since a transient outage should leave the last known good values in place rather than taking down a running application.

Q: When would you use a configuration provider versus a repository for database-backed settings?

The question is whether it is configuration or data. Configuration is application-wide, read at startup, and the same for every request — a provider suits that. If the values change during normal operation, or vary per user or per tenant, they are data and belong in a repository you query. A repository is also better practically: it can be async, it uses normal DI so it can have caching and logging, a database outage does not prevent startup, and errors are handled normally rather than inside a provider that must not throw.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Providers run before DI exists. You cannot inject services into one.
  • A throwing Load() prevents the application starting. Support an optional flag.
  • Data must use a case-insensitive comparer, or lookups fail inconsistently.
  • Load() is synchronous. There is no async version — it runs before the host starts.
  • Forgetting OnReload() means IOptionsMonitor never sees your changes.
  • Calling OnReload() unconditionally runs every subscriber's callback even when nothing changed.
  • Nested keys need : and arrays need indexed keys, or your provider behaves differently from the built-in ones.
  • A polling timer must be disposed, or it keeps the provider alive for the process lifetime.
  • Per-request or per-tenant values are data, not configuration. IConfiguration is loaded once and shared.

docs.title: 7.11 — Feature Flags and Feature Management
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 7. Configuration and Options Prev: 7.10 Custom providers · Next: 8.1 Endpoint routing

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A feature flag is a switch that turns a piece of functionality on or off without redeploying.

  • It separates deploying code from releasing it — you can ship a feature turned off and enable it later.
  • Microsoft's Microsoft.FeatureManagement builds on configuration, so flags can come from appsettings.json or a remote store.
  • ⚠️ Flags are technical debt with a shelf life. Every one is a branch you must eventually delete.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Feature flag a runtime switch A boolean controlling whether functionality is active. Also called a feature toggle. Microsoft.FeatureManagement a NuGet package Microsoft's feature flag library. Reads flags from configuration. IFeatureManager an interface Asks whether a feature is enabled. IsEnabledAsync("Name"). IVariantFeatureManager an interface Returns a variant rather than a boolean. For A/B testing. [FeatureGate] an attribute Puts a controller or action behind a flag. Returns 404 when disabled. <feature> tag helper a Razor tag Shows or hides markup based on a flag. Feature filter an IFeatureFilter Decides whether a flag is on, using rules — percentage, time window, user. PercentageFilter a built-in filter Enables a feature for a percentage of evaluations. TimeWindowFilter a built-in filter Enables a feature between two dates. TargetingFilter a built-in filter Enables per user or group. The basis of a real rollout. Kill switch a use case A flag whose only job is to disable something quickly during an incident.

docs.title: Deploy is not release
docs.text:
Without flags, shipping a feature and turning it on are the same event. That forces all-or-nothing deployments: the code goes live for everyone at once, and if it misbehaves your only remedy is a rollback.

Feature flags separate the two:

  1. Deploy the code with the flag off. Nothing changes for users.
  2. Enable it for internal staff. Test in production, with real data.
  3. Enable for 5% of users. Watch the error rate.
  4. Ramp up to 100%.
  5. Delete the flag and the old code path.

If step 3 goes wrong, you turn the flag off. No deployment, no rollback, seconds not minutes.

A picture: a dimmer switch rather than a light switch. You can bring the new thing up gradually and take it back down instantly, without rewiring the room.

docs.title: ⚠️ The cost nobody mentions
docs.text:
Every flag adds a branch to your code, and branches multiply:

if (await features.IsEnabledAsync("NewCheckout"))
{
    if (await features.IsEnabledAsync("ExpressShipping"))    // 4 combinations
    { }
}

Three flags is eight paths. Most of them are never tested, and some are never reachable.

Flags are technical debt with a shelf life. A flag that has been at 100% for six months is not a flag — it is dead code plus an if statement. The discipline that makes flags work is deleting them, and it is the part teams skip.

Practical habits: record the date and owner when you add one, and treat a flag older than a release cycle or two as a bug.

docs.title: The simple version
docs.text:
dotnet add package Microsoft.FeatureManagement.AspNetCore

// appsettings.json
{
  "FeatureManagement": {
    "NewCheckout": false,
    "BetaSearch": true
  }
}

builder.Services.AddFeatureManagement();

public class CheckoutService(IFeatureManager features)
{
    public async Task<Receipt> CheckoutAsync(Cart cart, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (await features.IsEnabledAsync("NewCheckout"))
            return await NewCheckoutAsync(cart, ct);

        return await LegacyCheckoutAsync(cart, ct);
    }
}

⚠️ Use constants, not string literals, or a typo silently disables the feature forever — IsEnabledAsync returns false for an unknown flag rather than throwing:

public static class FeatureFlags
{
    public const string NewCheckout = "NewCheckout";
    public const string BetaSearch  = "BetaSearch";
}

docs.title: Gating an endpoint
docs.text:
[FeatureGate(FeatureFlags.NewCheckout)]
[HttpPost("checkout/v2")]
public async Task<IActionResult> CheckoutV2(CheckoutRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // ...
}

When the flag is off the action returns 404, as though it does not exist.

That is deliberate — a 404 leaks nothing. A 403 would tell a caller the endpoint exists but is disabled, which is information you may not want to give.

docs.title: How it actually works — feature filters
docs.text:
A boolean in a file is the simplest case. Filters make a flag conditional:

{
  "FeatureManagement": {
    "NewCheckout": {
      "EnabledFor": [
        {
          "Name": "Percentage",
          "Parameters": { "Value": 10 }        // 10% of evaluations
        }
      ]
    },
    "BlackFridayBanner": {
      "EnabledFor": [
        {
          "Name": "TimeWindow",
          "Parameters": { "Start": "2026-11-27T00:00:00Z", "End": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z" }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

builder.Services.AddFeatureManagement()
    .AddFeatureFilter<PercentageFilter>()
    .AddFeatureFilter<TimeWindowFilter>();

⚠️ PercentageFilter is evaluated per call, not per user. So one user hitting the page five times can get the feature on three of them and off on two — which is useless for a real rollout and actively confusing for the user.

For a real percentage rollout you need TargetingFilter, which hashes a stable user identifier so a given user consistently gets the same answer:

builder.Services.AddFeatureManagement()
    .WithTargeting<HttpContextTargetingContextAccessor>();

{
  "FeatureManagement": {
    "NewCheckout": {
      "EnabledFor": [{
        "Name": "Targeting",
        "Parameters": {
          "Audience": {
            "Users": [ "beta@example.com" ],           // always on for these
            "Groups": [ { "Name": "InternalStaff", "RolloutPercentage": 100 } ],
            "DefaultRolloutPercentage": 10             // 10% of everyone else
          }
        }
      }]
    }
  }
}

That distinction — per-call versus per-user — is the thing worth knowing, because PercentageFilter is the obvious-looking choice and the wrong one.

docs.title: The deeper detail — where flags should live
docs.text:
Flags in appsettings.json have a problem: changing one requires a redeploy, which defeats the point.

Options, in increasing order of capability:

Source Change without deploy? Notes appsettings.json ❌ Fine for permanent config, not for flags A mounted ConfigMap ✅ Reloads on a kubelet interval (7.9) Azure App Configuration ✅ Purpose-built, with a UI and push refresh LaunchDarkly / Flagsmith ✅ Full platforms — audit, targeting, analytics 
// Azure App Configuration with a refresh interval
builder.Configuration.AddAzureAppConfiguration(options =>
{
    options.Connect(connectionString)
           .UseFeatureFlags(flags => flags.SetRefreshInterval(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)));
});

⚠️ Whatever the source, flags rely on configuration reload — so all the limits from 7.9 apply. IFeatureManager reads the current configuration on each call, so it does see changes, but the underlying provider must actually be reloading.

docs.title: Kill switches
docs.text:
The most valuable flag is often the simplest:

{ "FeatureManagement": { "EnableExpensiveReports": true } }

if (!await features.IsEnabledAsync(FeatureFlags.EnableExpensiveReports))
    return Results.Problem("Reporting is temporarily unavailable.", statusCode: 503);

During an incident, turning off one expensive feature can keep the rest of the application alive. That is a kill switch, and it is worth adding proactively to anything that hammers a shared database or a third-party API.

Unlike rollout flags, kill switches are permanent and should not be cleaned up.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic setup:

// Program.cs
builder.Services.AddFeatureManagement()
    .AddFeatureFilter<PercentageFilter>()
    .AddFeatureFilter<TimeWindowFilter>()
    .WithTargeting<HttpContextTargetingContextAccessor>();

public static class FeatureFlags
{
    // Rollout flags — DELETE these once they reach 100% and settle
    public const string NewCheckout = "NewCheckout";       // added 2026-08, owner: payments team

    // Kill switches — PERMANENT
    public const string EnableReports = "EnableReports";
    public const string EnableEmailNotifications = "EnableEmailNotifications";
}

public class CheckoutService(
    IFeatureManager features,
    ILogger<CheckoutService> logger)
{
    public async Task<Receipt> CheckoutAsync(Cart cart, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var useNew = await features.IsEnabledAsync(FeatureFlags.NewCheckout);

        // Log which path ran — essential when comparing error rates during a rollout
        logger.LogInformation("Checkout using {Path} flow", useNew ? "new" : "legacy");

        return useNew
            ? await NewCheckoutAsync(cart, ct)
            : await LegacyCheckoutAsync(cart, ct);
    }
}

That logging line is worth including. During a percentage rollout, "is the new path producing more errors than the old one?" is the question you need answered, and you cannot answer it without knowing which path each request took.

// A kill switch, checked before doing expensive work
[HttpGet("reports/annual")]
public async Task<IActionResult> AnnualReport(CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (!await _features.IsEnabledAsync(FeatureFlags.EnableReports))
        return Problem("Reporting is temporarily unavailable.", statusCode: 503);

    return Ok(await _reports.GenerateAsync(ct));
}

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text:
Once NewCheckout is at 100% and stable:

// Before
var useNew = await features.IsEnabledAsync(FeatureFlags.NewCheckout);
return useNew ? await NewCheckoutAsync(cart, ct) : await LegacyCheckoutAsync(cart, ct);

// After — flag gone, legacy method deleted, constant removed, config entry removed
return await CheckoutAsync(cart, ct);

Four things to delete, and teams routinely do only the first. A leftover config entry and an unused constant are harmless; a leftover legacy method is dead code that someone will eventually try to maintain.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a feature flag and why use one?

A runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without redeploying. The value is that it separates deploying code from releasing it — you can ship a feature turned off, enable it for internal users, then for a small percentage of real users while watching error rates, and ramp up from there. If something goes wrong you turn it off in seconds rather than rolling back a deployment. It also gives you kill switches, so during an incident you can disable one expensive feature to keep the rest of the application alive.

Q: What is the cost of feature flags?

Every flag is a branch, and branches multiply — three flags is eight code paths, most of which are never tested and some of which are unreachable. So flags are technical debt with a shelf life: a flag that has been at 100% for six months is not a flag, it is dead code plus an if statement. The discipline that makes them work is deleting them once they have settled, including the old code path, the constant and the configuration entry — and that is the part teams skip.

Q: What is wrong with PercentageFilter for a gradual rollout?

It evaluates per call rather than per user, so a single user refreshing a page can get the feature on some requests and off on others. That is useless for measuring a rollout and confusing for the user. For a real percentage rollout you want TargetingFilter, which hashes a stable user identifier so a given user consistently gets the same answer, and which also supports always-on lists for specific users and groups alongside a default rollout percentage.

Q: Where should feature flags be stored?

Not in appsettings.json for anything you want to change quickly, because changing it means a redeploy, which defeats the purpose. A mounted ConfigMap works and reloads on the kubelet sync interval. A purpose-built store like Azure App Configuration or LaunchDarkly is better, because it gives you a UI for non-developers, an audit trail of who changed what, and push-based refresh. Whatever the source, flags depend on configuration reloading, so all the usual reload limits apply.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• An unknown flag name returns false, so a typo silently disables the feature forever. Use constants.
  • PercentageFilter is per call, not per user. Use TargetingFilter for real rollouts.
  • Flags in appsettings.json need a redeploy to change, which defeats the point.
  • Flags multiply code paths. Three flags is eight combinations, mostly untested.
  • Old flags become dead code. Record the owner and date, and delete on a schedule.
  • [FeatureGate] returns 404, not 403 — deliberately, so it leaks nothing.
  • Cleanup means four deletions: the branch, the old method, the constant, the config entry.
  • Flags depend on configuration reload, so all of 7.9 applies.
  • Not logging which path ran makes a rollout impossible to evaluate.

docs.title: How to grow this file
docs.text:
Add a question every time one of these happens:

  1. You're asked something in a real or mock interview — write it down the same day, verbatim, before you rewrite it in your head into something you answered well
  2. You read a note and think "how would this get asked?"
  3. You fumble a follow-up — the follow-up is the real question, not the original

Aim for roughly one question per 🔥 topic. That's about 120 questions, which is a realistic target over the full study period and far more useful than a downloaded list of 500 you've never spoken aloud.

docs.title: Drill format
docs.text:
Solo: cover the answers, work through one section, mark every fumble in PROGRESS.md under Weak spots.

With a partner: hand them this file. Ask them to pick randomly and to always ask "why?" once after your answer. The follow-up is where interviews are actually won and lost — a confident first answer followed by silence when probed is worse than a hesitant answer that survives two levels of "why."

Out loud, alone: record yourself. Painful, effective. You will hear the filler words and the places where you trail off, and you can't hear either while you're speaking.

docs.title: System Design Practice
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Topic 25.5 🔥 🎯

System design rounds are increasingly common for mid-level .NET roles and standard for senior. They are not testing whether you know the "right" architecture — they're testing whether you ask about constraints before you draw boxes.

docs.title: The method (use this every time)
docs.text:
1. Clarify requirements — functional and non-functional. Never start drawing first. Ask about scale, read/write ratio, consistency needs, latency budget.
  2. Estimate — requests per second, storage growth, bandwidth. Rough is fine; showing you think in numbers is the point.
  3. Define the API — endpoints and their contracts. This forces concrete thinking.
  4. Data model — entities, relationships, and the access patterns that drive the schema.
  5. High-level design — draw the boxes. Client, gateway, services, data stores, queues.
  6. Deep dive — the interviewer picks a component. Be ready for any of them.
  7. Bottlenecks and scale — where does this break at 10×? What do you fix first?
  8. Tradeoffs — say out loud what you gave up and why.

Step 1 is the one candidates skip and the one interviewers score hardest. Jumping to a diagram before establishing constraints is the most common failure in this round.

docs.title: Worked examples to write
docs.text:
Each gets its own file in this folder. Write them out fully — a design you've written is one you can improvise from; one you've only read is not.

  • [ ] URL shortener — hashing, collisions, redirect performance, analytics
  • [ ] E-commerce checkout — inventory reservation, payment idempotency, order saga
  • [ ] Notification service — fan-out, delivery guarantees, retries, dead lettering
  • [ ] Rate limiter — algorithms (token bucket, sliding window), distributed state
  • [ ] File upload service — presigned URLs, chunking, virus scanning, CDN
  • [ ] Chat / real-time feed — SignalR, backplane, presence, message ordering
  • [ ] Multi-tenant SaaS API — tenant isolation, per-tenant data, noisy neighbours
  • [ ] Job scheduler — durability, exactly-once-ish semantics, poison messages
  • [ ] Audit log service — write volume, immutability, retention, query patterns
  • [ ] Read-heavy product catalog — caching layers, invalidation, search

docs.title: .NET-specific things to bring up
docs.text:
These are what make it an ASP.NET Core system design round rather than a generic one. Working one or two in naturally shows depth:

  • IHttpClientFactory + Polly for service-to-service resilience → 19.11
  • HybridCache or Redis for the caching layer → 19.3
  • Background processing: BackgroundService vs Hangfire vs a queue consumer → 21.1, 21.3
  • Outbox pattern for reliable event publishing from EF Core → 23.8
  • YARP as gateway/BFF → 23.10
  • Health checks driving Kubernetes probes → 18.5, 24.6
  • OpenTelemetry for cross-service tracing → 18.7
  • Stateless app servers so you can scale horizontally → 24.12

docs.title: Numbers worth knowing
docs.text:
Rough orders of magnitude. Precision isn't the point — being able to estimate at all is.

Latency In-memory cache read ~100 ns Redis round trip (same DC) ~0.5–1 ms Database query (indexed, same DC) ~1–10 ms Cross-region round trip ~50–150 ms Disk seek (SSD) ~0.1 ms Scale One well-tuned ASP.NET Core instance thousands of req/s for simple endpoints 1M requests/day ~12 req/s average, plan for 5–10× peak 1 KB per row × 100M rows ~100 GB
